9ce0ad809d82ca75: KOTA BARU: A surgeon involved in the bone donation procedure of the late Muhammad Aidil Ahmad Zupardi, 23, at the Universiti Sains Malaysia Specialist Hospital (HPUSM), has shared his emotional experience of carrying out the operation.
Dr Syahr Musafir said he struggled to contain his emotions as he reflected on the trust placed in him by the deceased and his family.
"From yesterday (the day before) until today (yesterday), I felt overwhelmed and tears kept welling up. Even in the operating theatre, my eyes could not stay dry.
"I had not eaten anything since morning, but even by noon, I did not feel hungry. I do not know where the strength came from.

"The deceased donated his bones. It is a trust for us to retrieve them carefully, return him to his family with dignity, and ensure the bones are properly preserved so they can eventually be used to treat other patients. All of this is a trust," he wrote in a Facebook post.
Dr Syahr, who was involved in coordinating the bone donation, said he repeatedly reminded himself that the procedure was a responsibility entrusted to him and that he had to give his best.
"Do the best you can because this is a trust from the deceased and his family, from our team members and, above all, from Allah.
"Tears may well up, but even through those tears, we must do our best," he said.
He said everyone had a role to play, including the deceased, who continued to make a difference as an organ donor even after his death.
"What a noble soul. Thank you. To his family, including his parents and siblings, who agreed to and consented to the donation, you are also wonderful people. Thank you all.
"His two kidneys, lungs, liver and corneas have already helped many people.
"The donated bones will also help dozens of people enjoy a better quality of life.
"I am humbled and deeply moved. May the deceased be granted a place in heaven," he said.
Aidil was involved in a road accident last Monday. He was later pronounced brain dead.
His family agreed to donate his organs, and the procedure was performed at HPUSM yesterday.
Hospital staff also paid their final respects through an Honor Walk, while the hospital building was illuminated in green as a tribute and symbol of the organ donation procedure.
df4b9cc621bb2c33: KUALA SELANGOR: Selangor must step up preparations for the high-tide phenomenon forecast from Nov 23 to 27, particularly as heavier and more frequent rain is expected until tomorrow.
Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari said preparations in flood-prone areas must be urgently reviewed following forecasts by the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia).
He said priority should be given to pumping water out of residential areas and monitoring river conditions and sea levels.
"Our priority now is to speed up water-pumping operations in residential areas and monitor river conditions and sea levels.

"More frequent rain is expected until Nov 21, while the high-tide phenomenon is forecast from Nov 23 to 27. I want preparations for both situations reviewed urgently to prevent conditions from worsening," he said.
He was speaking after visiting the temporary relief centre at Sekolah Kebangsaan Dato' Maharaja Lela here last night.

Amirudin also presented compassionate cash aid to 377 flood victims from the Ijok and Jeram state constituencies, identified as the worst-affected areas as of yesterday, particularly homes around Parit Mahang.
Commenting on the prolonged flooding in Parit Mahang, which has persisted for nearly two weeks, he said the river bund had been breached twice by irresponsible parties despite earlier repair works.
He said a police report had been lodged over the intrusion into the river reserve, and a suspect had been detained to assist investigations.
The bund is being repaired again, while additional water pumps have been deployed to speed up the draining of floodwaters.
Earlier, Amirudin visited 157 flood victims from 42 families at the SK Sungai Binjai relief centre in Meru, which was opened for the first time this year.
He said the centre had previously been opened at least two to four times annually.
He attributed the improvement to the Flood Mitigation Plan (RTB) project, which involved river widening works by the Drainage and Irrigation Department (DID).
"This shows how our RTB projects can reduce the impact of flooding, even though several areas are still affected by high tides.
"The overflow is coming from other areas, not Sungai Binjai, as the RTB project there has significantly reduced the impact of flooding compared with previous years," he said.
6ee229501972171a: HONG KONG: Asian shares slid on Friday to be on track for their worst week since 2020, as Anthropic's debut failed to restore investor faith in AI trades, while the dollar extended a rally on safe-haven flows.
MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares lost 2.5%, poised for a six-day losing streak. The gauge has now declined 7% this week, its worst performance since March 2020.
Japan's Nikkei tumbled 4.1% and was headed for a 6.8% weekly drop, while South Korea's KOSPI fell 4.7% and was set to end the week 7.5% lower.
The moves in Asia followed losses of more than 2% for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite.
Anthropic, the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company, saw its shares surge more than 30% in a historic debut but the euphoria failed to lift other boats.

"Anthropic's blockbuster IPO proved not enough to assuage the overall concern about the outlook for the AI trade and equities more broadly," said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.

The wider AI sector has been bruised by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia as well as additional momentum for the anti-data-centre movement in the wake of the Democrats' sweep of the US midterm elections.
Unease about mounting debt loads in the sector and warnings that AI threatens human extinction have also hit sentiment.
Rodda said that with the AI trade fading and Fed rate hikes seen likely, general market sentiment is shaky and the risk is that this bearishness begins to drag stocks even lower.
US stock futures also point to further losses, with the S&P 500 futures down 0.4% and Nasdaq futures down 0.7% in Asia on Friday.
Dollar extends rally, treasury yields dip on risk aversion
As risk sentiment took a beating, the US dollar extended its rally, also supported by growing expectations of a more hawkish Federal Reserve.
The dollar index last traded steady at 103.86, after hitting its strongest level since April 2025 this week.
Fed funds futures imply that a quarter-point rate hike next month is essentially locked in, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

In government debt, US Treasury yields eased as the sharp equity selloff pushed investors toward safe-haven bonds. The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes held steady at 5.026%, near a one-week low. The two-year yield touched 4.749%, compared with a US close of 4.779%.
Oil prices were mostly steady after an earlier spike, as reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz offset pressure from rising US crude inventories and forecasts for a global oil surplus.
Brent crude futures settled flat at US$91.98 a barrel, on track for a third straight week of decline.
Non-interest-bearing gold dipped 0.6% to US$3,601.40 an ounce and was headed for a 7.3% weekly loss.
159b342b4d274dcb: BRUSSELS: UK prime minister Andy Burnham and the EU's top officials hope to seal deals to ease trade and youth mobility at a Brussels summit Friday, billed as a first step in his push to rebuild ties after Brexit.
Since taking power this summer, Burnham has smashed through the taboos in Britain's toxic debate over relations with Europe – going as far as to float rejoining the bloc one day.

For now the summit with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa will focus on much smaller steps to help turn the page a decade after the UK voted to leave – while Burnham saves for later the bigger decisions on what could come next.
"It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive – to deliver a win-win for Britain and the EU," Burnham said this week.
"After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship."
On the table in Brussels are three main agreements: a deal cutting red tape for food exports, another linking the two sides' emissions-trading schemes and a third on a "youth experience scheme".
Burnham argues those moves – which were in the pipeline long before he entered Downing Street – will help fix some of the damage Brexit inflicted.
British firms will export to Europe more easily again, and thousands of under-30s will be allowed to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel.
But while the mood music at the meeting with EU chiefs von der Leyen and Costa may be much improved, old habits still die hard.

Brussels and London wrangled ferociously down to the wire over the details, with EU states greenlighting the deal package late Thursday night, according to multiple diplomats, but a final sign-off is still needed from the UK side.
One key sticking point was on pinning London down to a future agreement on cutting fees for EU students at UK universities to the level paid by their British counterparts.
Maros Sefcovic, the EU's veteran pointman on UK talks, insisted the atmosphere had stayed "very positive" – "even if the negotiations are very detailed and sometimes very, very hard".
'Tread carefully'
Burnham pledged not to "re-run" the Brexit debate if he became prime minister but has risked doing just that since succeeding Keir Starmer in July.

Having previously said he'd like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, the former Manchester mayor has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.
The strategy is in part because polls now regularly indicate most Britons regret Brexit and would vote to re-enter the bloc if a referendum was held tomorrow.
It is also reflective of Britain's weak economy, damaged by Brexit, and how much the world has changed since 2016, with Europe firmly behind Ukraine in its war against Russian aggression.
Burnham hopes friendlier EU relations will help build a broad centre-left coalition to win the next general election, not anticipated until 2029.
But the strategy comes with huge risks, not least because his own party – never mind the country – is divided on how to proceed.
For now, the prime minister appears to have tempered his early urgency.
"I'm happy with closer ties, but he does need to tread carefully," one Labour MP told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Burnham's push leaves him open to accusations of Brexit betrayal from the opposition Conservatives and hard-right Reform UK party of Nigel Farage – who will give his own press conference in Brussels Friday.
The prime minister has committed to Starmer's "red lines" on Europe for this parliament, meaning no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

But calls to go further are getting louder – with former deputy prime minister David Lammy becoming the highest-profile Labour figure to urge putting rejoining the EU in the party's next election manifesto.
In Brussels, meanwhile, there is little expectation the UK will return to the fold any time soon.
"I doubt he'd take the risk of a major step that would be so radioactive," said one senior EU diplomat.
"He'll probably keep on trying to nibble away around the edges to improve ties – and we are open to having as close a relationship as possible."
158cbe512b578a74: KUALA LUMPUR: Malayan Cement Bhd's operating margins in the coming quarters are expected to remain stable despite the rise in Indonesian coal prices.
Hong Leong Investment Bank Bhd (HLIB) said that Malayan Cement's use of alternative fuels and waste heat recovery system is able to mitigate further margin squeeze.
The firm said the elevated Indonesian coal prices of US$85 per tonne have largely been reflected in Malayan Cement's results for the first quarter (Q1).
Bulk cement prices that saw a slight decline to RM400 per tonne in recent months also added further pressure to the company's margins.

"Nevertheless, we think the margin pressure is manageable, mitigated by Malayan Cement's usage of alternative fuels and waste heat recovery systems. Malayan Cement also benefits from competitive procurement costs for low-calorific coal, supported by economies of scale and stable supply from Indonesian state-owned suppliers.
"As such, we believe operating margins in the coming quarters should remain broadly stable," it said.
Malayan Cement's core earnings came in at RM223.7 million in Q1, in line with HLIB and consensus' expectations at 26 per cent of the financial year 2027 (FY27) forecast.
HLIB trimmed its earnings forecasts for the company by one per cent and three per cent for FY27 and FY28, respectively, and also introduced earnings of RM953 million for FY29.
HLIB kept a "Buy" call on the stock with a target price of RM7.
34ebadbd103ca03b: KUALA LUMPUR: Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil has urged parents and the community to help children build healthy digital habits by reducing screen time and encouraging real-world activities.
In a Facebook post marking World Children's Day today, he said children had the right to grow up in a safe and protected environment, including online.
"An increasingly digital world requires us to help them build healthy habits. Cut screen time and make more room for play, movement, learning and interacting with the real world.
"Our responsibility is not just to protect them today, but to ensure they grow up healthy, confident and ready to face the future," he said.
World Children's Day is observed every Nov 20 to raise awareness of issues affecting children worldwide.
7bd06dc87c510c01: KUALA LUMPUR: Sunway Construction Group Bhd is poised to deliver stronger earnings in the financial year 2027 (FY27), supported by faster project recognition following record contract wins and a growing unbilled order book, says Hong Leong Investment Bank Bhd (HLIB).
The construction group has secured nearly RM10 billion in contracts year-to-date, lifting its unbilled order book to a record RM12.5 billion as of September 2026.

HLIB said the group's sizeable tender book of RM15.7 billion, including data centre (DC) projects with a combined capacity of more than 600 megawatts (MW), would provide strong visibility for further order book replenishment.
It expects earnings to accelerate in FY27 as contributions from the newly secured projects gain momentum heading into 2027.

The firm also expects the impact of new restrictions imposed by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on access to advanced US artificial intelligence technology to be limited for local contractors.
While the restrictions could slow the development of data centres operated by Chinese-linked companies in Malaysia, HLIB said such projects typically engaged China-based contractors.
It noted that the group had predominantly secured data centre contracts from US hyperscalers, which were expected to remain insulated from the new restrictions.

On its financial performance, Sunway Construction recorded core earnings of RM104.7 million in the third quarter ended Sept 30, 2026 (Q3 FY26), up 25.4 per cent from RM83.5 million a year earlier and 1.4 per cent from the preceding quarter.
This brought its nine-month core profit after tax and minority interests (Patami) to RM323.1 million, an increase of 19 per cent year-on-year.
HLIB said the results were within its expectations, accounting for 78 per cent of its full-year forecast, and 73 per cent of consensus estimates.
The quarterly earnings were adjusted mainly for net foreign exchange losses of RM3 million and a reversal of receivables impairment losses amounting to RM3.4 million.

Sunway Construction also declared a third interim dividend of 7.9 sen per share, bringing its financial year-to-date dividend to 34.7 sen, compared with 41.5 sen in the corresponding period last year.
Following the results, HLIB has maintained its earnings forecasts and "Buy" recommendation on the stock, with an unchanged target price of RM10.
The target price is based on 23 times FY27 earnings per share, representing a premium of 0.5 standard deviation above its two-year average price-to-earnings ratio of 22 times.
HLIB said the premium valuation was justified by Sunway Construction's strong exposure to the data centre growth theme, execution capabilities and consistent margin delivery.
This is alongside higher returns on equity and an attractive dividend yield of six per cent, based on a 150 per cent payout ratio.
b9f072ea79ba38ce: KUALA LUMPUR: Petronas Gas Bhd is poised to sustain its earnings trajectory, supported by the upcoming commercialisation of several key projects and rising demand for gas-powered electricity generation amid the rapid expansion of data centres.

In a note, Hong Leong Investment Bank Bhd (HLIB) said the group is expected to benefit from the commercialisation of its Pengerang Cold Energy air separation unit in November 2026, followed by the Kimanis 2 and Sipitang power plants by the end of 2026.

Other projects include PG Lingkaran Fibre, expected to commence operations in the first quarter of financial year 2027 (Q1 FY27); the Labuan power plant in late 2027 to early 2028; and the Third Regasification Terminal (RGT3) Lumut project in 2029.
The firm noted that Petronas Gas was also evaluating plans for a new biomethane facility.
It added that the group stood to benefit from Malaysia's transition towards gas-powered electricity generation, which was accelerating to support the rapid expansion of data centres.

On its financial performance, HLIB said Petronas Gas' Q3 FY26 core net profit rose 7.6 per cent year-on-year to RM477.1 million, bringing its nine-month FY26 core net profit to RM1.37 billion, up 0.8 per cent.
For the nine-month period, stronger gas transportation and regasification contributions were offset by weaker gas processing and utilities performance, as well as higher net finance costs.
HLIB said the nine-month performance was within expectations, accounting for 74.2 per cent of the firm's full-year forecast and 75.1 per cent of consensus estimates.

The group also declared a second interim dividend of 18 sen per share, bringing its cumulative financial year-to-date interim dividend to 50 sen per share. The shares will go ex-dividend on Dec 9, 2026.
Overall, HLIB maintained its earnings forecasts and a "Hold" call on the group, with an unchanged sum-of-parts-derived target price of RM17.83.

HLIB said Petronas Gas' earnings were expected to remain stable as most of its business segments were protected under the regulated asset base framework, while its utilities segment was partly insulated by the imbalance cost pass-through mechanism.
It also expected the group to maintain its annual dividend payout of 72 sen per share, supported by a healthy annual free cash flow of between RM1.5 billion and RM2 billion.

61184b556b86f17f: PETALING JAYA: Perikatan Nasional (PN) dikatakan berada di landasan untuk membentuk kerajaan yang lebih baik di Putrajaya, berdasarkan prestasi pemimpinnya di peringkat nasional dan negeri sejak empat tahun lalu.

Setiausaha Agung Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan), Saifuddin Abdullah, berkata ketika Ketua Pembangkang Hamzah Zainudin memberikan perbahasan yang bernas dan pedas di Dewan Rakyat, Ahli Parlimen Masjid Tanah Mas Ermieyati Samsudin mempengerusikan Jawatankuasa Kira-kira Wang Negara yang 'paling berkesan dalam sejarah'.
Katanya, portfolio yang pembangkang tubuh untuk membayangi kerajaan kelihatan 'agak setara' dengan sesetengah kementerian dalam hal tertentu.
"Contohnya, portfolio pendidikan, dengan dokumen ‘Cadangan Reformasi Pendidikan’, mampu sparring dengan Kementerian Pendidikan," katanya dalam ruangan 'Merentas Ruang' terbitan Sinar Harian.
Di luar Parlimen, Saifuddin berkata, Hamzah tahun lalu membentangkan Konsensus Nasional Baharu sebagai 'gagasan ke arah Malaysia yang lebih baik'.

Di sebalik pencapaian di peringkat nasional, negeri ditadbir PN turut menunjukkan prestasi yang beliau sifatkan sebagai menggalakkan.
"Kedah, contohnya, adalah antara negeri utama di Malaysia dari segi tarikan pelaburan," katanya yang juga Ahli Parlimen Indera Mahkota.

Kedah merekodkan pelaburan diluluskan berjumlah RM194.8 bilion dalam tempoh 2020 hingga Jun 2026, menurut Urus Setia Penerangan Darul Aman. Pemimpin PAS iaitu Sanusi Nor menjadi menteri besar negeri itu sejak Mei 2020.
Saifuddin berkata, beliau optimis apabila melihat pencapaian-pencapaian ini.
"Pada saya, kita harus terus dengan gambaran besar, iaitu perjuangan yang berasaskan nilai, untuk membentuk kerajaan baharu yang lebih baik di Putrajaya. Demi kebaikan rakyat."
e7607665c67e8342: SHAH ALAM: A residents’ association cannot automatically impose membership on homeowners or compel them to pay retrospective security fees, a sessions court has ruled.
Judge Zuhrina Nor Hakim allowed a civil claim brought by homeowner Abdul Farid Abdul Kadir against Persatuan Penduduk Jalan Hijau Pelangi and its chairman, Saaidal Razalli Azzuhri.
In a decision delivered on Monday, Zuhrina also dismissed the counterclaim by the association and its chairman in its entirety.

The dispute arose from the association’s insistence that Farid was automatically a member and liable for outstanding security charges dating back to 2013, although he maintained that he had never voluntarily applied for membership.
Farid argued that membership required an application in accordance with the association’s constitution and could not be automatically imposed on homeowners.
He also disputed the demand for retrospective security payments for a period when he was living overseas and not occupying the property.
In his statement of claim, Farid said he returned to Malaysia in July 2020 and applied to join the association, offering RM1,410 towards membership and security services.
However, his application was rejected after the association insisted that he first settle outstanding charges accumulated over previous years.
The dispute also involved access arrangements at the Cahaya SPK residential development in Shah Alam.
Farid claimed that residents who did not pay security charges were required to leave their vehicles and operate the boom gate themselves, even when security guards were on duty.
He argued that this discriminated against non-members and interfered with their access to their properties.

Another issue was the legality of the guarded and gated arrangement, including guardhouses and automated boom gates allegedly erected on government land without approval from the Shah Alam City Council (MBSA).

Farid argued that the original arrangement established by the developer was a guarded community scheme, and that its subsequent conversion into a guarded and gated arrangement required compliance with the relevant local authority guidelines and procedures.
In allowing the claim on the balance of probabilities, Zuhrina granted the declarations sought in Farid’s statement of claim.

Among other things, she declared that the association could not automatically impose membership on homeowners without an application, compel residents to become members or demand retrospective fees as a condition of membership.
She also ruled that non-member residents could not be required to operate the boom gate themselves without assistance from security personnel, contrary to the applicable guarded community guidelines.
The defendants were ordered to provide Farid with an access card to enter through the guardhouse and boom gate within 30 days of the order.

The judge also ordered a refund or set-off of the RM1,410 Farid previously paid towards the disputed security charges. She further granted relief concerning threats to report the names of him and his wife to credit reporting agencies, including CTOS and CCRIS.
Zuhrina awarded Farid RM20,000 in general damages, with interest at 5% per annum from the date of judgment until full settlement.
The defendants were also ordered to pay RM7,000 in costs.
Colin Andrew Pereira and Edwina Ti represented Farid, while Shah Nurul Afzan Abdullah appeared for the defendants.
6f0047ed501b68b8: PORTIMAO: Marc Marquez has a date with history this weekend when he can retain his MotoGP crown at the Portuguese Grand Prix and in the process claim a record-equalling eighth world title in the premier class of motorcycling, 13 years after his first.

Just 14 points from the final two race weekends, in Portimao and then Valencia, will be enough for Ducati's Marquez to draw level with Giacomo Agostini, who won his 500cc championships between 1966 and 1975.

Marquez could seal the deal as early as Saturday if he wins the sprint race, but with a 60-point gap separating him from his closest rival and compatriot, Jorge Martin, it would need a total disaster for him to not finish top of the pile come the end of next weekend in Spain.
Marco Bezzecchi is still technically in the fight, but, trailing by 74, the Italian needs maximum points from Portimao and Marquez to not score any in order to stay in it.
"It's true that we are in a very good situation, but in MotoGP everything can happen... We have many different moments over a race weekend," said Marquez on Thursday.
"I have a number in my mind which is 14, 14 points. If I achieve 14 points in the next two weekends, this weekend and Valencia, it doesn't matter what the others do."
Marquez's record in the sprint races gives him a good chance of heading into Sunday's GP already the 2026 champion, with 10 wins and four podiums this year.

That's in comparison with seven wins and one other podium finish in the actual GPs in a year in which he hasn't dominated quite like he did last season when he won his first title in six years with five rounds remaining.
Ducati has been a happy home for Marquez, who has returned to top form in the last two years, following a long recovery from a broken arm suffered at the start of the 2020 season.

He moved up to the factory team from Gresini at the start of last year and took the reins as principal rider from two-time world champion Francesco Bagnaia, a disciple of Marquez's great rival Valentino Rossi, who also has seven MotoGP titles.
The difference between the pair has been stark, with Bagnaia languishing ninth in the riders' championship and scuttling off to join Bezzecchi at Aprilia next season.

Marquez became the youngest ever MotoGP champion in his debut season in 2013 and then went on to win the title in five of the next six seasons, and he wants to make up for the time he lost to injury as he heads into his mid-30s.
"The life of an athlete is short, so you need to take the maximum," said Marquez.
"The fastest Marc was 2013. 2013, or maybe 2019. The best Marc is now, 100%. I would have liked to have the mentality I have now at 20 years old."
Marquez will get his weekend underway on Friday with two practice sessions, at 1045GMT and 1500GMT.
ac73dec4c36b6a7b: PETALING JAYA: A car parts warehouse in Jalan Chan Sow Lin, Kuala Lumpur, was mostly destroyed in a fire early this morning.
The Kuala Lumpur fire and rescue department said it received an emergency call at 5.53am and dispatched firefighters from the Pudu fire and rescue station, supported by teams from six other stations.
Firefighters arrived at the scene at 6.03am and found the warehouse engulfed in flames. The blaze was brought under control at 7.03am.
The fire affected an estimated area of 70ft by 150ft, with about 90% of the premises destroyed. No casualties were reported.

The department said firefighters conducted offensive and defensive firefighting operations from all four sides of the building and established firebreaks to prevent the flames from spreading to nearby buildings.
A total of 75 firefighters were deployed, supported by six fire engines, three emergency medical rescue services units, two water tankers and other specialised vehicles.

"Limpahan sebenarnya datang daripada kawasan lain dan bukan limpahan Sungai Binjai kerana RTB Sungai Binjai ternyata dapat mengurangkan sangat banyak kesan banjir berbanding tahun-tahun sebelum ini," katanya.

61cc3b0563f3216a: LAS VEGAS: Ticket prices for Saturday's Las Vegas Grand Prix are on course to be their lowest since Formula One debuted on the Strip in 2023, secondary-market platform TickPick said, as a lack of championship suspense and chilly weather weigh on demand.
The average purchase price for Saturday race-day tickets stood at US$781, down 12% from US$889 last year and 36% below the US$1,214 paid for the inaugural event in 2023, according to TickPick.
The cheapest available ticket for Saturday's race was US$470, while entry to Thursday's practice session was available from US$67.
This year's event comes after Mercedes secured both the drivers' and constructors' championships, removing the title implications that can help fuel late-season interest.
The first Las Vegas race drew fans partly because of its novelty, while the 2024 edition saw Red Bull's Max Verstappen clinch a fourth successive drivers' title on the high-speed street circuit.

"When the Las Vegas Grand Prix was first introduced in 2023, it generated tons of excitement from F1 fans across the US, and demand was reflected in the US$1,214 average purchase price for a ticket that year," said Kyle Zorn, TickPick's director of content.
"Now in its fourth year, some of the initial excitement surrounding the Las Vegas Grand Prix has faded, and ticket prices have consistently declined since that first year."

Cold and wet weather added another variable in the buildup, with rain and low temperatures on Thursday ahead of first practice. Conditions are expected to be dry but cool for Friday qualifying and Saturday night's race.
"I feel like the destination is buzzing," Emily Prazer, Formula One's chief commercial officer and president and chief executive of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, told reporters on Wednesday.
She noted the number of activations across the city had reached an all-time high, and said the challenge for organizers was to improve on the previous year's event.

Formula One signed a 10-year extension in June to keep Las Vegas on the calendar through 2037. The race is unusual in that Formula One itself promotes the event rather than relying on a third-party promoter.
"It feels like it's really Formula One's home in North America," Prazer said.
"And expectations are high when you're Formula One putting on the race."

Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who this month became Formula One's youngest world champion, said the low temperatures could make the race an "outlier," with tire management likely to play a decisive role.

"Having tires in the right temperature is going to be key," said the 20-year-old Italian, who named Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari as Mercedes' main rivals for the weekend. "Track evolution is going to be massive."

b00d2094481c93e7: Now that the Melaka state election is done and dusted, here are six harsh truths Malaysians need to confront.
The first is this: like it or not, the Barisan Nasional (BN)-Perikatan Nasional (PN) bloc won resoundingly.
There is no other way to describe it.
Many of the majorities recorded were astronomical, suggesting that Malay voters remain firmly behind these two coalitions, particularly Umno and PAS.
The prospect of BN and PN forming the next federal government, aided by voter transference between the two coalitions, appears increasingly likely with each passing day.
The second harsh truth is one we are often reluctant to acknowledge: many Malay voters appear largely indifferent to corruption.
The Tabung Haji and Felda controversies associated with Umno barely registered at the polls and did little to dent the party's support.

Meanwhile, PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang, who commands considerable influence among the religious electorate, continues to advance the narrative of Malay-Muslim political dominance with relatively little challenge.
It is a simple yet powerful message. The idea that Malay-Muslims must remain in power is easy to understand and sell.

Against such populist narratives, the Madani government's successes in attracting investments, creating jobs and improving fiscal management have struggled to gain traction, even when the achievements of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's administration were communicated effectively.
The third harsh truth is for a specific group of Malaysians: those in Bersama.
Twice now, despite their hard work, sincerity and idealism, they have come away empty-handed.
Bersama may yet have something to learn from Umno and PAS and their marriage of convenience.
The relationship between the two parties is far from a fairy-tale partnership. I suspect there remains deep distrust between them. After all, what became of Muafakat Nasional?
Nevertheless, both parties recognised that cooperation was necessary for political survival.

Rafizi Ramli may have serious differences with Anwar, but if the PKR president was once able to set aside his differences with mentor-turned-nemesis Dr Mahathir Mohamad to wrest Putrajaya from BN's iron grip in 2018, why can't Rafizi do the same?

There is also a reason figures such as Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, Mahathir, Hadi and Anwar have remained relevant for decades. Rather than dismissing them as political dinosaurs, Bersama might do well to study the lessons they offer.
The fourth harsh lesson is for PKR itself.
The time has come for Anwar to do something bold if the party hopes to survive the next general election.
He must begin laying the groundwork for a new generation of leaders and gradually step back from centre stage.
Unless fresh faces are given room to emerge, public enthusiasm for PKR may continue to fade.
There is little point talking about a second term for Anwar and his administration if the party remains unwilling to reinvent itself.
The fifth lesson is that Pakatan Harapan must strike meaningful deals with the ruling coalitions in Sabah and Sarawak.
Those arrangements must go beyond simply addressing demands under the Malaysia Agreement 1963.
Anwar still possesses something neither BN nor PN is likely to offer: the possibility of an East Malaysian prime minister.
Such a commitment could fundamentally reshape the political landscape.
The sixth and final harsh lesson concerns voter turnout.
During the Melaka election, it was reported that about 80% of Malay voters turned out, compared with only 60% of Chinese voters.
Overall turnout stood at 70%.

It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.
Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.
The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

d1d261c28db95c75: The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.

"Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them."

Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime.

"At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption."

Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering.

Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained.
Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network.

"Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life."
At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play.

Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content."

Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements.

"I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device."
If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success.
But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky.

Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose.

"On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app.

"And so the way that we're marketing and growing right now is [by offering] end-to-end encrypted messages for Bluesky users. You log in with your handle into our app. We pull your friend graph so you can see your mutuals that already have Germ in the app."

Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option.
At some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®

b9181880dad68760: The last few weeks haven’t been good for the US tech industry. The recent US midterms elections signalled strong pushbacks against AI, data centres and big tech in general. Then there’s last week’s breakdown of Microsoft services followed almost immediately by an outage that grounded civilian flights across the US for hours.

Donald Trump's aggressive policies in his second presidency – tariffs, embargoes, sanctions and even military actions against many countries including those once considered allies – are beginning to register loudly in the risk assessments of many countries. The latest incidents bring even more intense focus on this matter.

China was the first to face US actions on its tech sector, especially those involving semiconductors, software and AI. However, China has the resources to deal with this. Chinese companies such as Huawei and DeepSeek are successfully overcoming these obstacles and showing they’re good at converting these problems into opportunities.

Europe is a bit late to the party, taking longer to realise they aren’t high on the US list of friends and allies any more. The inertia and in-fighting in its huge coalition of disparate European nations slowed things down a lot. But even there the logjam is breaking.

A particular shock was Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Trump administration's overt siding with Russian president Vladimir Putin is unnerving Russia’s European neighbours. They realise they depend too much on the US, whether for office productivity tools, weapons, satellite capabilities or semiconductor chips that power their AI ambitions.
A wake-up call

The recent incidents where SpaceX withheld its Starlink and Starshield services to Ukraine’s war efforts are wake-up calls on the perils of depending too much on an increasingly unreliable partner. The same goes with the repeated US threats of annexation of Canada, Greenland, Panama as well as the de facto annexation of Venezuela.
There’s a growing international desire to reduce dependence on US technology, especially critical ones for defence, finance and businesses.

That we can have service breakdowns such at Microsoft and at the US Federal Aviation Administration shatter the decades-old illusions of the superiority, invincibility and desirability of American technology.

Now Malaysia is not China. We don’t have the resources to build cutting-edge tech we can use for ourselves and perhaps sell to the world. But neither do most countries out there,for that matter. We still have to rely on external technologies and services for many areas, even critical ones.
But change must happen. While we’re good at producing everything from agricultural commodities to manufactured goods, we have never been known for being particularly technologically innovative.

But given Asean’s 700 million people and over US$4.5 trillion in GDP, and given the need for economic and security blocs to deal with aggressive and even predatory superpowers, we have the ability, resources and motivation to achieve our goals.

That the overheating global AI markets could crash has been on everybody’s mind lately. Recent events, such as grave warnings about the potential dangers of AI going rogue and harming humanity, coming from AI's biggest boosters themselves, as well as scandals and personnel changes that can potentially alter the tech landscape, may accelerate such an economic scenario.

What’s not on anybody’s bingo cards, however, were the Microsoft and FAA outages. They reveal the dangers of both transitioning complex current systems to new technologies as well as concentrating it in the hands of a handful of American tech giants so much of the computing power that the world needs.
Computing as a service

Over the past few decades the world had increasingly relied on computing hardware and software being made available on subscription from remote data centres owned and operated by mostly US tech giants. Such “cloud computing” means users rent computing services rather than owning the hardware and software themselves. They’ve become tenants rather than landlords, and their landlords have a near-monopoly.

We are seeing the perils of being tied to massive, remote cloud computing capabilities, as when Ukraine and Iran bombed some of Russia’s and the US’s data centres. We’ve always thought having giant tech companies offering capital, expertise and multiple redundancies would guarantee us from those dreaded “single points of failure”.

We were wrong. We are now seeing how single points of failure can and do indeed fail and shut things down. And the human part of the deal – a president or a CEO – can actually be that single point of failure and cause havoc such as we’ve never planned for or insured against.

Another lesson over the recent past has been that middle powers – such as Ukraine and Iran – that had their backs against the wall can show amazing resilience and innovation. They are both successfully holding back global superpowers, lobbing actual bombs and missiles at them, and even bloodying up some noses in return.

There are no reasons that Malaysia, already a reasonably-sized economic middle power, can’t create the tech and infrastructures that can provide us with some sovereignty and hence protection against hostile nations. If Malaysia is to be Boleh at anything, this is certainly an area where we must Boleh.

Meanwhile, I came across a wonderful term used to describe the ability of some systems to degrade under attack but still provide some reduced, predictable functionality, rather than totally collapsing like what happened at Microsoft and the FAA. It's called graceful degradation, a term I wished I’d invented to describe myself growing old.
I'm degrading for sure, with the occasional outage, though whether it's graceful or not still remains to be seen!

b9b68b51845fc3b9: Japan is yet to establish the Human Rights Protection Bill and a independent national human rights institution
Originally published on Global Voices
Anti-immigration policy protest in Oct 2026. Screen capture from the Japan Unfiltered YouTube Channel. Fair Use

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
A newborn Black baby delivered at a clinic in Tokyo’s Meguro Ward became the target of a barrage of racist harassment online.

The clinic published the baby’s photo with a congratulatory message on its social media account as part of its routine “babies born this month” photo series. A screenshot of the post spread widely on X, gaining more than 1.3 million views within a day. The post attracted many hateful comments loaded with anti-immigrant sentiment and racial discrimination against non-white and non-Japanese people. Some of the hateful comments received thousands of likes.
All comments have since been removed from the post, and the clinic has disabled commenting on its Instagram.

This incident sheds light on two issues within Japanese society. On one level, it reflects how racist hate speech still remains rampant in Japan. But more broadly, it exposes a missing layer of justice infrastructure: Japan has no independent human rights commission empowered to handle discrimination complaints, no enforceable national hate speech law, and no effective way to force platforms to remove hate speech targeting entire groups.

While some cultural critics argue that the widespread racial discrimination in Japan stems from the younger generation’s inadequate interest in foreign cultures and development, others argue that the prevalence of online hate speech is to a large extent related to a lack of effective domestic legislation and human rights education.

Despite being a signatory to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) since 1995, Japan has not passed the Human Rights Protection Bill or established an independent national human rights institution to investigate human rights violations and penalize perpetrators. While there have been numerous attempts to pass such a bill, it was tabled multiple times in the 2000s and early 2010s. Critics say the efforts failed because the public feared it could violate the freedom of speech protected by the Constitution.
Toothless anti-discrimination national laws

Thus, instead of passing a comprehensive set of laws, it addresses discrimination and human rights through issue-specific laws, such as the Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Human Rights Awareness-Raising (2000), the Act for Eliminating Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (2013), the Act on the Promotion of Efforts to Eliminate Unfair Discriminatory Speech and Behavior against Persons with Countries of Origin other than Japan (2016), the Act on the Promotion of the Elimination of Buraku Discrimination (2016), as well as the Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of the Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (2023), which aim to raise public awareness about human rights and providing government support rather than criminalizing hate speech and discrimination.

For example, while the Hate Speech Elimination Act was enacted to curb xenophobic street rallies that terrify ethnic minorities residing in Japan, such as the series of protests against Kyoto Korean Elementary School between December 2009 and March 2010, it does not declare hate speech illegal, nor penalize offenders with fines or jail sentences.

Moreover, the law only protects foreigners with a legal status, but excludes undocumented migrants, asylum seekers, and Indigenous peoples, including the Ainu and Ryūkyūans. The law’s legal scope is at odds with the United Nations’ recommendations, which state that a signatory of the ICERD must “ensure legislative guarantees against racial discrimination apply to non-citizens regardless of their immigration status, and that the implementation of legislation does not have a discriminatory effect on non-citizens.” Legal experts have criticized the restrictive clause of the law for, as Shuji Oda, president of the Dai-Ichi Tokyo Bar Association, says, “giving rise to a false reverse implication that hate speech directed at individuals without legal residency status is permissible.”

The toothless anti-discrimination laws only manage to contain explicit discriminatory actions against disabled people, Burakumin (feudal outcasts), LGBTQ+ people, and foreigners with legal status; they have not eliminated hate speech. Meanwhile, street rallies against immigrant and imported labor have surged amid stagnant local wages, inflation, and rising living costs. Though these protests are usually small in scale, they attract a large number of social media comments, with plenty of discriminatory remarks and hate speech against foreigners.

Additionally, none of the aforementioned laws has a mechanism to force internet platforms to remove harmful content; this results in the spread of xenophobia, homophobia, hatred against social minorities, and a racist online culture.
Kawasaki model

As Japanese national politics has stalled the enactment of the Human Rights Protection Bill, some local governments have started building the legal framework from the bottom up to address local unrest targeting ethnic minorities.

Kawasaki City, which is home to a large Zainichi Korean population in Kanagawa Prefecture, was the first municipality in Japan to introduce punitive local laws to curb protests that “injure the human dignity of others,” as described by the city’s Justice Department.

Since the national Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Awareness was passed in 2000, the city enacted its own Children’s Rights Ordinance in 2000 and Human Rights Ombudsperson Ordinance in 2001, which paved the way for the establishment of a local independent Human Rights Ombudsperson system for receiving and investigating complaints on bullying, abuse, and discrimination.

Following a surge of demonstrations calling for the exclusion of people of foreign origin around 2013, the city enacted the Ordinance for the Creation of a City that Respects Human Rights and is Free from Discrimination in December 2019, which prohibits discrimination based on race, nationality, ethnic origin, gender, sexual orientation, and disability. The ordinance also bans using loudspeakers, placards, or flyers that induce hatred against people originating from outside Japan and their descendants. Under the Ordinance, repeat offenders would have their identities publicly disclosed, and they could be fined up to JPY 500,000 (approximately USD 3,130). The city would also keep a record of hate groups and ban them from using public facilities, such as sports venues and parks.

Furthermore, the ordinance established an expert panel empowered to review hate speech and instruct online platforms to remove extreme content targeting a specific group of people and disclose the abusers’ identities.

While the ordinance has managed to reduce discriminatory protests against Korean-Japanese communities within Kawasaki City, it is powerless when the protests take place in neighboring jurisdictions. Moreover, thus far the criminal penalty of the local ordinance just punishes abusers targeting people originating from outside of Japan; LGBTQ+, disabled, and indigenous communities have remained unprotected. It cannot penalize landlords or employers who discriminate and has limited power over online abuse, as internet companies are not legally bound by local laws.
Human rights education translated into moral education

Various UN bodies have repeatedly criticized Japan for failing to enact a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and establish an independent commission to investigate and prosecute abusers in line with the “Paris Principle,” the official international standards for national human rights institutions. Yet, to date, Japanese society still lacks the consensus and determination to pass the Human Rights Protection Bill.
While proponents of stalling the legislation cite potential violations of free speech, a deeper reason relates to local xenophobia and perceptions of human rights.

The concept of human rights was introduced to Japan about 150 years ago, during the Japanese modernization period beginning in the late Edo and early Meiji era. However, when the Constitution of the Empire of Japan was promulgated in 1889, it defined citizens’ rights not as inherent human rights, but as “rights of subjects” granted by the Emperor.

Only after World War II was the concept of universal human rights re-introduced and localized to criticize Japan’s wartime militarization of society and crimes against non-Japanese people. Yet, human rights education in schools is often confused with conventional moral education, which emphasizes individual responsibility to family, society, and the country, and the need to maintain harmonious human relations through interpersonal politeness and consideration.

However, the individual morality approach overlooks the structural causes of discrimination and fails to empower individuals as rights-holders to address the problem of systematic discrimination, as pointed out by a group of Japanese teachers from the Institute of Global Education and Culture in a proposal to better integrate moral and human rights education in 2014:
日本では人権教育・啓発の場で「おもいやり」「やさしさ」などが強調される一方で、権利そのものを学習することは低調である。[…]
[…]具体的な「権利」という側面も、また「社会的に」問題を解決しようという側面も極めて弱い。「思いやり」を強調する抽象的・心情主義的教育は、私的な人間関係の中での問題解決ばかりを強調し、権利を具体的に考え実現しようとする力をむしろ弱めているといえる。
In Japan, human rights education and awareness-raising campaigns have kept emphasising concepts like ‘consideration for others’ (omoi-yari) and ‘kindness’ while downplaying education on rights. […]

It’s extremely weak in addressing different aspects of individual rights and the social resolution of rights-related problems. The emphasis on ‘understanding’ is both abstract and sentimental; as such, education relies solely on problem-solving within private interpersonal relationships and will hence weaken the ability to think concretely about rights and exercising one’s rights.

Earlier this year, Human Rights Watch urged the newly elected prime minister Sanae Takaichi to legislate a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and create an independent national human rights body to address the rise of xenophobic sentiments against immigrants. Although the right-leaning government has no intention of resurrecting the Human Rights Protection Bill, a civic coalition has formed to advocate for an independent National Human Rights Institution with investigative and corrective powers to address discrimination and human rights abuses by 2028.
Written by Jo Carter

36f6a66393bf4897: OTTAWA: Canada is still seeking an interim arrangement with the United States to ease some US tariffs on its goods, but Washington has shown little movement, the Canadian minister responsible for trade with the US, Dominic LeBlanc, told an advisory committee on Thursday, two people familiar with the briefing said.

US tariffs on Canadian autos are set to rise in January to 50% from 25%. Companies and industry associations have warned prime minister Mark Carney’s government that the increase could dismantle decades-old supply chains and lead to job losses and factory shutdowns.
Speaking to CBC News, LeBlanc reiterated that Ottawa had made some progress in trade talks with Washington but not enough to sign a deal.
"We're not yet at a point where we think we have a deal that is good enough for the economic interests of the country, but we have made progress," LeBlanc said.
LeBlanc also noted that even with a deal, the US would likely keep some sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and autos.

"I think we have to be realistic with Canadians in those particular sectors; there is an element of those tariffs that are going to remain, but they have to be in a circumstance that ... the long-term economic viability of these sectors is assured," he said.

Earlier, LeBlanc told the Advisory Committee on Canada-US Economic Relations, which includes business leaders and politicians, that he is in regular contact with his US counterparts, but there has been little progress since talks broke down in August, said the people, who are committee members and spoke on condition of anonymity because the briefing was private.

"The US understands what our red lines are and our people are saying that if the US makes movement, then we can move quickly. But so far the US has made no movement," one of the people said, summarising LeBlanc's briefing to the committee.

LeBlanc's office confirmed in a statement that LeBlanc briefed the committee on trade talks and reaffirmed Canada's commitment to strike a mutually beneficial agreement with the US. It did not respond to a request for comment on further details.

One of the people familiar with the briefing said LeBlanc has been speaking with US Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department plays a central role in administering and negotiating tariffs imposed under a US law that lets the president restrict imports deemed a threat to national security, including those on steel and autos.
LeBlanc has also been speaking with US Trade representative Jamieson Greer, who led most of the dialogue in August before the talks collapsed, the person said.
The commerce department and office of the US Trade representative did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The US midterm elections, in which president Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of the House of Representatives and the Senate to the Democrats, have not changed the course of trade negotiations, the other person familiar with the briefing said.

023c96572d69f0f2: It has to be Anfield, of all places. The fixture list is up to its wicked tricks again.
Just as it did for Manchester City after the guilty verdict was announced, Sunday’s big game sees United go to that simmering cauldron of hostility at a critical moment in their history.
Mauricio Pochettino takes charge, fresh from guiding the USA to an 8-0 aggregate win over Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League.
From Haiti to hate, you might say, and instead of just 24,000 at Cincinnati’s TQL Stadium, the world and a good chunk of the universe will be watching.
But is Anfield still the forbidding fortress it is cracked up to be?
We know what happened with City, who ran out comfortable winners after two harsh yellow cards gave them a man advantage.
But it’s not just star-studded City we’re talking about: only Crystal Palace, who are bottom, and Nottingham Forest (16th) have worse home records than Liverpool.
A paltry five points is all the Reds have mustered from five games despite the wall of sound that is supposed to make opponents weak at the knees.
They have played all three teams above them in the table, but it is only due to having the best away record that they sit in fourth place.
Even more relevant, though, is that United do not seem intimidated by the place.
Indeed, the Devils have a good record here despite Liverpool’s recent overall superiority.
Kopites may still think fondly of the 7-0 annihilation of 2023, but since then Liverpool haven’t won there in three games, and just once in seven meetings in all competitions.
However, if the Devils have found some steel, Pochettino himself will only have reason to dread the Anfield roar.
The Argentine has won only one game there, and that was when he was at Southampton.
In 19 games against Liverpool in total, with the Saints, Chelsea, and mostly Tottenham, he has won only three times, with five draws and 11 defeats.
At Spurs, he won only once and his greatest disappointment in football was the Champions League final of 2019, when a second-minute penalty distorted the game.
Pochettino had relished the underdog role with Southampton, beating United as well in just his fourth game in charge.
The trick seemed to be making a fast start, which took the big boys by surprise.
After a maximum of three training sessions since landing on Wednesday, the 54-year-old will hardly be able to transform United.
Still jet-lagged, a fast start may be beyond his powers to engineer, but there is no doubt that this will be another occasion where he’ll be the underdog.
Three of his staff did arrive earlier, but it will be expecting an awful lot of the ‘new manager bounce’ to match a Liverpool side that is showing signs of becoming an Andoni Iraola team.
An interesting aspect of Poch’s appointment is that he was not Jim Ratcliffe’s choice, but that of the Glazers, who pulled rank on the minority owner.
CEO Omar Berrada and Football Director Jason Wilcox wanted Eddie Howe but were overruled by the family in Florida, who had been impressed by Pochettino’s stewardship of the American national team.

Ratcliffe has been strangely quiet of late and, with the protests against the owners showing no sign of abating, you wonder if he’ll carry out his promise to walk away should he get the abuse the Glazers endure.
He’s already very close to that level and now he’s been firmly put in his place by the majority owners.
A hedge fund billionaire pal of the Glazers, Ken Griffin, helped to pay Pochettino’s salary at cash-strapped US Soccer.
Even before he crossed the Atlantic, Poch was already talking about signings in the January transfer window.
He’s widely expected to add Folarin Balogun and Antonee Robinson from his US team to fill the gaping holes at striker and left-back.
It will be fascinating to see if United find funds for him that Ratcliffe denied Michael Carrick.
This is not to say that he won’t give everyone a chance at Old Trafford. In the US job, he tried no less than 77 players and unearthed several teenage starlets before honing down his squad.
This augurs well for United’s academy traditions, but it came too late for wonderkid J.J. Gabriel, who has gone to Real Madrid.
Liverpool are also being linked with more recruits to bolster Iraola’s promising first three months.
The Spaniard is more of a slow starter, having gone 10 games before he notched his first win at Bournemouth, but we know the rest.
And there are welcome signs that despite injury disruptions, he’s getting his message across.
He’s certainly more in tune with Jurgen Klopp’s heavy metal than the more patient Arne Slot ever was.
He must feel that the lightning breaks of Bradley Barcola, Cody Gakpo and Victor Munoz could overwhelm a United defence that has been ragged of late.
Indeed, the jitteriness of the back four even spread to Sanne Lemmens in the last game.
And you can’t help but feel that if Florian Wirtz can’t flourish against this defence, he never will cut the mustard in the EPL.
He scored two in Germany’s 5-0 rout of the Netherlands, so he’s primed.
But the focus will inevitably be on the visitors’ dugout to see the new would-be saviour.
He’s already promised to make the players run and ‘unblock’ their brains.
It sounds like he has half a chance, but maybe not on Sunday.

e5aeafa36fd39838: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 20 — The excitement of taking a new train service is really about the experience and discovering what amenities await. As the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) prepares to connect communities across the east coast when commercial passenger services begin next month, here’s what passengers can expect from the onboard six-car electric train experience. One of the first things passengers may notice is the generous legroom. The surprise is it serves a purpose beyond passenger comfort. It actually allows the seats to swivel and face each other, giving families and groups travelling together greater flexibility in their seating arrangements. Beyond the swivel seating arrangement, passengers can also choose between two travel classes: Economy and Business, each offering its own level of comfort and amenities. All seats feature patterned blue upholstery and fold-down tray tables that can support up to 25kg, with Business Class arranged in a 2-2 configuration and Economy Class in a 3-2 layout. The main difference? The Business Class seats come with headrests, a plusher, more cushioned feel and a wider seat base for added comfort. An onboard bistro in the middle section of the train also allows passengers to purchase pre-heated meals, refreshments and beverages, with train crew available around the clock to serve them.

In addition, passengers travelling in Business Class receive full meal service served by crew members trained at the Malaysia Airlines Academy, bringing airline-style dining service to the rail journey. Despite travelling at speeds of up to 160km/h, passengers can also expect a relatively quiet ride, with minimal noise from outside the train. Other amenities include a dedicated prayer room, hot and cold water dispensers, a diaper-changing area and wheelchair-accessible facilities throughout the train.
