3121ae048a876fc6: PRACHINBURI (Thailand), Nov 20 — Father of four Adisorn Lakonburee used to catch fish for his family’s dinner, but stopped after floodwaters brought oil slicks and foul chemical smells into his village in eastern Thailand. “Now I’m too afraid to catch or eat them,” the 43-year-old homebuilder told AFP at his home in Prachinburi province, adding that he and his family are also too scared to drink the tap water. Located between the capital Bangkok and Thailand’s flagship industrial zone further east, Prachinburi has long faced concerns over waste pollution. But heavy flooding in September and October exposed the scale of the problem, spreading foul, rainbow-coloured water across rice paddies and waterways. In water sampled near one landfill in October, Thai authorities found “unusually high” levels of petroleum hydrocarbons — chemicals associated with oil and fuel — as well as toxic concentrations of aluminium. The landfill operator, Green Environment Technology, denied any wrongdoing, but after resident complaints, the industry ministry ordered it temporarily closed. The ministry also suspended operations at two other waste facilities in the surrounding area and ordered a nationwide inspection of 3,000 similar plants across Thailand — with 300 already found to have breached regulations. As residents protested against the pollution, Prachinburi’s then-acting governor ate locally caught fish to show residents it was safe. But Navaporn Sanguanmoo, director of industrial waste management in the government’s Department of Industrial Works, said authorities needed to do more. “Prachinburi is a lesson that makes us rethink many things,” she told AFP. Garbage dump Farmland stretches as far as the eye can see in Prachinburi, a major food-producing province known for rice, sugarcane, cassava and fruit orchards, as well as livestock and fish farming. But among the fields are waste facilities and illegal dumping sites. During a visit this month, AFP saw a pile of electronic scrap mixed with chicken manure in the middle of a sugarcane plantation, and a massive landfill hidden inside a forest. A burning stench hung in the air near some of the sites, akin to machine oil or weedkiller. Environmental researcher Somnuck Jongmeewasin said the area had been a “garbage dump” for the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC), a flagship industrial zone spanning the neighbouring provinces of Rayong, Chonburi and Chachoengsao. An adviser to the Thai parliament’s industrial sub-committee, he has conducted research that identified more than 60 suspected illegal dumping sites in Prachinburi in recent years. Dawan Chantarahassadee, an activist with environmental watchdog EARTH Thailand, blamed cheap land and lax law enforcement for what she described as an “empire” of waste facilities. The floods have “clearly shown that government oversight has not been strict enough”, she said. Campaigners trace the problem to a 2016 military junta order that exempted waste facilities from town-planning laws, allowing them into agricultural green zones. “This area is designated for agriculture,” said local activist Sumet Rianpongnam, 54. “Yet (waste-processing) factories have been built right next to our homes.” Last year, Thailand banned the import of plastic waste and strengthened controls on electronic waste to help protect the environment and public health. But Navaporn, from the industrial works department, said the country still deals with around three million tonnes of hazardous industrial waste each year, and over 30 million tonnes of non-hazardous waste. She said some can be sold, including scrap metal, but waste with little resale value, such as oil-contaminated water or low-grade plastics, was particularly vulnerable to illegal dumping because of high treatment costs. “That is precisely the type of waste we find illegally dumped across multiple areas,” Navaporn said. She added that the penalties for dumping were too low, meaning “breaking the law makes economic sense” for violators. At a Buddhist meditation centre near a suspected dumping site, nun Suparpron Tapowpong, 64, said they have had to wash with rainwater and drink donated bottled water. “We just don’t know where to get safe water anymore,” she said, adding that “this has become a serious crisis, the worst I’ve ever faced”. Food security The contamination has caused immediate health concerns, with academics warning the chemicals could cause skin irritation or breathing difficulties. There are also longer-term issues. “Don’t forget, if the land and water are contaminated, we lose our food security,” said Dawan. For farmer Chalida Mongkon, the fallout is already visible in her once-verdant rice paddies, which turned black and rotten after floodwaters receded. “We don’t even know if we’ll be able to grow anything next year,” the 60-year-old said. “We’re afraid to set foot in our rice fields because we’re worried about toxic chemicals.” The government pledged in early November to expand testing to riverbed sediment for heavy-metal contamination, but many say it is moving too slowly. “In the end, we might lose the forensic evidence we need to identify who’s responsible,” said Somnuck, adding: “Delay is injustice.” — AFP
ee581ca7c7bf2b84: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 20 — Malaysia’s food is more than a gastronomy experience. It tells a story of diversity and unity, where different but complementing flavours, ingredients, and culinary traditions reflect a shared national identity. This distinctive character is what captivates Italian chef Alessia Morabito, who hailed the country’s food culture as an expression of how different communities preserve their culinary individuality while contributing to an unmistakably Malaysian identity. “What I love in this country is that you have three souls together, the Malay, Chinese, and Indian together and the food is expressed in three different moods but when you taste a Malay, Chinese, or an Indian food, every time you understand the same identity,” she told Bernama in an exclusive interview. At the interview, Morabito, who was in Malaysia in conjunction with the Week of the Italian Cuisine in the World 2026, also demonstrated the preparation of Trippa Finta, a classic home-style Italian dish that uses thin, sliced cheese omelettes simmered in tomato sauce to mimic the look and chewy texture of animal tripe. The recipe, which dates back to post-war central Italy, is featured in Reti e Archivi del Gusto (RAGU), a cookbook digitisation project she has led since 2021 with food historian Mila Fumini. Different cultures, shared values Morabito, who also teaches migrant women culinary arts at Roots, a social enterprise restaurant in Modena where she is based, said while Italian cuisine enjoys wide international reach, Malaysia’s rich culinary diversity is largely discovered only by those who visit the country. “Malaysia gastronomic identity is very inner (deep-rooted). So, to taste Malaysian food, I have to come here. Italian food is different because can find it everywhere,” she said. Despite their distinct culinary traditions, Morabito said Malaysians and Italians share a deep appreciation of food as an expression of generosity, family bonds, hospitality, and human connection, making it an integral part of their cultural identity. She noted that this appreciation of food as part of cultural identity is also reflected in Unesco’s recognition of Italian cooking as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. She added that both kitchens share surprising similarities in ingredients and techniques, comparing local beef stews to northern Italy’s brasato, dumplings to tortellini, and water-and-flour handmade pastas like Tuscan pici to Asian noodles. Recipes that adapt On adapting Italian dishes for local tastes, Morabito said chefs should view recipes as “alive” rather than rigid. She said, even within Italy, cooking practices for traditional food such as ragù (slow-cooked meat sauce) and tortellini vary from town to town depending on local ingredients. “Authentic food, for me, is not so important, because if you have a recipe, recipes are alive. So you have to change the recipe because the ingredients are changed during the time and in the places too,” she said. Citing an example, she noted that Italian restaurants abroad often cater to Italians living there while also offering local diners an introduction to the country’s food traditions. Expanding Italy-Malaysia culinary exchange Morabito also sees potential for Malaysia and Italy to deepen culinary cooperation, with food offering a platform for cultural exchange, professional development, and closer people-to-people ties. She expressed optimism about expanding bilateral culinary exchanges through diplomatic channels such as the Italian Embassy in Kuala Lumpur by way of joint workshops, chef training, and ingredient showcases in both countries. Such initiatives, she said, would allow chefs from both countries to share techniques, explore each other’s culinary heritage, and gain greater exposure to ingredients and food products. “We can organise kitchen courses and invite Malaysian chefs to Italy for exhibitions, collaborations, and ingredient showcases for instance, with iconic Italian products like Parmigiano-Reggiano. “We have everything needed to create strong Italian-Malaysian collaborations,” she said. — Bernama
096fc96b01a2f439: PORT DICKSON, Nov 20 — The beaches in Port Dickson are gaining popularity as training grounds for divers seeking to obtain diving licences, boosting efforts to develop marine biodiversity-based tourism products in the district. Negeri Sembilan Fisheries Department director Kasim Tawe said the initiative, launched in collaboration with several diving centres and certified instructors last year, aims to establish Port Dickson as one of the country’s diving training destinations. He said Port Dickson’s proximity to Kuala Lumpur and the Klang Valley made it a convenient option, eliminating the need for aspiring divers to travel to other states for training. “Previously, those seeking diving licences had to complete their open-water dives at destinations such as Pulau Redang, Pulau Tioman or islands in Sabah. They can now undergo training at Port Dickson’s beaches, particularly around Tanjung Biru, Teluk Monyet (Monkey Bay) and Barbosa Cove in Tanjung Tuan. “Our coral reefs are also beautiful, with unique varieties comparable to those found around the country’s renowned islands,” he told Bernama after the 2026 Port Dickson Marine Biodiversity and Conservation Programme at Tanjung Biru here today. He added that the clear waters off Tanjung Biru and Teluk Monyet allowed divers to see coral reefs from as close as five metres away, although rainfall could sometimes reduce underwater visibility. The effort to develop Port Dickson as a diving training destination is also expected to showcase its marine attractions beyond its traditional appeal for swimming and beach activities. Kasim said Port Dickson’s coastal waters were home to 46 coral species, five of which were classified as endangered, as well as two turtle species - the hawksbill and green turtles. Meanwhile, on the Marine Biodiversity and Conservation Programme, Kasim said it sought to raise public awareness, particularly among younger generations, about the importance of protecting marine ecosystems. As part of the programme, six adult turtles aged between three and eight years were released into the sea, alongside about 5,000 seabass fingerlings to replenish fish stocks and attract more anglers to Port Dickson’s waters. To protect turtle populations, the department had appointed three turtle egg collectors to monitor turtle landings along the Negeri Sembilan coastline, from Glory Beach Resort in Pantai Gemuk to Tanjung Tuan and Pantai Cermin. There are currently no plans to gazette turtle landing sites. However, Kasim urged the public not to disturb turtles coming ashore to ensure their natural processes are not disrupted. — Bernama
2e71f13f3cdb0ff7: Malaysia’s ports handled 33.07 million 20-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, in 2025. Through September 2026, they had already moved a provisional 25,713,471 TEUs, up 4.8% from the corresponding nine months last year.
That expanding flow of containers provides an encouraging backdrop for everyone whose business depends on moving, storing and delivering goods.
At the centre stands Port Klang.

Its throughput reached 11,804,541 TEUs, growing 5.4% and contributing 45.9% of the national total. More tellingly, Port Klang supplied approximately 50.8% of Malaysia’s additional container volume over the period. It is not merely the largest contributor; it is driving a disproportionate share of national growth.
Already ranked the world’s 10th busiest container port in Lloyd’s List’s 2026 table, based on 2025 throughput, Port Klang is demonstrating why its international standing matters to Malaysia.
More than a transshipment success
Port Klang’s strength lies in the combination of international connectivity and Malaysian gateway trade.

Imports and exports together reached 5,265,991 TEUs, representing 44.6% of throughput. Exports grew 6.2% to 2,625,382 TEUs, while imports increased 4.3% to 2,640,609 TEUs. Combined gateway growth was approximately 5.2%.
These figures measure container activity, not trade value. Nevertheless, they show expanding demand for the port’s services in both directions.
For manufacturers, importers, freight forwarders and warehouse operators, this is the commercially significant story: Port Klang’s growth is not confined to cargo changing ships.
Transshipment also advanced, increasing 5.5% to 6,538,550 TEUs. Its 55.4% share of throughput underlines the gateway’s substantial international connecting role.
Serving Malaysian commerce while connecting global shipping networks gives Port Klang two important foundations for growth.
Two terminals, complementary strengths

Westports remains the anchor, handling 8,546,840 TEUs and contributing 72.4% of Port Klang’s throughput. Its 1.3% overall increase included export growth of 2% and transshipment growth of 2.2%, although imports declined 1.9%.
Its scale remains formidable. Westports handled 68.8% of Port Klang’s gateway cargo and 75.3% of its transshipment business.

Northport, meanwhile, supplied exceptional momentum. Its throughput rose 17.9% to 3,257,701 TEUs, contributing approximately 82% of Port Klang’s additional volume. Imports grew 19.6%, while exports and transshipment volumes increased by 17.7% and 17.1%, respectively.
That breadth deserves recognition. Northport’s gateway cargo reached 1,640,511 TEUs, alongside 1,617,190 TEUs of transshipment. Its progress strengthened both sides of Port Klang’s business.
Westports’ larger base and Northport’s acceleration demonstrate the value of complementary terminal strengths.
Scale backed by capability
Global leadership requires infrastructure that shipping lines can use with confidence.

Westports states that its facilities can accommodate container ships of 24,000 TEUs, supported by a natural deep harbour reaching up to 18 metres. Its expansion programme is expected to increase annual capacity from 14 million to 28 million TEUs.
That is future capacity, not cargo already secured. However, it provides a credible platform for defending Port Klang’s top ten position.
The decisive test will be execution: dependable vessel handling, efficient clearance, productive yards and reliable connections beyond the terminal gate.
A stronger national network
Johor reinforces Malaysia’s maritime weight.

Port of Tanjung Pelepas (PTP) handled 10,973,966 TEUs, up 5.4%, while Johor Port at Pasir Gudang handled 793,279 TEUs, down 0.6%. PTP contributed approximately 93.3% of their combined 11,767,245 TEUs, with Pasir Gudang supplying 6.7%.

Together with Port Klang, these gateways accounted for approximately 91.7% of the provisional national total. Their concentration of activity makes continued investment and operational resilience nationally important.

Penang remains a gateway for the northern corridor and southern Thailand trade. It handled 987,857 TEUs, down 2.5%, although September recorded growth of 1.4%. Its strategic role extends beyond one period’s softer performance.
Elsewhere, Kuching grew 9.9%, Rajang 9%, Bintulu 4.3% and Sabah 4.1%. Malaysia’s maritime progress includes these regional connections, not only its largest hubs.
From port activity to business value
Daiso’s newly opened RM1.2 billion Global Distribution Centre on Pulau Indah adds another layer to Port Klang’s proposition, serving 27 countries and regions.
Alongside IKEA’s distribution centre on Pulau Indah, it strengthens the connection between maritime access and international distribution.
Elsewhere, Volkswagen’s regional parts distribution centre at PTP demonstrates the wider Malaysian opportunity.
For warehouse operators and logistics providers, the prize is capturing more value around cargo through storage, consolidation, fulfilment and specialist services.
Port Klang’s leadership is therefore more than a ranking. It is a platform for Malaysian enterprise.
For investors and stakeholders, the message is encouraging: the volumes are growing, the capabilities are substantial, and the opportunity reaches well beyond the quay.

Malaysia’s next maritime achievement should be measured not only in containers handled, but in the businesses, careers and possibilities they help carry forward, making Malaysia a nation that moves not just cargo, but people and prosperity too.

b83436b2b80978cb: Karim Ibrahim’s departure from Malaysia Athletics (MA) should have happened years ago. That it took intervention from World Athletics and a constitutional overhaul to end his presidency says plenty about the federation’s failure to put its own house in order.

The lifetime ban imposed on Karim in 2018 was never lifted. The Court of Arbitration for Sport upheld the findings against him. Yet he returned as MA president in June 2025, relying on a domestic constitutional provision that limited disqualification to five years.
World Athletics continued to regard him as permanently ineligible. MA’s rules, meanwhile, gave him a route back.
That contradiction should never have been allowed to stand.
A national federation cannot claim to represent its sport internationally while maintaining eligibility rules that conflict with those of its international governing body.
World Athletics’ intervention in January this year exposed a failure that MA should have recognised and addressed long before it was forced to do so.
But Karim was not the only person responsible for this episode.
Where were the watchdogs?
MA’s executive council, made up of representatives from its state affiliates, cannot escape scrutiny.
The five-year disqualification provision did not simply find its way into the constitution. It went through the executive council before being put to the affiliates and approved at the AGM.
The very people entrusted with overseeing the federation were part of the process that created the provision allowing Karim to return.

What questions were raised along the way? Did anyone challenge how a domestic five-year disqualification could coexist with a lifetime ban imposed by World Athletics? Did the council consider the consequences for Malaysia’s standing in international athletics?
These are not minor oversights. They go to the heart of what an executive council is supposed to do.
Its members are not there to fill seats, attend meetings or wait for the next overseas competition. They are there to govern, scrutinise decisions and hold the administration accountable.
That means challenging proposals when they threaten the federation’s credibility.
The affiliates cannot now treat the affair as somebody else’s mistake. Their representatives were part of the process, and the provision was approved at their AGM.

An executive council that fails to question decisions of this magnitude is not doing its job. MA needs fewer passengers and more watchdogs – people prepared to challenge the leadership, even when the questions are uncomfortable.
A new rulebook is not enough
The amended constitution is a necessary correction. It is not, by itself, proof that MA has turned a corner.

The federation must now apply its eligibility rules consistently, conduct transparent elections and make its executive council answerable for the decisions it takes. It must also clarify how the new requirements affect its state affiliates.

Karim remains president of the Perak Athletics Association. His disqualification from holding office within MA raises an obvious question about whether he can continue in that state role. MA and Perak must clarify the position rather than leave it to assumption.
But governance is only part of the job. Malaysian athletics has a sporting purpose that has too often been overshadowed by its administrative troubles.
MA must develop athletes, support coaches, strengthen grassroots programmes and build a credible pathway to international competition.
These responsibilities cannot keep taking a back seat while office bearers argue over positions and control.
There is more to being an office bearer than travelling with delegations, attending functions and occupying a seat at meetings. The job is to serve the sport.
The 2027 SEA Games will offer another measure of the country’s ambitions, but the federation’s performance should not be judged by medals alone.
It should also be judged by the quality of the system that produces the athletes and supports those who work with them.
Karim’s exit should be a turning point, not a victory lap for those who remain.
The executive council must examine its own record: the provision it helped put through, the questions it asked or failed to ask, and the consequences that followed.
State affiliates must decide whether their representatives are there to protect the sport or simply occupy positions within its administration.
Karim is gone from the MA presidency. The people who helped create the conditions for his return are still there.
It is time they stopped being passengers.

697df9fe24ea1705: WASHINGTON: Meta said Thursday it was reconsidering its 2030 deadline for net zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence boom, the latest in a broad retreat by corporations on global warming targets.

"We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones – including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal," Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company's annual sustainability report.

The company reported its net carbon equivalent emissions increased 45% in 2025 to 11.8 million metric tonnes – a figure that is itself based on accounting methods viewed sceptically by climate advocates.

"When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex," the executives wrote, adding that delivering on Meta's vision "requires building the infrastructure that powers AI."

In 2020, Meta set a goal of net zero emissions across its entire value chain by the year 2030 in order to align with the Paris Agreement, which seeks to hold long-term warming to 1.5°C to avert climate catastrophes.
This involves eliminating emissions as far as possible and purchasing credits from carbon removal projects where emissions cannot be eliminated.
The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services and capital goods – equipment, machinery, buildings, facilities and vehicles.

A study published in Nature Sustainability this week found that 403 of the United States' most powerful data centres accounted for around 2% of the country's electricity consumption and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark – figures that are only growing.
Around 1,200 such "hyperscale" data centres are now online, and hundreds more are planned.
Under President Donald Trump's second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.
Though the explosion of AI data centres looms large over the trend, it is not confined to Big Tech, with car makers, retailers and beverage companies also offenders.
In January 2021, GM set a target of 100% zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035.
While it technically maintains this target, the company this year backed the Trump administration's weakening of a fuel economy rule to a level that would require no further improvement.

In 2020 retail giant Walmart committed to cutting emissions by around a third by 2025 and two-thirds by 2030 from a 2015 baseline. But in a 2024 report, it acknowledged it would miss the first target as well as its recycling goals.

Also in 2020, Google pledged to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, in what CEO Sundar Pichai heralded as a "moonshot". But by 2024 it had stopped claiming its operations were carbon neutral, and this year it acknowledged its emissions were still rising.
Beverage giants Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions reduction targets and weakened their ambitions.

4665289b81f88c7a: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated?  Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work.  “Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.” While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code.  This is where an international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute sought to help, by examining how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies. Such studies develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes, such as the risk of developing a disease. Because these models inform decisions about patient care, researchers need to be able to scrutinize how they were built and tested. Using large language models (LLMs), the researchers examined nearly 4,000 papers to identify statements about shared code. They then followed the statements to assess hundreds of associated code repositories. Their review revealed two key gaps: Code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings, recently published in Nature Medicine, are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Following the code TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. To understand current code-sharing practices, the team identified studies citing either guideline. The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models, and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central’s open-access collection.  “The challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent. First, we had to identify whether or not a paper shared code” says Thomas Sounack, the study’s first author. He adds that authors “discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways.” The team used an LLM to help screen papers, identify statements about code availability, and extract links. Software then retrieved the linked repositories — online collections of code and related files — for further assessment. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed. It also assessed repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. “The real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text. These models helped us work with information that was scattered across papers and software repositories, rather than neatly organized in a table,” says Pollard, who is a senior author of the study. “That allowed us to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies.” Human reviewers evaluated the work of the LLMs. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results.  Agreement was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Because classification errors remain possible, the authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact. Inconsistent code sharing Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Where code was shared, the contents of repositories varied widely. Some repositories were “extremely well-organized and -documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all,” Sounack says. Good code sharing, he explains, means “giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper.” Practices also varied substantially across journals and countries. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice. Some researchers, for example, provided synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where the original patient records could not be shared publicly. Setting a standard for code sharing Researchers who share code are already making an effort to make their work transparent. But clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ. TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. “We want to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code, and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors,” Pollard says. “The review gives us evidence to inform those discussions."

That view has been clouded a bit by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's fall from grace: Back in July, he came to the defense of open-weight models as a defense against the hegemony of purveyors of closed-weight commercial models like Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. Nonetheless, PAN clearly sees a future for open-weight models.

"Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, in a statement. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional."
The company expects the $4.5 billion all-stock transaction to add more than $1 billion to the company's Next Generation Security business by FY 2029.
Arora, on the company's earnings call, explained the pricey bet as recognition of the corporate desire to avoid vendor lock-in and to retain control of data.

"We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open-weight and open-source models," he said. "Early signs of that shift are clear, with open-weight models growing from under 5 percent of token traffic to more than 60 percent over the past year."

cdf026b73ca8cb64: Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it's worth looking at how they handle climate change.

But there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual users, confined to their chat session. A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer.

LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list in the report.)
540bcf5f777b11b5: China's Xi Jinping places himself firmly in the center of the trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Doug Mills/Getty ImagesIt was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders. Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them. But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver? As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping looks on in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026. Iori Sagisawa/AFP via Getty Images What were the key takeaways from the meeting? The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order. And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president. And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades. A rare airport hug from Xi Jinping. Mandel Ngan/Getty Images It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen. In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds. So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body. And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.” All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter. What wasn’t discussed? The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations. For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged. But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting. At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi. Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings. British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin sit together at the Yalta Conference. AP Photo This was touted as Yalta II – was it? There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table. Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years. Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed. Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary. What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that. 3e0614a078a7f423: New Linux distros seem to appear daily, but far too few distinguish themselves by being smaller and simpler.

XXRI OS is a fairly new desktop Linux distro. It has a snazzy-looking website, complete with an amusing URL, and along similar lines, its GitHub page has a very heavily formatted README. Nonetheless, this is not another over-complex opinionated slopfest of an OS with built-in AI, bizarre keystrokes, and several proprietary components. It's almost the reverse.

The main download is just 287.4 MB, and that's the full distro, not a minimalist installer that fetches most of the OS over your internet connection. We installed it in a VirtualBox VM. It took 675 MB of disk space, and in the graphical desktop, when we opened a terminal window, it reported just 75 MB of RAM in use with the desktop and terminal running. We are restraining ourselves hard when we say that those are unusually low numbers for the 2020s. We would expect most cut-down lightweight Linux distros to use around five to 10 times as much disk space or memory.

The current release of XXRI-OS is version 2.7. XXRI OS 1.0 came out in May 2025, making this a young project with five published releases already behind it. It also has much deeper roots: it is based on the existing and much older Tiny Core Linux. The Reg FOSS desk last looked at Tiny Core Linux 15 back in March 2024 and the project is still going strong: the latest version is version 17.1.

Tiny Core Linux is a marvel, but there are prices to pay for somehow getting a graphical Linux desktop into a 23 MB download. It runs from RAM and uses its own extension-based package system, which can make adding components and managing updates unfamiliar territory. XXRI OS takes TCL and turns it into a slightly more conventional desktop.

It installs to disk in the usual way, and it includes the core functions that most people would expect from their OS in 2026. It has a file manager, a text editor, a media player, a simple app store for adding further components, and a settings app including an update manager. It even includes its own web browser, and there are both x86-32 and x86-64 variants.

The desktop layout has a floating dock at bottom center, and the icons are unlabelled. To save you some guesswork, though, floating just to the left of the dock is an icon with a grid of dots, which is an app launcher. The icons in that do have text labels underneath, so you can learn which symbol denotes which function from here.

We plan to experiment more with this remarkable little OS and see how well it runs on the oldest, slowest boxes in the Irish Sea wing of Vulture Towers, but we like what we see so far. It's an impressive experiment in how low Linux can go and remain useful. While Tiny Core Linux goes down to Windows 95 levels of resource usage, XXRI OS has a more usable Windows 2000-level baseline. Over a quarter of a century later, that is nearly unbeatable. ®

d61da2d07a5dfa33: <!--kg-card-end: html--> This article was produced in collaboration with Court Watch, an independent outlet that unearths overlooked court records. Subscribe to them here.
Federal prosecutors say the FBI posed as both a ransomware victim and threat actor during an undercover operation targeting a Florida-based company.
The company, run by defendant Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar and an unnamed business associate, began in 2020 and claimed to offer data recovery services for victims of ransomware.

An indictment filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island on Wednesday alleges that Palacio’s business, listed as “Company A,” purported to have "advanced cryptographic tools" that could be used to "restore 100%" of a victim's data. Yet prosecutors say Palacio, charged with three counts of wire fraud, had no such capabilities and instead secretly negotiated with the ransomware gangs to obtain the decryption keys himself. Palacio, the indictment adds, would then bill clients for an amount greater than what the ransomware gangs charged in order to turn a profit."It was part of the scheme and artifice to defraud that PALACIO used Company A to intentionally misrepresent to companies in the United States who were victims of ransomware attacks that Company A could help them decrypt and recover their files without paying a ransom," the indictment says.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> As part of the investigation into the company, an undercover FBI agent in June posed as a representative for a fictitious Rhode Island-based business that alleged it had fallen victim to a ransomware attack.Another FBI employee posed as a member of a ransomware gang and encrypted several files on a computer operated by the fictitious company. The federal employee also left a ransom note on the computer with contact information.The fictitious business then contacted Palacio's company and held an initial meeting on June 8 in which an agent said it did not want to pay the ransom. Palacio during subsequent discussions charged the fictitious company $2,750 to conduct an initial forensic assessment.

After offering the undercover FBI agent a contract outlining his company's services, Palacio on June 14 contacted the federal employee posing as the ransomware threat actor over email. Palacio requested the "lowest possible price for the decryptor," the indictment says, before accepting a 0.2 bitcoin offer, worth roughly $13,000 at the time. On June 16, Palacio's business associate reached out to the fictitious FBI-run business posing as the victim, and said the files could be decrypted for $13,260, which the FBI paid. The following day, Palacio once again contacted the fake ransomware operator, which the FBI was also running, and asked to reduce the payment from $13,000 to $4,000 in an attempt to increase the company’s profit.The FBI employee, posing as the ransomware threat actor, counter-offered with $6,000.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> On June 19, Palacio paid the FBI employee 0.0948 bitcoin, worth $6,003 at the time. Five days later, the undercover FBI agent gave Palacio the decryption key. In total, according to the indictment, Palacio's company netted $10,010 in profit as part of the FBI sting.

Numerous legitimate companies are also listed as victims in the indictment, including a Kansas-based business that Palacio allegedly charged $720,000. In that case, prosecutors say Palacio kept all remaining funds after paying a ransomware gang approximately $445,000 in bitcoin for the decryption key.

If convicted, Palacio would be required to forfeit any proceeds and property obtained through the company’s alleged fraud.The case against Palacio is not the first time the FBI has targeted individuals in the ransomware recovery space. In April, a Florida man who previously worked at a cyber incident response company pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit ransomware attacks against U.S. companies. The man, according to the DOJ, abused his role at the company to provide the BlackCat ransomware gang with “confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his company’s clients” in order to maximize ransom payments.

6dd93e791f56c5c8: Welcome to the world of public AI frontier labs: Anthropic is now a publicly-held company with its Thursday IPO, and investors are clamoring for a piece of the pie, for now anyway.

That $83 IPO price didn’t last long, with shares rocketing to $111.50 by the time the public could get their hands on them at the end of the initial auction. That means that the company was valued at around $2 trillion as of the public availability of the 980 million shares it put up for sale, a 34 percent increase over the IPO price.

At just under six years old, Anthropic’s meteoric rise to that valuation has sent investors into a frenzy despite uncertainties surrounding the company’s future profitability. As we’ve noted, Anthropic is on the hook for nearly $1 trillion in compute obligations that could drag its profitability prospects down if any one of a number of scenarios happens to materialize.
Amodei was on hand to address some of those questions with CNBC this morning following the opening of markets on his company’s big day.
When asked about the risk Anthropic’s massive compute bills to its bottom line, Amodei admitted the company’s needs are difficult to predict, and that - get this - they try to err on the low side.

That’s right: The $900 billion in infrastructure and compute commitments that Anthropic revealed in a recent regulatory filing, which could end up surpassing $1T in short order, might just be an underestimate of what the company will need in coming months and years.
Not to worry, though, the Anthropic CEO insisted: It’s worth it.

“We’re willing to put into place these very large compute spends because, historically, we’ve seen that it pays off,” Amodei told CNBC’s Ross Sorkin, adding that the returns on the cognitive capabilities of its new models are “so high” as to make all that spending worth it - eventually, one would assume based on his comments, Anthropic is sure to come out on top.

But what of the threat of open models that could undermine the constant push at Anthropic and other frontier labs to create the most power-hungry, resource-intensive, and powerful AI? Bah, that’s not a problem either.

Frontier model makers like Anthropic, Amodei said, have already proven that they can do the heavy lifting at the bleeding edge, so you can trust it to make reliable models that are cheaper and less capable, too.
“Anthropic can compete both at and away from the frontier,” The Anthropic CEO said.

Whether that’ll mean long-term success for investors is another thing altogether. Mozilla president Mark Surman doesn’t think valuation translates into long-term success, for one. He told The Register this morning that the one thing he consistently hears from developers is that they want AI they can control, not rent from a frontier lab. As Amodei suggested in his comments, Anthropic is aware that those with less intense AI needs might not choose its models, and that could harm the company.

“Pushing AI toward open source matters so much right now,” Surman said in an email. “Mozilla’s own research this year found that open source models account for a third of all tokens, while the gap with the best closed models is down to about 3.3 per cent.”
In other words, keep an eye on that Anthropic stock - it might be hot now, but reality could still catch up to the company with the biggest-ever IPO.
“The market is already moving,” Surman said. “No valuation changes that.” ®
c9454e5a96356183: International Court of Justice President Iwasawa Yuji reads the court's judgment in The Hague on Nov. 19, 2026. Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty ImagesThe International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not. The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar. But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases, particularly the case of South Africa v. Israel. Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. 19, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images What the court ruled Gambia’s case focused on actions that Myanmar’s military government called “clearance operations” in the course of its decades-long violent persecution of the country’s Muslim Rohingya minority. The Tatmadaw, as the Myanmar military is known, justified these actions as a counterinsurgency operation. Yet in the course of those attacks, soldiers were found to have destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages, and to have committed widespread rapes, torture and summary killings. While the precise death toll of the 2017 attacks may never be known, at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians are thought to have died, and roughly 750,000 Rohingya fled to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined other Rohingya in what is now the world’s largest refugee camp of over 1.2 million people, comprised of those who had already fled years of the Myanmar government’s persecution and attacks. The court’s ruling that the Tatmadaw’s attacks amounted to genocide rested on its interpretation of the crime of genocide in the 1948 U.N. Genocide Convention, the first major international treaty approved by the United Nations General Assembly. For an attack to be genocidal, it must be directed against an ethnic, religious, racial or national group, and must include at least one of five prohibited acts: killing members of a group; inflicting serious physical or mental harm on members; deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about its destruction; imposing measures intended to prevent births; or forcibly transferring children from the group. Beyond these factual requirements, genocide requires that the perpetrator specifically intended these acts to destroy the group, in whole or in part. In its ruling, the court agreed that the facts of Myanmar’s attacks met the legal definition of genocide. For the notoriously difficult and demanding requirement for proving the “special intent” to destroy a group, the court determined that the pattern, selective targeting and lethality of the attacks on Rohingya villages could not plausibly be explained as a counterinsurgency operation. Instead, the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the military’s actions, the court determined, was the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya ethnic minority. A series of historic firsts The court’s decision is unprecedented in many important respects. In an influential previous ruling on violations of the Genocide Convention, in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro in 2007, the court found only that Serbia had not met its legal duty to prevent genocide by failing to use its influence to restrain the Bosnian Serb army in the Srebrenica massacre of 1995. In the Myanmar ruling, by contrast, the court ruled for the first time that a country is legally responsible for committing genocide – not merely failing to prevent it. Further, the court ruled for the first time that a country that has committed genocide also has multiple obligations toward the victim group. Those include designing and implementing a comprehensive program of reparations and compensation for victims; creating conditions where Rohingya can make a safe, voluntary and dignified return to their homes; and restoration of their citizenship status after national legislation from 1982 rendered them stateless. Rohingya Refugees cross a river at Tambru, a no-man’s land on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border. Majority World/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Finally, the court also demanded that Myanmar take steps to investigate all those involved in the genocide to determine individual criminal responsibility. Since the International Court of Justice is not a criminal court and only hears cases between states, this order explicitly connects the ruling to other courts where individual perpetrators can be held accountable. These include the International Criminal Court – which had already requested an arrest warrant for Tatmadaw leader Min Aung Hlaing – as well as national courts that may pursue prosecution according to the doctrine of universal jurisdiction. The ruling’s broader implications The court’s ruling in Gambia vs. Myanmar is also likely to have huge ramifications far beyond the case itself. In filing its complaint, Gambia appealed to an innovative argument to establish that it had legal standing. It argued for what’s known as “erga omnes partes,” roughly translated as “toward all parties to a treaty.” According to this line of reasoning, the Genocide Convention imposes such strong legal duties to prevent and punish the crime of genocide that any state, even one that has not in any way been directly harmed, has the standing – in fact, the obligation – to seek legal remedies. In accepting Gambia’s “erga omnes partes” approach, the court opened a pathway for other cases centering on violations of the Genocide Convention. Of these, the most significant by far is the ongoing case of South Africa v. Israel, which charges the Israeli government and the Israeli military of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in the Gaza Strip. Going forward, other nations would now also have a legal tool for holding perpetrator states accountable for committing the most serious international crimes. The International Court of Justice has no enforcement arm. As such, the Myanmar government cannot be compelled to abide by its rulings, whether to cease any further attacks or persecution on the Rohingya, make efforts to repatriate them or design a comprehensive reparation and compensation plan. But even if Myanmar chooses to ignore the court’s specific orders, the ruling is a major defeat. The reputational damage of being the first country found guilty of state-sponsored genocide is likely to be considerable. Further, the ruling will support claims that other nations have a duty not to assist Myanmar in any way that might support or enable further attacks on Rohingya. While that doesn’t automatically mean other countries will fulfill their duties under international law, many are nonetheless likely to use the ruling to bolster multilateral efforts to impose political, economic and social costs on the Tatmadaw. That could include targeted economic sanctions, financial restrictions, prohibitions on arms sales and other forms of cooperation with Myanmar’s government. The ruling thus comes with a potentially hefty price tag for the military junta. Given the general weakening of international legal institutions over the past 20 years, a dysfunctional U.N. Security Council and an International Criminal Court under siege by the Trump administration, the court’s ruling is a rare victory for international justice and opens new routes for international genocide prevention and accountability efforts. Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. 19, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images Before all else, though, it is also a victory for the Rohingya – a people who have suffered decades of persecution. Thousands gathered in their Bangladeshi refugee camps to watch and cheer as the court’s president, Judge Iwasawa Yuji, read the court’s judgment. Camp inhabitants held aloft signs and chanted a simple message as the verdict came down: “Thank you Gambia.” Max Pensky does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
51f4381ba318ead5: NAND flash prices could start falling next year as Chinese cloud operators cut enterprise SSD orders, helping push the market toward oversupply.
Taiwan-based market intelligence firm TrendForce says Chinese cloud service providers are grappling with GPU shortages, high inventories, and fierce competition over AI token pricing.

As a result, they have reduced their total enterprise SSD orders for 2027 by a substantial amount. Although TrendForce doesn't specify any figures, it says the cutbacks in China are large enough to outweigh the additional demand coming from US-based cloud operators.

But don't get too excited: TrendForce forecasts overall NAND flash contract prices falling by 0-5 percent quarter on quarter in early 2027, with all product categories entering a downturn from the second quarter.
Falling orders are only half the story. Manufacturers are also increasing output, while weaker consumer electronics sales could further depress demand.

Strong demand for high-performance storage in the US continues to drive manufacturers to expand capacity and upgrade to newer process technologies. At the same time, the rising adoption of quad-level cell (QLC) technology and increasing number of layers in the NAND chips will further boost bit output, TrendForce observes.

Some suppliers may go slower on their expansion plans in response to sluggish consumer demand, but the firm still expects global NAND flash output, measured in storage capacity, to grow by 25 to 30 percent in 2027.

US restrictions on access to advanced AI chips could put Chinese cloud operators under further pressure. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has introduced new restrictions on sales of GPUs, and on remote access to them via the cloud.
The new restrictions "set everyone back in China," as The Register reported.

TrendForce adds the caveat to its forecast that its market outlook depends on factors such as the pace of inventory reduction among Chinese CSPs, further changes to the restrictions on overseas GPU procurement, and whether device makers continue reducing storage capacities in 2028.

Sadly, cheaper NAND wouldn't resolve the separate squeeze on DRAM supplies. The situation, caused by memory makers opting to produce high-margin products for the AI market rather than mainstream chips, has already increased prices of PCs in Europe by double-digit percentages, leading to a fall in shipments as buyers balk at the cost. ®

2c7821a53685b1bc: A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech company in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes.

Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent.

After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company.
Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war.
While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation.
D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July.

The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the company’s employees.
In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device.

The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims.
D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so.
One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong.
D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots.
The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler.

Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date.
Inside recruitment

The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations.

According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 showed that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US.

Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram.

A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp.

The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico.

Records obtained from Google showed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the company's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints.

The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto company’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers.

Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing.

D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash.

The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco.

The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed company's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed.

Contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else.

The affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept.

These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a New York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns."

He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing.

One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there.
FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being:
The forged ID documents
Two Russian passports
$18,035 in cash
Two laptops
Two iPhones
Two T-Mobile SIM cards
Wi-Fi equipment
A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for company employees’ homes

Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses.
Suspicions and charges

Per the affidavit, D'iu was said to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex.
"D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated.

At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the company he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government.

Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources.
"D'iu's targeting of the company and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine."

The Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®

c24721e4bcb27fca: Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the company insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production.

Equinor, Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, first disclosed the attack on Tuesday evening, saying it had called in the relevant resources to deal with the intrusion and had found no indication that any data had been stolen.

In an update on Wednesday, the company said it had a better handle on how the attack was carried out and which of its systems had been compromised, though it stopped short of sharing either of those details.

"As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading," Equinor said. The company added that it had found nothing to suggest the incident would affect employees, partners, or suppliers.

In a further update on Thursday, Equinor said the attack remained ongoing but did not appear to be specifically targeting the company. Production continued normally, with no indications that data had been stolen or altered. The incident has been reported to police.

What kind of attack Equinor is dealing with remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified those responsible, disclosed whether it's received any demands from the hackers, or said when it expects the affected systems to be fully restored.
The Register has asked Equinor to elaborate, including whether any of its UK operations have been affected and whether the hackers managed to venture beyond its corporate IT network.

Equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told Norwegian news agency NTB that the company hadn't lost access to its IT systems, though staff could have trouble accessing some corporate applications and services. Email appears to be among the casualties, with Reuters reporting that the company's internal email system was down.

Equinor, which traded as Statoil until 2018, is still largely in the hands of the Norwegian state, which owns 67 percent of the company. The oil and gas biz employs around 25,000 people and operates in more than 20 countries.

The bulk of Equinor's oil and gas production takes place off the coast of Norway, but the company also pumps oil and gas in the UK, US, Brazil, and Canada. It's one of the companies behind Dogger Bank, the enormous offshore wind project off England's northeast coast, and is also in the business of capturing and storing carbon dioxide.
Equinor's assurances about production will be particularly welcome in Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on Norwegian gas since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The attack comes just weeks after Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) raised its cyberattack risk assessment to four on a five-point scale. The agency said the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian businesses had tripled over the preceding six months and warned of potential disruption to essential services, including water and electricity supplies.

Europe has already had a few nasty reminders this year of what happens when hackers get their hands on industrial equipment. Last week, the French government pinned a series of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites in October on a hacking unit affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The crooks turned up the temperature in supermarket fridges and freezers, ruining tens of millions of euros' worth of food and starting fires at some premises.

Nothing suggests Equinor's hackers have similar ambitions, or that they've got anywhere near the kit used to extract and transport oil and gas. Given how much of Europe depends on that kit continuing to work, a little more detail from the Norwegian energy giant wouldn't go amiss. ®
