93bf51b7b8a77fda: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “no way”. Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple, Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Continue reading...
f60109a4a5b864ab: JAKARTA, Nov 19 — Indonesian lawmakers passed a long-awaited bill Thursday allowing the state to seize criminal assets even without a conviction, as the archipelago nation moved to address a longstanding problem with corruption. Indonesia, the biggest economy in South-east Asia, has long struggled to stamp out corruption despite appointing a special commission and arresting several high-profile suspects in recent years. On Thursday, the country’s first-ever asset forfeiture law was approved unanimously by parliament, 18 years after it was first introduced. Previously, assets could only be seized from individuals and companies convicted of corruption, lawmaker Habiburokhman said during a plenary session. The final text was not made public but a draft seen by AFP said asset forfeiture without a criminal conviction can be carried out if a suspect had died, was sick or at large, and covers assets valued at a billion rupiah (about RM225,641) or higher. The law covers assets gained through corruption, drug trafficking, financial fraud, terrorism and human trafficking, said Habiburokhman, who like many Indonesians uses one name. An independent body, its members nominated by the president and approved by parliament, will be set up to ensure that the bill is not abused for political purposes, Habiburokhman added. In August, demonstrators rallied outside parliament to push for the passage of the bill. Indonesia scored a low 34 out of 100 on watchdog Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index for 2025. — AFP
5bb1d77a59dc4b5d: SYDNEY, Nov 19 — Fiji and Tonga have declared that severe droughts fueled by the El Nino weather phenomenon are reaching crisis levels in the South Pacific. Drought in the region is strongly linked to the El Nino pattern, which dries up the rains that typically keep tropical islands lush and green. El Nino warms surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in wind, heat and rain. The current El Nino is expected to become one of the most powerful on record, experts have warned. The Fiji government said “the ongoing El Nino drought has reached crisis thresholds”, forcing the declaration of a nationwide disaster. “Families across Fiji are concerned about the availability of water and the impacts of prolonged dry conditions on their daily lives,” Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said on Wednesday. “Farmers are worried about their crops and livestock. These concerns are real.” Under the emergency measures, the Fiji government has the power to ration water, force evacuations and reallocate public funds to disaster assistance. Water sources across much of the country have dropped to worrying levels, local media reported, with scores of trucks dispatched to re-supply parched villages. “We cannot control the climate, but we can act early, use our resources responsibly and stand together through its impacts,” Rabuka said. Tonga has meanwhile declared a 27-day state of emergency as a prolonged drought causes water shortages across the country. Acting Prime Minister Viliami Latu said the declaration would help emergency services coordinate and deliver drought assistance. “Recent reports have shown the devastating impacts on people, water resources, agriculture and livestock, with potential consequences for the health of people across Tonga,” he said, according to local media. — AFP
ea6ad4a562751f40: MIAMI, Nov 19 — Eager gamers in Miami sprang into action as the clock hit midnight on Thursday, diving into the highly anticipated launch of the latest installment of the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) video game. Millions of fans have been waiting for more than a decade for GTA VI, and nowhere less than in the US city that serves as the backdrop for the new edition of the multi-billion-dollar crime franchise. Ryan Jones, a 32-year-old Miami resident, had set up his PlayStation, where a clock counted down the minutes until the game dropped at midnight (0500 GMT). GTA VI began like a Hollywood movie and, almost immediately, placed Jones on what could have been any street in the South Florida city. “It’s cinematic,” said Jones, who works as head of a civil protection office. “It’s the best start they ever had.” Jones was excited at the prospect of exploring the city’s iconic landmarks on his PlayStation. In the world of GTA VI, he’ll do so behind the wheel of a car. “I’m going to jump in a car and explore. I’m going to make sure I open up the entire map and see everything I can”, he told AFP. “And I’m probably going to steal an airplane.” The series lets players live out gangster fantasies, smash up cars and fight whoever they choose in a fictionalised city populated by lowlifes, sex workers and thugs. Billed as bigger, better and more realistic than its predecessors, GTA VI follows a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style couple trying to survive in Vice City, a crime-ridden city modelled on Miami. It comes 13 years after the last full edition broke sales records and became one of the most profitable entertainment products of all time. ‘Surreal’ A few miles (kilometers) from Ryan’s house, a launch party was in full swing at a bar, with staff sporting GTA T-shirts and Vice City’s neon-pink inscription splashed across the walls. The venue set up computers and consoles and handed out caps and merchandise. Even before the midnight launch, fans were already playing the game on Xbox consoles, having gained access by changing the system location settings to New Zealand. The game first dropped in the country thousands of miles away, and is rolling out around the world as each market reaches midnight. GTA fan Alex Martinez said the experience was “surreal.” “I think it has to do with when GTA V came out,” he said, referring to this edition’s 2013 predecessor which shifted 230 million copies. “For me specifically, I was still in my teenage years and it was a foundational part of my childhood,” the 25-year-old said, as one of his friends tried out the latest installment. “Since I’ve lived here my whole life, seeing this is just, like, you can’t describe the feeling,” he added. Near Martinez’s table, 34-year-old Veronica Chicola was celebrating the launch with her friends. A Miami-Dade County employee, she even took time off from work to binge on the game. “I got all my work done before I left today and I’m ready to sit down at midnight tonight and play all day tomorrow,” she said. Like other fans, Chicola said she was excited about the fictionalised version of Miami that serves as the new edition’s backdrop. But for now, she has no plans to indulge in a crime spree or steal a car, preferring instead to follow the story of the main characters as they fight to survive in Vice City. “I’m not trying to go too crazy,” she said. — AFP
95a1e101132c1af6: SHENZHEN (China), Nov 19 — The original documents of the Pardons Board are classified as confidential, but their declassification is not unusual if they are challenged through court proceedings, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim. He said applications or challenges through the courts involving such documents could normally lead to their declassification, while the date of implementation would be determined later. “The original documents are indeed confidential, but usually, if they are brought to court, they are declassified. That was also the case in my previous case. “They were initially classified, but once there was a court challenge. In my case, I did not challenge the Board’s decision; I challenged the process,” he told a press conference after attending the 2026 Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting here today. Anwar said any further questions or issues relating to the matter could be referred to the Cabinet. He was commenting on reports concerning the minutes of a Federal Territories Pardons Board meeting, which discussed granting house arrest to former Prime Minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak and have since been declassified. — Bernama
a153ff01be906453: Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.

The confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it.

The problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like users to migrate to Planner but, by the company's own admission, there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private plan, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not currently planned for the replacement experience," and so on.

Existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data.

Personal Microsoft account holders are left in an even worse state: Planner isn't available to them, including Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers. Microsoft's advice is to choose another task-management app and prepare to export their data. Export instructions are still to come, and exporting won't necessarily produce something another app can import.
Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out."

Unifying tasks and plans is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist (acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme.

Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier."

Some users responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent."
Indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do.
The message for To Do users appears to be: Get with the Plan(ner) or just get out. ®
6922adfa77cdfe45: PONTIAN, Nov 19 — The Johor state government has ordered an immediate halt to land reclamation works at a project site suspected of using construction waste believed to have originated from a neighbouring country at Jalan Kampung Tenggayun, Mukim Rimba Terjun, here. State Housing and Local Government Committee deputy chairman Zaidi Japar said the order was issued following the detection of various regulatory violations, including carrying out works without approval of Form B from the Pontian Municipal Council (MPPn) president. He said the violations identified at the site, which had been active for the past week, included non-compliance with traffic management requirements, the installation of hoarding and signboards, waste management, and carrying out works without Form B approval. “Johor is not a dumping ground for construction waste or a landfill. We are also concerned about technical safety, as the use of such materials could cause the piles to become unstable. “In the future, this could potentially cause buildings to tilt, develop cracks and other structural problems,” he told reporters after inspecting the site at Mukim Rimba Terjun here today. He said the contractor should have submitted Form B to MPPn president before commencing work, but the application was only submitted yesterday and has yet to receive approval. He said apart from the closure order, legal action and fines could also be imposed depending on the offences, including carrying out works without approval. He added that a report on the case would be submitted to the state executive council for further assessment, including possible follow-up action against the contractor. “Stricter action will be taken as it is clear that they have disregarded the state government’s decision. This case will serve as an example to others,” he said. Meanwhile, Johor SWCorp director Zainal Fitri Ahmad said no permit has been issued to allow construction waste from a neighbouring country to be brought into Malaysia. However, the authorities had detected the possibility of a loophole, with the waste believed to have been brought into the country using other permits. Zainal Fitri said SWCorp is currently working with the Royal Malaysian Customs Department and the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry to investigate the matter. He said SWCorp has records of vehicles entering the country, as well as information on the owners of the companies believed to be involved in the activity. According to Zainal Fitri, the site is a newly identified location for such activities, and closure action would be taken to prevent them from continuing. Those involved could also face legal action under the provisions of Act 672, in addition to being ordered to clean up the site and remove all construction waste dumped there, he added. “A notice ordering the site to be cleaned up will be issued this week. We also want the dumped waste to be removed and the site restored to its original condition. “The site owner has agreed to clean up the area, but we will monitor the implementation,” he said. However, he stressed that SWCorp’s priority at present is to ensure that all locations used for illegal dumping are cleaned up and no longer used for such activities. Yesterday, the media reported that 10 lorries linked to several companies had been detected during an enforcement operation at a reclamation site in Rimba Terjun here, which was suspected of being used to dump construction waste believed to have originated from a neighbouring country. — Bernama
dae6f5d8afc635c4: THE HAGUE, Nov 19 — Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the International Court of Justice said on Thursday in an historic ruling, ordering refugees be given safe passage home and awarded compensation. The ruling by the top UN court was the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges have determined that a state committed genocide, and is likely to be seen as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar’s brutal 2017 crackdown. “The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” said ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa, delivering the verdict in the court’s Great Hall of Justice in The Hague. For nearly three hours, Iwasawa laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority during the campaign, which forced hundreds of thousands to flee into neighbouring Bangladesh. Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, Iwasawa said. Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, said the ICJ, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide. ‘Safe’ return The court ordered Myanmar to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence” for those who fled the violence. Judges also told Myanmar it must investigate and punish anyone suspected of committing genocide, providing for compensation to be determined at a later date. While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders. But the ruling will likely heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing. He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup. This year, he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy—which may be complicated by the ruling. The landmark ICJ verdict was also being closely watched by legal experts for clues into how the court will rule in another high-profile case before it—whether Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. ‘I want justice’ For the more than one million Rohingya now living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the ruling offered a glimmer of hope for accountability. “I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor said before the verdict in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family. “There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity. Survivors of the violence brought with them harrowing tales of gang rapes, mass executions, and cruelty towards families and children. Far from the squalor of the refugee camps, the panel of 15 judges has been weighing for seven years whether Myanmar’s actions constitute genocide. The case was brought by The Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II. Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead. “Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein,” its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings on the case in January. The Gambia’s justice minister said the country filed the case “after reviewing credible reports of the most brutal and vicious violence imaginable inflicted upon a vulnerable group that had been dehumanised and persecuted for many years.” The Gambia has the “full backing and support” of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation for its efforts at the ICJ, said the minister, Dawda Jallow. “It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” added Jallow. Speaking before the verdict, survivor Mohammed Osman said he was hoping the ruling would allow him to go back home and perform last rites for his parents and younger brother killed by the Myanmar military. “They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead,” Osman, 20, told AFP. — AFP
24a63d0290cf3133: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 19 — The RM8.4 billion Capacity Charge payable over 40 years under the Bulk Water Supply Agreement (BWSA) between Penang and Perak represents deferred payments to recover the construction costs of a water treatment plant built specifically to supply water to Penang. Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow said the charge, amounting to RM210 million annually, was an “availability payment” for the plant’s capacity. It is a standard payment mechanism in long-term bulk water supply agreements and is separate from charges for the actual volume of water supplied, he said. He explained that the water treatment plant, with a capacity of 500 million litres per day (MLD), was constructed exclusively to supply the Penang Water Supply Corporation (PBAPP), at an estimated construction cost of RM3 billion. “When financing costs and plant renewal works over the 40 years are taken into account, the total amount comes to RM8.4 billion. This figure has undergone scrutiny and review by financial consultants appointed to conduct due diligence on the project. “Prasarana Air dan Irigasi Perak (PAIP) is responsible for securing the financing and bearing the construction risks, while PBAPP is not required to make any upfront payments or capital contributions to PAIP,” he said in a statement today. Yesterday, Bagan Member of Parliament Lim Guan Eng, who is also a former Penang Chief Minister, questioned why PBAPP was required to pay RM210 million annually for 40 years, amounting to RM8.4 billion, despite no treated water having been supplied to Penang to date. Chow, who also chairs PBA Holdings Berhad (PBAHB) and PBAPP, explained that the plant’s construction costs would be recovered through the annual Capacity Charge over 40 years, beginning when water supply commences. This arrangement, he said, would spread the financial commitment over the agreement’s duration, making the payments more manageable for PBAPP. He added that the BWSA also provides for a separate Supply Charge, amounting to RM16.2 billion of the total RM24.6 billion payable under the agreement, which represents the cost of the water itself. Addressing concerns raised by five PBAHB directors who had expressed reservations about certain aspects of the agreement, Chow said they generally acknowledged the need to secure the water supply but had raised concerns over the payment terms. These concerns included the possible invocation of the “Perak State Interest Clause” and the implications of a prolonged suspension of water supply. Chow stressed that several safeguards had been incorporated into the agreement to protect Penang’s interests, particularly those of PBAPP. He said that under the agreement, PBAPP is only required to pay the Supply Charge based on the actual volume of water received that meets the stipulated quality standards. Furthermore, PAIP is required to compensate PBAPP at an agreed rate for every cubic metre of water shortfall or supply that fails to meet the required quality standards, as verified by an independent laboratory. He said PBAPP also retained the right to terminate the agreement and claim damages if PAIP breached its contractual obligations and failed to rectify the breach within 90 days. In the event of a water supply suspension lasting more than three months, provided the disruption was not caused by PBAPP, either party would be entitled to request a renegotiation of the agreement. This could include referring the matter to their respective state governments for mediation. “Either party may terminate the agreement only if the renegotiations fail to reach an agreement after a further three-month period. “In such circumstances, PBAPP would only be required to make a one-off payment equivalent to the outstanding balance of the Capacity Charges, discounted at a rate of four per cent per annum, instead of continuing to pay RM210 million annually until 2072,” he explained. Chow emphasised that the BWSA, which provides for a balanced allocation of risks between PBAPP and PAIP, was a strategic measure to secure Penang’s long-term water supply, particularly as the state’s existing surface water resources are projected to reach full utilisation by 2030. — Bernama
d81b81e8c116927c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 19 — A total of 86 classrooms at 48 schools in the Federal Territory of Kuala Lumpur have been prepared to accommodate six-year-old pupils entering Year One from 2027. The Ministry of Education (MOE), through the Federal Territory of Kuala Lumpur Education Department (JPWPKL), said the classrooms were prepared using the “Modify and Upgrade” (USNT) approach and the Industrialised Building System (IBS). “As of November 17, 2026, a total of 81 classrooms have been completed, while the remaining five, which are being constructed using the IBS method, are expected to be ready by the end of December 2026 at the latest,” the ministry said in a Facebook post today. The ministry said the initiative was expected to benefit 3,820 pupils in three districts, namely Bangsar Pudu (45 schools), Keramat (25 schools) and Sentul (16 schools). Meanwhile, the 2027 Academic Calendar for National Schools and Government-Aided Schools will run from January 4 to December 2, 2027, for schools in Group A states, and from January 4 to December 3, 2027, for those in Group B states. Group A comprises Kedah, Kelantan and Terengganu, while Group B involves Johor, Melaka, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang, Perak, Perlis, Penang, Sabah, Sarawak, Selangor, the Federal Territories of Kuala Lumpur and Labuan, and Putrajaya. — Bernama
c66fd6e4f18db99e: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”
232a74eadf93328f: LAS VEGAS, Nov 19 — Lando Norris is confident Formula 1 bosses are not putting the sport’s 2,000-strong travelling circus at risk by ending the season in West Asia, PA Media/dpa reported. Following Saturday’s race on the Las Vegas Strip, the grid’s 11 teams — 10 of which have bases in the UK – will head to Qatar for the penultimate round on November 29 before a concluding fixture in Abu Dhabi the following weekend. Imola had been placed on standby to host the final race amid the ongoing United States-Iran conflict. However, F1 chiefs confirmed last week that they will push ahead with completing the 23-round season, as planned, in West Asia. UK’s current Foreign Office advice says the situation in the region “remains deeply unpredictable and the risk of escalation is high.” It adds that “British nationals in, or planning to travel through, the Middle East should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” as well as “a risk of further attacks across the region at short notice.” But speaking in Las Vegas, 27-year-old Norris, who won the previous race in Sao Paulo, said: “I am looking forward to going. From my side, I am fine. It is a big team that we travel with, and it is more, ‘what do they think?’ “But I have my friend’s wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there anyway, and then going on to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. “So, from my side, it is not a concern. I just don’t believe that this sport would put us at risk.” The rounds in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled earlier this year, although a ‘Bahrain Grand Prix’ was relocated to Malaysia’s Sepang venue last month. Next year’s calendar is due to begin in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. “I don’t have any hesitation to go or know of anyone that is concerned,” said Mercedes driver George Russell ahead of the concluding two rounds. “I am sure some people have their reservations. But I know people who live in the region, and they have said it quite bluntly, that if they didn’t feel comfortable, they wouldn’t remain there with their families. “There are a lot of terrible things going on in every region of the world, and you have got to trust in the people that say it is safe. F1 are not stupid, so there is zero concern from my side. Fingers crossed it’ll all be fine.” Kimi Antonelli was crowned world champion last month in Mexico, while his Mercedes team wrapped up the constructors’ title the following weekend in Sao Paulo. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen leads the battle to finish as runner-up in the drivers’ standings. The four-time world champion is 17 points clear of Russell and 18 ahead of Lewis Hamilton ahead of Saturday’s night race. — Bernama-PA Media/dpa
4324a80b17abe87b: SHENZHEN, Nov 19 — The death of a student at a boarding school in Perak should be a reminder to all parties of the importance of shared responsibility in ensuring the well-being of children, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim. Anwar said he had discussed the incident with the police and Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek, describing it as something he had never imagined could happen. “This is a matter that deeply troubles us. May Allah SWT protect us and remind us all — parents, friends and peers — that this is an issue we must address together as one big Malaysian family,” he told a press conference after attending the 2026 Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting here today. As such, he called for a transparent and independent investigation rather than relying on existing departmental channels, to identify the actual cause of the incident. He added that the investigation should examine the background and factors that led to the incident, including possible family issues, peer relationships or other aspects. Anwar also questioned the supervision and care provided to students at boarding schools, particularly when students are absent from class or staying in areas such as the sick bay. “In my experience, students at boarding schools are monitored. If they do not attend class, they are usually in the sick bay. Boarding schools have designated areas for students requiring care in the sick bay. “But how come no one is assigned to look after the sick bay?” he said. c97d7de75b39a7c1: SHAH ALAM, Nov 19 — A premises in Puchong, suspected of operating as a non-Syariah-compliant chicken slaughtering and processing centre, is expected to face charges next week for several offences, including offences under the state’s Syariah enactment. 866c236a92cc7cbe: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them.
Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days.
Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable."

News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday.
Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6.
Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days.
The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them.
The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types:
Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames
Business Identifier Codes (BICs)
International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs)
Sort codes
Payment references
Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers
Payee addresses

Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds.
St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach.
The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data."
He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations.

"We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses."
Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services.
Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said.
Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations.
Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time.
"What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said.
Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday.

The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

6fef8c47ef555446: KUALA LUMPUR, November 19 — Forget the blue wave — Bukit Jalil is drowning in an emo wave tonight as My Chemical Romance (MCR) kicks off the first night of The Black Parade 2026 in KL. The TM National Stadium in Bukit Jalil, serving as the tour’s penultimate venue, will host the rock band on November 19 and 20 with an estimated 120,000 fans attending both days. By early this morning, fans had already begun arriving, many clad in all-black outfits, some complete with MCR-themed face makeup and face paint. The hype for MCR has been building since the KL stop was announced last year and despite the postponement that moved the original April and May dates to November, fans are still going above and beyond to welcome MCR back to Malaysia after nearly 19 years. From an MCR-themed running event and an after party to trading customised fan freebies packs, Malaysians are ready for The Black Parade 2026. Twenty-six-year-old Akmal Hady is one of the founders of a Klang Valley-based running community collective called Langgar Limit, and the group recently organised an MCR-themed running event in Petaling Jaya. “The idea for The Black Parade run came from one of our crew members, Muaz, back in July 2025 when tickets first went on sale. “Basically, it’s a short run followed by a DJ after-party at Underturntable in PJ. “We had a great turnout — around 80 people showed up,” Hady told Malay Mail. Hady added that many participants even came in their best emo-style sporting getups with some wearing band tees, chains, boots, makeup and eyeliner. “Growing up, I listened to a lot of emo music, and MCR is easily one of the biggest icons of the subculture. “After going to so many emo night gigs over the years, my team and I finally managed to organise one ourselves — and I’m honestly so proud of us,” Hady said. Meanwhile, 19-year-old Danny is one of the admins of the @fansprojectmcr_msia Instagram page and is currently on a mission to execute a fan project, a hybrid physical and digital fan light-up project in collaboration with a couple of local MCR fan pages, including @mcrxmalaysia and @MCRmymsia. The fan light-up project uses a mix of 20,000 red paper cutouts (printed with QR code instructions for the seating zones) and red-and-blue digital backgrounds that fans display on their phone screens at full brightness. They are asking participating fans to light up their phones or put up the cutouts during several songs throughout the concert. “We started planning about two weeks after tickets dropped last year for the original April date. At first, around 80 people volunteered, but after the postponement, many members backed out quite late. “Now we’re down to about 20 people, which made our original plan of printing 160,000 two-coloured papers impossible. Instead, we printed 20,000 red cutouts with QR instructions mainly for the seating zones, and switched to digital red and blue screens that fans can screenshot and display at full brightness,” Danny said. Danny was inspired to do the fan project after seeing MCR frontman Gerard Way’s reaction towards another light-up fan project at their previous concerts. He even made a new circle of online friends through Aling and Aiman over their shared love for MCR and, having never met face-to-face, the first night of the concert will mark their first real-life meetup. “Two weeks after tickets went on sale, I searched to see if any Malaysians were doing something similar (fan project) and found a post by Aling that barely had any engagement. “I reached out to her and the only person who commented on her post, Aiman, and we started a WhatsApp group to recruit more people. “What’s crazy is that we’ve never met in real life — we’ve only ever talked online, and today will be our first time meeting,” Danny said, adding that the rest of the team consists of members from various age groups, ranging from Millennials to Gen Z. While most fans have been supportive, the team has faced gatekeeping from rock purists calling the project “too K-pop” and questioning whether they are “real rockers” — criticism the team takes in stride. “The reception has been a bit of a mixed bag. “Most people are backing us and sharing our posts, but there are definitely a few calling us ‘not real rockers’ or saying we’re acting like K-pop fans. “Some people agree with that take, and honestly, we get it — you can’t please everyone,” he said. Bringing a heavy dose of early-2000s nostalgia to Bukit Jalil, 34-year-old small business owner Teh Fatimah Md Sidik — founder of custom printing brand Tehreka Studio — is handing out free retro cassette cover inserts and selling custom cassette fan packs across both nights of the concert. Inspired by fans sharing handmade crafts online and the lasting memories attached to physical music memorabilia, she wanted to create tangible keepsakes that would remind concertgoers of the night they finally saw MCR live after nearly 19 years. “I started this project on Saturday, November 14, with around RM70 in capital for 200 freebie packs. “I handled everything myself, from designing and mock-ups to printing, cutting, and packaging and it’s been completely worth it. “Beyond introducing Tehreka Studio, I didn’t expect so many people to love the cassette concept because it brings back their teenage memories,” Teh told Malay Mail. There is no shortage of fans dressing up in their gothic and emo outfits in Bukit Jalil today, and one of them is 31-year-old Nur Fatin Shafiqa Mohd Norman from Batu Pahat, Johor. Shafiqa came clad in a black jacket, a handmade red songket tailored by her mother just a couple of days earlier, along with a black veil adorned with a black rose and gothic-themed makeup. “We arrived in KL from Johor yesterday and we stayed at a hostel in KL and will be heading back to Batu Pahat tonight after the concert. “We arrived at the stadium around 9am this morning because we were afraid that the parking would be full here. She also revealed that she had to wake up at around 4.45am this morning to start dressing up for the concert. It took her around two hours to finish her look today. “I’ve been listening to MCR since my school days. “Even though the postponement dampened the hype for a bit, the excitement definitely came rushing back as the new date got closer,” she said. Tonight marks the first night of MCR’s The Black Parade 2026 in KL. The concert opened with a performance by local rap-rock group Pop Shuvit at 7.15pm before MCR takes the stage at 8.30pm.

11c1f6c108023853: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
e1a149bd991cbc8c: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.

The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise.

"We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident."

TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did.
TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected.

Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over.

Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too.

TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems.

Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back.
"We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said.

TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised.

Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related.
Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

3d858e2a650679b4: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”

a2c0df1404e712c0: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note.

Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see.

During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not.

"Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door."

Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee.

Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries.

The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically.
The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records.

"At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said.

After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in.

The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information.

"The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

6b61b4736011fe25: Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety.

Researchers affiliated with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have analysed 22,096 ULLMs collected from five major LLM hosting platforms.

As described in their paper, "Characterizing the Ecosystem of Open-Source Uncensored Large Language Models: Supply Chain, Governance, and Risks," authors Zilong Lin, Zichuan Li, Xiaojing Liao, and XiaoFeng Wang found that uncensored LLMs are easy to obtain from hosting platforms like US-based Hugging Face, Kaggle, and John Snow Labs, and China-based OpenCSG and ModelScope.

What's more, these unrestrained models have been deployed through applications, GitHub projects, and model routing platforms like Open Router, and users of those apps or services may not be aware of the nature of the underlying LLM.

"Uncensored LLMs generally refer to LLMs whose content filtering or refusal safeguards are absent, removed, or weakened, allowing them to respond to requests that aligned models may refuse," the paper explains.

Zilong Lin, lead author and assistant professor of computer science at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, told The Register that open source LLM hosting platforms like Hugging Face play a similar role to code hosting services like GitHub, GitLab, and Codeberg in the open source community by enabling sharing, modification, and redistribution of code artifacts.

"However, unlike traditional software, whose behavior can often be examined through source code analysis, the safety alignment of LLMs is difficult to assess directly from their model files," Lin explained. "Evaluating whether an LLM has adequate safety safeguards typically requires deploying the model and testing its responses to potentially harmful prompts, which involves substantial computational and financial costs."

Lin said this makes the identification and assessment of LLM safety particularly challenging, particularly given the large number of models available. That's why he and his colleagues chose to study the space through publicly available model metadata.

Even popular commercial LLMs that are purportedly "aligned" – to some standard not everyone accepts – may respond to prompts with content deemed harmful. The US Government Accountability Office just released a report that found Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, and Gemini can be coaxed to provide information that would help with the planning of a terror attack.

To highlight the consequences of AI advice, the GAO points to news reports indicating that generative AI helped enable the creation of an explosive device in a January 2025 attack on a Las Vegas hotel and the planning of a February 2026 mass shooting in British Columbia, Canada.

The issue with open weight LLMs is that anyone with modest technical skills (or just cluelessly assisted by a compliant LLM) can apply techniques like toxic training/fine-tuning (TTFT) or de-aligned training/fine-tuning (DTFT) to datasets that haven't been safe, in order to produce models with reduced or removed refusal behavior. Examples include toxicqa-Llama2-13B and WizardLM-7B-Uncensored. A more recent technique called refusal-direction ablation (or abliteration, e.g., Daredevil-8B-abliterated) dilutes refusal training to make the model less likely to refuse requests.

Uncensored (or simply less restrictive) models have legitimate uses, sometimes ironically because commercial models are insufficiently permissive and refuse legitimate security analysis. Hugging Face, for example, had to resort to using Z.ai's less rule-encumbered GLM-5.2 to analyze the hacking of its infrastructure by OpenAI's irresponsibly unsupervised AI agents.
But ULLMs can just as easily be misused to provide guidance about illegal activity, assist with malware development, or emit content that's harmful, malicious, or manipulative in some way.
"We identified more than 11,000 ULLMs appearing across multiple platforms, with Hugging Face serving as the dominant upstream source," Lin said in a blog post.

"This movement exposes an important governance gap: models can travel more easily than the information needed to assess their risks. Only about 13 percent of the ULLMs we identified carried moderation warnings, and security threat indicators were not consistently preserved across platforms.
"This creates a supply chain problem: a model can be copied across platforms while the information needed to understand its risks is lost along the way."

The ULLMs were evaluated for text output and not images. The issues raised by text-to-image LLMs, such as the ability to generate illegal images (e.g. CSAM), were beyond the scope of this particular study.

"The uncensored LLMs we evaluated were generally more likely to comply with harmful requests and generate harmful content than non-uncensored models," Lin said. "Our evaluation covered 11 categories of harmful requests, including child abuse, illegal activities, and fraud.

"However, the ability of an individual model to generate harmful content varies depending on several factors, including its training data, development methods, and the extent to which its refusal direction has been ablated."

A small portion of these ULLMs (27 of them, which have been downloaded 136,000 times) exhibited threat indicators from security scans. Many of these, authors say, had signatures associated with malware, exhibited suspicious binary patterns, or contained unsafe deserialization mechanisms that could allow arbitrary code execution.
From trickle to flood

The number of ULLMs has been rising rapidly, according to the paper, from about 100 per month in May 2023 to more than 1,000 per month presently. And some of these models have been downloaded millions of times. The uncensored model dolphin-2.9.1-yi-1.5-34b has more than 53 million downloads, and more than 4.8 million just last month.

The authors note that many ULLMs violate the licensing terms of the models on which they've been based, not that source code licensing has had any meaningful impact on the behavior of the AI industry.

Asked whether the safety concerns arising from the availability of ULLMs might prompt a replay of the 1990s when authorities tried to limit the availability of cryptographic code, Lin said, "It is difficult to predict whether model abliteration tools will face similar legal challenges.

"As shown in Section 5.1 of our paper, refusal-direction ablation (i.e., abliteration) appeared in 2024 and quickly gained popularity within the open-source LLM community. Within approximately two years, a growing ecosystem of publicly available tools had emerged to support this technique.

"In the meantime, techniques for both removing and mitigating LLM safety alignment have also become active research topics in academia, with many researchers releasing open-source tools and artifacts to support their studies."

Dealing with the risks posed by uncensored models isn't easy because it depends on divining the intent of the user's prompt. When is a question about terrorism intended as a plan and when is it guidance for writing a thriller? When is a question about hacking intended for theft and when is it cybersecurity education?

The current approach taken by commercial labs — limiting powerful models to favored paying insiders and offering hobbled models to the rest — doesn't work for those left out. Applying some similarly censorious regime to open weight models isn't likely to achieve any more success than efforts by law enforcement to make cryptography available only to "the good guys."
Lin expects that greater transparency, auditability, and verification of models will help.

"As discussed in Section 8 of our paper, our approach to identifying uncensored LLMs relies on publicly available model metadata, such as model cards, to identify models that explicitly disclose their uncensored characteristics," he said. "Our findings demonstrate the value of such transparency for identifying potentially unsafe models.

"Regulatory frameworks have also increasingly emphasized AI documentation and transparency. For example, the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI models to maintain technical documentation covering model characteristics, capabilities, limitations, and evaluation results. Similarly, the Colorado AI Act recognizes model cards and dataset cards as possible documentation supporting AI impact assessments."
Hugging Face, in the process of being acquired by Nvidia, did not respond to a request for comment. Nor did Kaggle or John Snow Labs, the two other US-based companies named in the study.
According to Lin, the research findings were responsibly disclosed to Hugging Face, John Snow Labs, OpenCSG, Kaggle, ModelScope, and Open Router.

Asked whether any of the companies responded, Lin said, "We received a response from OpenCSG, which expressed appreciation for our work on identifying and measuring uncensored LLMs, stating that 'your research is meaningful and supports the development of a safe and trustworthy LLM ecosystem.'"
OpenCSG, the report says, has committed to enhance its service based on the research findings. ®
