06c0f277b32b5cf9: Google periodically tables new AI models named after elements, and its latest offering has the noble name "Neon."

"Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity," explained Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, in a blog post.
Neon emerged after Google last week emitted Hydrogen, after delivering Carbon two weeks earlier and wafting Argon out the door in late September.
Unlike OpenAI's celestial more intuitive model naming scheme – Astra, Sol, Luna, and Terra – which maps celestial position to capability, Google's chemical soup doesn't suggest a specific hierarchy.
To judge by price, Carbon or Argon would be Google's top tier model, based on non-discounted price that takes effect next month, each priced at $4/M input tokens, $20/M output.

The Chocolate Factory refers to Carbon as "Our most capable reasoning model" while Argon is "Our efficient Gemini 4 frontier reasoning model … with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon across complex coding, agentic, math, and science tasks."

Yet Neon, the latest element in the mix, surpasses both in Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, scoring 61 compared to Carbon at 60, Hydrogen at 54, and Argon at 50. At the same time, Neon costs less, at $3/M input tokens and $15/M output.

That favorable pricing is all the more surprising in light of Google's willingness, as of two days ago, to let users of its Gemini services opt out of generative AI model training without losing their chat histories.
Kavukcuoglu evidently recognizes the need to clarify its model rankings, an issue addressed in a blog post section titled "Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family."

"While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency," he explains. "Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently."
That may not really clarify which model is appropriate for which task and frankly Google is fine with that.

As noted, Google Antigravity comes with an Orchestrator that decides how to spend your money for you by swapping models on the fly. As the company describes it, a developer might start a task using Carbon, which would write a plan, and hand the task off to Hydrogen to benefit from its token thrift.

Antigravity does support model pinning, for those who know what they want. But Google, like other companies exploring model routing and orchestration, is fine with developers delegating decisions that affect billing to their trustworthy service provider. ®
74fbfcd64d12556a: In the Guria region, an organization is helping people recover a history the Soviets tried to erase
Originally published on Global Voices
Resort in the Guria region of Georgia. Photo by Tinari.totoro on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Guria is a region in Georgia, situated in the southwestern part of the country. It has a coastline on the Black Sea to the west, which is about 22 kilometers (13 miles) long, and the region is bordered by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region to the north, Imereti to the east, and the Autonomous Republic of Adjara to the south. It has a rich history and a historical tradition of democracy.
Today, in the region, independent media access is limited and digital literacy remains low. However, Guria has a civic tradition that most of its own residents do not know about in detail.

In 1904, locals organized protests against imperial (Russian, at the time) institutions, formed institutions of self-governance, and proclaimed the Gurian Republic, an early experiment in participatory democracy.

The republic was violently suppressed first by the Russian tsarist empire, and later all the memories of it were fragmented further by decades of deliberate erasure under Soviet occupation of Georgia (1921–1991) and by repressions.
This is exactly what the Digital Spark Spotlight project in Georgia focused on: history and memory in the Guria region.
Global Voices interviewed Lika Mergaladze, head of the organization Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, about their project: what they have done and what they learned through it.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Lika Mergaladze (LM): Our organization, Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, works to preserve local history, strengthen civic engagement, and promote sustainable development in the Guria region of Georgia. We use exhibitions, workshops, digital storytelling, and collaborative activities to connect communities with their history and encourage active participation in civic life.

We chose to get involved in the Digital Spark project because we saw an opportunity to combine local history with modern digital technologies. We wanted to help community members document and share their family stories, develop digital skills, and better understand the connection between the past and present. We believe that preserving historical memory and encouraging critical thinking are essential for building an informed and active community.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

LM: One of the main challenges in Guria is that many important historical stories have been forgotten or remain untold. These stories were purposely erased during the Soviet Union. Many families who were the victims of a series of repressions in the 1920s and 30s learned to remain silent about their past in the 50s after World War II. As a result, younger generations often know very little about their ancestors and the region’s democratic traditions, including the Gurian Republic of 1904.

Another challenge is limited access to independent media and low levels of digital literacy in local communities. The dominance of social media and television as information sources makes media literacy and critical thinking particularly important.

We undertook this project to address these challenges by helping local people preserve their history, recognize misinformation and propaganda, and use digital tools to share their stories with a wider audience.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

LM: Through the project ‘From Understanding the Past to the Digital Future,’ implemented from April to October 2026, we organized several activities across the three municipalities of Guria: Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. Our main activities included a public discussion. On June 24, we organized ‘What Drove Gurians Crazy? Propaganda Now and Then,’ exploring Guria’s democratic history, Soviet occupation, propaganda, and contemporary challenges. We also did digital storytelling workshops, an AI and Digital Creation workshop and a theatrical performance: on August 12, we presented “My Days and My Father’s Diaries,” dedicated to Meri Chanukvadze and her father, Amberki Chanukvadze, whose life reflected the impact of Soviet repression. These activities helped strengthen participants’ digital skills, encourage historical research, and create opportunities for community members to share their stories online.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

LM: The project generated strong interest across all three municipalities, reaching nearly 50 community members, with particularly strong participation from women and young people. Locals participated in the digital storytelling workshop, including 12 women. These activities gave participants practical opportunities to develop their digital skills and explore new ways of communicating important ideas. Another meaningful example was the theatrical performance dedicated to Meri and her father. More than 35 people attended and participated in a discussion afterwards. The performance encouraged people to reflect on the experiences of families affected by Soviet repression and the importance of preserving historical memory.

The project also laid the foundation for a cross-municipal network of young people, activists, and aspiring digital storytellers. This network can help community members continue documenting local history, sharing civic information, and engaging in public discussions beyond the project itself.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

LM: Our participation in the project strengthened our understanding of how digital technologies can support civic engagement and democratic participation. We gained greater awareness of the importance of digital storytelling, media literacy, and critical thinking in helping communities understand their history and respond to contemporary challenges. We also explored how AI-assisted content creation can provide new opportunities for preserving local stories and making them accessible to wider audiences. The project reinforced our belief that digital tools are not simply communication technologies; they can also help people participate in public life, challenge misinformation, and contribute to community development. Most importantly, we recognized that connecting historical memory with modern digital tools can help create a more informed, active, and engaged society.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

LM: One of the most valuable lessons was that many people are interested in learning about their history when they are given a welcoming space to ask questions and share experiences. Family stories can open up broader conversations about democracy, human rights, repression, and civic responsibility.

We also learned that practical workshops and collaborative activities are effective ways to introduce digital tools to community members. The strong participation of women and young people demonstrated the potential for inclusive, community-based learning.

Another important lesson was the value of combining traditional storytelling with digital technologies. Personal stories, family diaries, public discussions, and theatrical performances can make historical events more relatable and meaningful.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?
LM: We plan to build on the experience and connections developed through the project by continuing to document, digitize, and share historical and civic stories from Guria.

We aim to encourage more community members, especially young people and women, to use digital storytelling and online content creation to preserve family histories and discuss local issues. We also intend to apply the knowledge gained from the workshops to future educational activities, community discussions, and collaborative initiatives.

An important priority will be to strengthen the network of local journalists, activists, and digital storytellers across Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. By supporting collaboration and knowledge-sharing, we hope to ensure that these activities continue beyond the project period.

c9e737dd8e066bae: HONG KONG, Nov 19 — Tech firms mostly rose today following a record IPO from Claude-creator Anthropic, but trading was cautious as investors deal with the fallout from the crisis engulfing AI titan Nvidia. In a highly anticipated initial public offering, Anthropic priced its shares at US$83 (RM341) each, raising more than US$80 billion, which could rise to more than US$100 billion — topping SpaceX’s blockbuster sale in June. Nvidia’s scandal has compounded growing concerns about the eye-watering sums pumped into the artificial intelligence buildout and when that would see a profit, if at all. Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department’s move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress would impose new regulations. 19d132bfd53eb32c: From MyPower Corporation

As delegates gathered in Vienna, Austria, for the 70th International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) general conference, geopolitical tensions continued to show how events thousands of kilometres away can disrupt energy markets, supply chains and fuel prices.
These are very different challenges, but they remind us of something Malaysia cannot take for granted: resilience and energy security.
How do we ensure that our electricity system remains reliable, secure and cost-competitive as demand grows, while also moving towards cleaner energy?
There is no simple answer, and no single technology can meet every need. Nuclear energy is one of the options Malaysia is examining, and this is not our first time doing so.

Malaysia joined the IAEA on Jan 15, 1969 as its 101st member. Over five decades later, the agency has grown to more than 180 member states, reflecting the expanding role of nuclear science and technology around the world.

For Malaysia, nuclear technology has never been solely about electricity generation. Nuclear science at the domestic scene is always about supporting peaceful applications in areas such as medicine, agriculture, industry, research and environmental monitoring.

We have explored nuclear power before. Earlier efforts included feasibility studies and the establishment of the Malaysia Nuclear Power Corporation (MNPC) in 2011 as the country's nuclear energy programme implementing organisation. That programme did not ultimately proceed as planned.
Today's assessment therefore does not mean Malaysia is starting from zero. Neither is it simply reviving an earlier project. We are revisiting the nuclear question, but in a very different world.

In tandem with the nation's economic growth, electricity demand is also growing. Data centres and new industries are intensely changing the shape of future demand growth. As Malaysia moves towards a cleaner energy system, energy security has become increasingly important amid geopolitical uncertainty.

Malaysia is not alone in taking time to consider nuclear power. Bangladesh first explored the Rooppur project in the 1960s, but construction only began decades later in 2017. Turkey also made several attempts before the construction of its first nuclear power plant at Akkuyu began in 2018. Many other countries have also taken long journeys towards nuclear power.

Closer to home, Vietnam has revived its nuclear power development plan and has requested an IAEA Phase 2 Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review mission, while the Philippines is also moving forward with preparations for a nuclear power programme.
Their experiences show that the path to nuclear power is rarely straightforward. Countries may pause, reassess and adjust plans as national priorities and circumstances change.

Their experiences do not mean Malaysia should follow the same path. Every country has its circumstances. They simply remind us that nuclear programmes rarely move in a straight line. Governments change, economies progress, technology develops and national priorities evolve.

That was the broader context for Malaysia's participation in the IAEA conference from Sept 14 to 18. The scale of the gathering is significant. The IAEA brings together more than 180 member states, and 36 ministers attended this year's conference alongside senior officials, regulators, scientists and representatives of international organisations.

Malaysia's delegation was headed by the energy transition and water transformation ministry (Petra) secretary-general, with representatives from the Malaysian permanent mission in Vienna, Malaysian Nuclear Agency, atomic energy department and MyPower Corporation.

Malaysia delivered its national statement, sharing the country's progress in the peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology, and the work under way to assess the possible role of nuclear energy in electricity generation.

Malaysia has also been elected to serve on the IAEA governors board for 2026-2028, giving it a greater role in the agency's governance and discussions on nuclear safety, security, safeguards, peaceful uses and international cooperation.
The general conference, bilateral meetings and side events provide a platform for countries to exchange experiences across the much wider world of nuclear science and technology.

A key highlight of Malaysia's engagement in Vienna was the bilateral meeting with IAEA director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi, which reaffirmed the importance of international cooperation in strengthening national nuclear infrastructure.
Malaysia shared its ongoing preparations and plans for an Integrated INIR Phase 1 mission to independently assess progress and identify areas for improvement.

For Malaysia, the priority is not deciding when to build a nuclear power plant, but ensuring that the country has the knowledge, institutions and capabilities to make an informed decision. Malaysia remains in Phase 1 of the IAEA milestones approach, with no firm decision yet on nuclear power deployment, technology, vendor or site.

Malaysians will understandably have questions. Is nuclear safe? How much will it cost? What happens to radioactive waste? Who pays for the plant and its eventual decommissioning? Are our institutions ready?
These are fair questions. They deserve clear answers. Studying nuclear does not mean advocating for it. Equally, we should not dismiss an option before understanding what it can, and cannot, offer.

Renewable energy will remain central to Malaysia's energy transition. But our challenge is broader than adding renewable capacity. We must also consider what the electricity system will need as demand grows and the role of coal declines.

The haze during the week of the conference was a visible reminder of our environmental challenges. Geopolitical uncertainty offers another reminder that energy security and resilience matter, too. There is no single technology that solves every problem.
Malaysia's presence in Vienna should therefore not be read as a signal that we have already chosen nuclear power. It means we are preparing to make an informed choice.
The IAEA can provide expertise, international experience and independent peer review. Countries that have travelled on this road can tell us what worked and, just as importantly, what did not.

Ultimately, the decision belongs to Malaysia. Our task today is not to rush towards a reactor but to ask difficult questions, develop our people, strengthen our institutions and understand the responsibilities involved.
For something that could shape Malaysia's energy system for generations, doing the homework first is not a delay. It is simply a pertinent process and a responsible action.
MyPower Corporation is the government agency coordinating electricity sector reforms and nuclear power planning.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

82784f45b9bc8eaa: PARIS, Nov 19 — The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the US and Israeli bombing of Iran has created the “largest threat” to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned today. The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies. The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave “lasting marks”, the agency warned. Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following US and Israeli strikes that sparked the crisis in February. Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the channel — which pre-crisis carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments — supply lines remain severely disrupted. “The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report. He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets. “Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply,” Birol wrote. The report said elsewhere that “increasingly it is falling to consumers — and high prices — to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down”. Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from “several cushioning factors”. ‘No pathway’ back The IEA’s report comes as nations meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal. The agency uses three scenarios for its energy outlook: a cautious one takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario looks at “stated” government policies including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050. In its middle scenario, the IEA forecasts that global oil demand will reach a peak around 2030 before a slow decline, while gas demand would increase until around 2035. For this report, it also adds two other scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists. “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” Birol said in a press release. “And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before.” — AFP

fd4601690c0a7216: PETALING JAYA, Nov 19 — Putrajaya has several ways to safeguard Malaysia’s dual 5G model beyond its golden share in Digital Nasional Bhd (DNB), including legislation and conditions attached to spectrum assignments, says an industry expert. Jake Saunders, vice-president for Asia at technology intelligence firm ABI Research, said the government’s golden share already provides one safeguard. “The Malaysian government does have its Golden Share in DNB, which gives the Malaysian government a vital say in the future endeavours of DNB,” he said. However, Saunders said different policy instruments offered different strengths if Putrajaya wanted to preserve Malaysia’s access to separate technology ecosystems over the longer term. “It is a complex topic. Legislation is a very durable solution; ministerial direction is always beneficial and can help direct and galvanise government agencies,” he said. “Going further, setting out spectrum conditions/ assignments can be more hardcoded. That is, set rights of access and/or limitations on transfers that can also applied for a guaranteed duration of time.” Saunders said maintaining access to a wide range of technologies was important as geopolitical developments, mergers and acquisitions could gradually narrow the options available to countries. “Throughout history, technology innovation has always accelerated in the most open and most diverse markets, and yet mergers & acquisition as well as geo-politics over time can inevitability constrain options.” He said Malaysia was well placed to benefit from technologies emerging from both China and Western-aligned economies. “Malaysia has always been at the crossroads of Asia and the rest of the world, and it would be prudent that the widest possible access to technologies — such as chipsets, smart devices, infrastructure hardware, for data centres, cellular networks, AI R&D and implementation — is kept open,” he added. “Offering a dual technology stack, or lane, would ensure DNB and indeed the wider Malaysian economy has competitive access to all technologies, the wider technology ecosystem and its opportunities.” DNB currently operates one of Malaysia’s two wholesale 5G networks, while U Mobile has been selected to operate the second network. DNB’s network was built by Ericsson, while U Mobile is being supported by Huawei and ZTE. The government is also transferring ownership of DNB to CelcomDigi, Maxis and YTL, although Putrajaya retains its golden share. Switching technologies not straightforward Saunders said DNB could technically change parts of its network technology over time, but replacing an established 5G system would involve more than simply changing equipment. In 2021, Ericsson signed a 10-year contract with DNB that covers an end-to-end network encompassing the core network, radio access network, transport systems, operations and business support systems, and managed services. Saunders said there was greater flexibility in the radio access network, where base stations and antennas could be replaced, although even this was not straightforward. “RAN base-stations and antennas could be swapped out but there would still need to be additional network planning, equipment testing, debugging and integration.” He said Ericsson also supported DNB’s operations layer through a dedicated network operations centre covering functions such as billing, faults, network performance and security. A complete replacement would therefore carry additional costs and operational complications. “A full-on swap out would certainly incur additional capital expenditure, ongoing integration costs, and longer-term debugging and network performance testing.” Saunders said there were also legal and financial considerations, including vendor financing, compliance with contractual milestones and support arrangements. He said DNB could nevertheless change its technology gradually rather than through a single wholesale replacement. Separately, Saunders said DNB would need to continue innovating following the handover, particularly as Malaysia develops its industrial automation and artificial intelligence capabilities. He said future upgrades could include newer radios at base stations in high-traffic urban areas, RedCap technology to support lower-cost devices and industrial internet-of-things applications, and greater use of available spectrum to increase capacity.

e5d8c3d4efd94fea: Burak Kara/GettyThis week, it was revealed that 100 corporations and industry groups tied to fossil fuel interests – including the US multinational ExxonMobil and French energy company TotalEnergies – have sent delegations to this year’s global climate summit COP31 in Turkey. These climate talks have a long history of lobbyist interference. More than 1,600 fossil fuel lobbyists attended the COP30 talks in Brazil last year, and more than 1,700 at the 2024 talks in Azerbaijan. This is a problem. The whole point of these long-running United Nations negotiations is to address human-caused climate change, which is primarily driven by burning oil, gas and coal – the very products these lobbyists are paid to promote. At COP31, fossil lobbyists will have been hard at work promoting fossil fuels. Their methods often draw on what academics call “discourses of delay”. This is how it works. To slow the shift away from fossil fuels, lobbyists spread disinformation, such as claiming fossil fuels are part of the solution (“gas is a transition fuel”), that future technologies will save us (carbon capture), or we’re doomed and it’s too late to act. Oil and gas companies have dramatically increased their Google ads in the month leading up to COP31, for example. Researchers have shown fossil fuel lobbyists use a two-pronged strategy. First, they point to a lack of international action as a reason for not acting on climate change at home. Second, they work to stymie progress at the same international talks. A new UN report says it’s now too late to hold the global temperature rise to 1.5°C. The world will likely pass this threshold in 2030. A big reason for this is obstruction by lobbyists of climate policies that target the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. So, why are fossil fuel lobbyists allowed into these talks? Pushback in Brazil At last year’s COP30 summit, host country Brazil tried to push back against fossil fuel lobbyists. Alongside the UN and UNESCO, Brazil launched an international partnership to counter climate change disinformation and misinformation. Thirty countries have since signed onto the declaration, which calls out the: growing impact of disinformation, misinformation, denialism […] and other tactics used to undermine the integrity of information on climate change, which diminish public understanding, delay urgent action, and threaten the global climate response and societal stability. Lobbyists gain access to the talks in different ways, including through affiliations with non-governmental organisations and industry groups and as part of official government delegations. While this year’s draft negotiating text makes reference to information integrity, there’s still no clear code of conduct or meaningful disclosure of fossil fuel industry ties for the thousands of delegates attending COP31. There are no clear, explicit rules against spreading climate disinformation. COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago (centre) listens to his advisers at the conference in Brazil last year. Brazil has since produced a global roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. Pablo Porciuncula/Getty A long history of lobbying Sadly, this story is all too familiar. For as long as there have been international climate talks, fossil fuel lobbyists have tried to persuade countries not to act with the urgency the science demands. It took more than a quarter of a century of climate talks before fossil fuels were explicitly addressed at the Glasgow COP in 2021. Until then, the focus was on greenhouse gas emissions – but not the fossil fuels causing them. Corporate fossil fuel lobbyists have been assisted by so-called petrostates, such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, whose economies are highly dependent on oil and gas production. And when the oil- and gas-producing states Azerbaijan and the United Arab Emirates hosted the COP talks in 2023 and 2024, respectively, both countries used the summit to push new fossil fuel deals. What are lobbyists targeting this time? There are more than 100 different agenda items up for debate at COP31, many of which are opposed by fossil fuel lobbyists. Negotiators are still discussing a UN initiative designed to rapidly increase efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, for instance. Alongside the official agenda, COP President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum released a separate “action” agenda organised around ten themes. Some of these, such as transitioning to clean energy, threaten fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel lobbyists will likely try to block calls for phasing out coal, gas and oil – just as they did last year, where Brazil’s efforts to formalise a roadmap transitioning away from fossil fuels ran aground. Another concern for fossil fuel interests is the electrification goal, aimed at boosting electricity’s global share of final energy demand to 35% by 2035. If this translates to more electric vehicles, batteries and heat pumps in homes and electric furnaces in factories, it would mean less demand for oil and gas. That would affect profits for companies such as ExxonMobil and Shell. Australia on the tightrope Australian Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen is acting as president of negotiations at COP31 as part of a co-hosting arrangement with Turkey (also known as Turkiye). This represents a tightrope walk for Australia. Domestically, the Albanese Labor government is attempting to speed up the energy transition. Policies such as subsidising home batteries have proven a strong success. More than 600,000 households have installed batteries since the program began last year. Electric vehicle uptake is rapidly accelerating. Internationally, however, Australia remains one of the world’s largest coal and gas exporters. State and federal governments keep approving new projects. Given this, many countries have questioned Australia’s climate credibility, especially its Pacific neighbours. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was heavily criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his opening COP31 speech. Just minutes before Albanese spoke, UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to make fossil fuels “go the way of the dinosaurs”. “The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do,” he said. Can progress be made despite lobbyists? As COP31 enters its final days, the eyes of the world will be on Australia and Turkey. Should the co-hosts fail to get agreement on concrete steps to advance Brazil’s latest efforts to transition away from fossil fuels, many countries will be left disappointed. But despite the best efforts of the fossil fuel industry, momentum for a shift away from oil, gas and coal is gathering pace outside the UN talks. In April, nations attended the first international conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, while the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative continues to gain members. As always, though, much more needs to be done, and quickly. Clamping down on lobbyists and climate misinformation is well overdue. Christian Downie receives funding from the Australian Research Council. William Kakenmaster receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

000c7eec3c44d2c9: Saya kira jika kita bercakap mengenai Umno yang berusaha di Negeri Sembilan untuk membetulkan keadaan bodoh yang mereka sendiri ceburi, kita akan menepuk dahi berkali-kali. Perbuatan Umno dan PAS di Negeri Sembilan sudah terlalu ‘ayoyo dan haiya’ untuk dimuhasabah. Apabila pelajar saya bertanya mengenai pusingan U 10 exco Barisan Nasional dan Perikatan Nasional saya memang kesal. Saya memang berdecit dan menggeleng kepala. Umno dan PAS tidak rajin membaca, dan belajar.

Sepuluh exco BN dan PN yang kurang cerdas itu terdiri Adun Linggi, Mohd Faizal Ramli; Zaifulbahri Idrisi (Chembong), Mustapha Nagoor (Palong), Siow Kong Choon (Chennah), Siti Nur Umaira Hasim (Labu), Mohd Asna Amin (Lenggeng), Mohd Razi Mohd Ali (Sungai Lui), Suhaimizan Bizar (Gemencheh), Mohd Fairuz Mohd Isa (Serting) dan Razali Abu Samah (Sikamat).

Memang terdapat perkembangan baharu susulan surat bertarikh 10 Nov 2026 yang mana Menteri Besar Ismail Lasim bersama 10 bekas exco berkenaan telah membuat pusingan U, tetapi soalnya, mereka adalah pimpinan politik yang dipilih rakyat. Mengapa pimpinan sebegini tidak rajin membaca dan belajar?

Kepada pelajar saya itu, saya menjawab begini; “Betapa bodohnya Umno dan PAS yang berusaha untuk menjatuhkan suami Tuanku Aishah Rohani, iaitu Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir. Bukan sahaja Tuanku Aishah Rohani adalah berketurunan anak gahara, baginda juga adalah anak daripada keturunan agamawan dan bangsawan yang baik-baik dari Terengganu. Ini sahaja memadai menjadi indikasi untuk menimbangkan banyak perkara.”
Umno dan PAS tidak rajin membaca, dan belajar.

Terlalu banyak telah dipertimbangkan mengenai kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz dari segi adat dan lain-lain; sekarang masanya tiba untuk menimbangkan kedudukan Tuanku Aishah Rohani, isteri Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz.

Kiat boleh faham jika penyokong Umno bebal. Al maklum perasuah pun masih mereka sokong, tetapi ahli PAS tidak sepatutnya bodoh. Oleh sebab yang menderhaka di Negeri Sembilan itu ada dalam kalangan mereka adalah Adun daripada PAS, saya ingin membawa pembaca PAS ke negeri Terengganu. Ini kerana Terengganu adalah negeri solid PAS. Terengganu juga adalah negeri presiden PAS. Justeru, dalam banyak keadaan Terengganu ada tempat istimewa dalam kepala ahli PAS. Ya, kalau mereka rajin membaca dan mahu belajar.

Leluhur Tuanku Aishah Rohani, iaitu Tuanku Ampuan Besar Negeri Sembilan berasal dari Terengganu. Nenda baginda Tuanku Aishah adalah Haji Su Mahmud (juga dikenali sebagai Che Su Mahmud). Haji Su adalah anak kepada menteri besar Terengganu yang pertama, iaitu Ngah Muhammad Yusof yang berasal dan bertapak di Kampung Batu Burok, Kuala Terengganu. Ibu Haji Su adalah Cik Teh Fatimah Ali.

Haji Su Mahmud dipandang terhormat di Terengganu yang mana sebelum kematiannya pada tahun 1940, beliau telah mewakafkan kediamannya untuk menjadi bangunan Sekolah Menengah Agama (Atas) Sultan Zainal Abidin (SMAASZA). Beliau juga adalah bekas pegawai daerah di Kuala Berang ketika pendudukan Jepun.

Anak perempuan Haji Su iaitu Zainun-Mariam binti Haji Su Mahmud, berkahwin dengan kerabat Terengganu, dan merupakan bonda kepada Tuanku Aishah Rohani (Duli Yang Maha Mulia Tunku Ampuan Besar Negeri Sembilan). Ayahanda Tuanku Aishah Rohani adalah Almarhum Tengku Besar Mahmud (Tengku Seri Utama Raja Tengku Besar Mahmud Sultan Zainal Abidin III Terengganu). Dalam erti kata lain, Tuanku Ampuan Negeri Sembilan adalah cucunda kepada Sultan Terengganu iaitu Almarhum Sultan Zainal Abidin III, merangkap cucu kepada menteri besar Terengganu.

Memahami nasab dan leluhur Tuanku Aishah baik dari jalur ayahanda atau bondanya ini sangat penting. Ini kerana baginda merupakan anakanda saudara kepada tiga orang Sultan Terengganu iaitu Almarhum Sultan Haji Muhammad II Muadzam Shah, Almarhum Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah, dan Almarhum Sultan Ismail Nasiruddin yang merupakan Yang di-Pertuan Agong keempat. Ini juga menjadikan baginda Tuanku Aishah Rohani bonda saudara kepada Sultan Terengganu iaitu Sultan Mizan Zainal Abidin dan juga bonda saudara kepada Raja Perempuan Perlis Tuanku Fauziah Tengku Abdul Rashid yang merupakan cucunda kepada Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah.

Keadaan ini juga meletakkan Tuanku Aishah Rohani sebagai sepupu kepada Almarhum Sultanah Asma Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah yang merupakan bonda tiri kepada Almarhum Tuanku Abdul Halim Mu'adzam Shah dan bonda kepada Sultan Kedah, Sultan Sallehuddin Sultan Badlishah. Sekali gus menjadikan baginda berpangkat bonda saudara kepada Sultan Sallehuddin.

Dalam konteks orang Melayu, dan adatnya, status anak gahara atau anak raja yang lahir daripada pasangan yang kedua-duanya berdarah diraja atau bangsawan sangatlah mustahak dipertimbangkan. Dalam hal melibatkan pewarisan takhta, anak gahara dianggap mempunyai jurai keturunan yang paling tulen. Justeru, mereka akan sentiasa diberikan keutamaan mutlak untuk menaiki takhta atau dilantik sebagai putera mahkota berbanding anak raja yang ibunya daripada orang kebanyakan (atau bukan berdarah raja). Hal ini adalah untuk mengelakkan konflik di mana pelantikan waris yang bukan anak gahara sering ditentang oleh kerabat diraja atau pembesar negeri. Ia juga merupakan petunjuk kepada keabsahan selain menjadi simbol kedaulatan.

Di Negeri Sembilan soal status anak gahara pernah sekali sahaja tidak dipertimbangkan. Kita faham sistem beraja di Negeri Sembilan mengamalkan sistem pemilihan oleh Undang Yang Empat. Ini misalnya terlihat setelah Almarhum Tuanku Munawir (anak gahara) mangkat pada tahun 1967, Undang Yang Empat ketika itu telah sebulat suara memilih Tuanku Ja'afar (bukan anak gahara) untuk menaiki takhta sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan ke-10. Tambahan pula usia anakanda Tuanku Munawir (yakni Tuanku Muhriz yang merupakan anak gahara) masih muda.

Namun demikian saya tetap percaya jurai anak gahara ini penting dalam masyarakat Melayu terutama apabila berlaku perselisihan menentukan siapakah yang lebih absah menjadi raja. Atas sebab itulah maka takhta Yamtuan Besar dikembalikan kepada jurai Tuanku Muhriz. Jurai yang ‘terbonam’ pula meletakkan keadaan menjadi rumit.

Seperti telah ditunjukkan, Tuanku Aishah Rohani mempunyai keterserlahan jurai baginda dengan cara tersendiri. Baginda bukan sahaja melengkapkan suaminya, Tuanku Muhriz, tetapi menjadikan kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan itu istimewa dengan cara unik. Bukan sahaja kehadiran baginda itu meletakkan Negeri Sembilan bertaut dengan keluarga diraja negeri lain, hari ini bahkan baginda adalah bonda kepada dua daripada empat Putera Berempat Negeri Sembilan. Mereka adalah Tunku Besar Seri Menanti Tunku Ali Redhauddin Tuanku Muhriz; dan Tunku Panglima Besar Tunku Zain Al-'Abidin Tuanku Muhriz. Pemilihan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan mendatang akan dipilih oleh Undang yang sah hari ini daripada Putera Empat.

Makanya, jawapan saya kepada pelajar saya memang valid dan relevan; bahawa ahli Umno dan PAS mesti terus membaca agar pandai. Malulah sudah diundi rakyat tetapi masih bebal. Supaya kita yang sedikit cerdik ini tidak menepuk dahi seraya mendecit ‘ayoyo atau haiya’ melihatkan tingkah laku mereka. Ini kerana dari segi Adat Perpatih, mahupun pertimbangan Adat Temenggung (disokong isterinya), Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir beroleh markah penuh.

24abcf689c6b9b5d: From Terence Netto
Former Sarawak DAP vice-chairman Wong King Wei has advised DAP to stay out of the Dec 12 Sarawak polls, citing the need for DAP to be friendly with the idea of state autonomy for Sarawakian parties.
Sarawakians want to assert the interests of their state after years of deferring to federal interests.
Decades-old reticence about their interests has in recent years been replaced by an assertiveness that Putrajaya cannot but respect.
The intensive battle between competing political coalitions in the peninsula makes the courtship of Sarawakian (and Sabahan) political parties imperative.
These days, the keys to Putrajaya, for peninsula aspirants, lie between Kuching and Kota Kinabalu.

Since the major Sarawakian parties have banded together into a fairly cohesive force in Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS), it does not make sense for DAP to be at cross-purposes with GPS components in the upcoming state polls.
As a single party, DAP may well emerge with the highest or second highest number of parliamentary seats in the next general election (GE16), which is due by February 2028.
No single party or coalition is expected to gain a simple majority in GE16.
This will require one or the other coalition in the peninsula to importune GPS to back them for the right to form the federal government.

DAP, as the anticipated holder of a sizeable number of seats in the peninsula, will be critical to negotiations with GPS, which is expected to sweep not only the state seats in the Dec 12 polls but also the parliamentary ones in GE16.
After seeing how the peninsula Malay vote is solidifying behind Umno and PAS-led Perikatan Nasional, DAP must think strategically about GE16.

Based on their performance in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka polls, DAP's Pakatan Harapan (PH) allies PKR and Amanah are struggling to make a dent in the Malay vote, and are no more confident of the non-Malay vote bank.
Fear of the evolving collaboration between Umno and PAS will keep the Chinese vote with DAP despite discomfort with DAP’s overly compliant attitude towards Anwar Ibrahim.

DAP secretary-general Loke Siew Fook, presently unencumbered by ministerial duties, will have more time to espouse the reforms championed by PH that have been neglected by Anwar's puzzling pussyfooting.
The path is open to a de facto premiership by Loke – by careful rhetoric and subtle gesture – given Anwar's continued tepidity in pursuing the reformasi agenda.
Nuanced rhetoric and statesmanlike gestures by Loke can restrain Sarawak DAP leader Chong Chieng Jen from remonstrating against a DAP decision to refrain from contesting in the Sarawak polls.

DAP should also signal to Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama to be realistic about its chances in GE16, which will require the PKR splinter to go only for the parliamentary seats – 10 at the most – that the Rafizi claque in PKR can win in GE16.
After two underwhelming outings in Johor and Melaka, Bersama ought to come down from the clouds and see that there is no point in overrating its chances.

So, it’s a rearguard action that DAP must undertake, running into GE16, to save what can be salvaged from the growing wreck of Anwar's myopia and Amanah’s failure to convince the Malays that moderate Islam is not a delusion but a viable proposition.
It’s the high road that beckons DAP which also happens to be the pragmatic road to take in the circumstances.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

2baef697661cb837: Dari kemelut tidak ada exco dan tak boleh buka persidangan Adun, membawa pula kepada kekalutan nama calon menteri besar baharu dikemuka kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar ketika menteri besar masih bertugas.

Kalau kita dengar penjelasan pengulas politik popular, Iswardy Morni, akan ada suatu naratif tentang the story behind the drama yang semacam menyokong hujah-hujah beliau. Saya tak mahu ulang di sini, tuan-tuan boleh pergi ke saluran YouTube beliau.
Jadi, apa akan jadi di Negeri Sembilan?

Ismail dan presiden Umno mengatakan mahu menyelesaikan kemelut yang entah siapa mulakan ini supaya rakyat boleh dijaga tanpa banyak drama. Dalam naratif ini, a new slate will be made untuk reset hubungan antara ahli politik dan raja berpelembagaan dengan peletakan jawatan si menteri besar. Sedap juga bunyi skrip ini. Ismail dan 10 orang ahli exco dah buat macam-macam yang mengundang murka Yang Dipertuan Besar -- yang kalau saya pun susah nak maafkan. Jadi baguslah Umno mahu buang yang keruh dan ambil yang jernih.

Tetapi skrip adegan baharu ini belum lengkap. Istana kata surat yang dihantar oleh seorang individu itu datang selepas pengumuman Umno. Menurut Istana, si empunya subjek dalam surat itu tak datang pun maka perkenan tidak dapat diberikan. Tentulah terkejut apabila Istana mahu semak ketulenan surat yang dikirim.

Pada ketika itu, Ismail pun tak tahu skrip apa perlu dibaca. Anaknya bersuara dan berkata dia tak meyakini surat perletakkan jawatan itu. Dengar khabar Zahid semacam menegur anak Ismail dan berkata ini soal pentadbiran dan bukannya soal bapanya. Saya rasa teguran Zahid itu betul tetapi kita pun keliru tentang surat itu.

Ketika kita dijamukan dengan adegan-adegan bercelaru ini, tiba-tiba peristiwa lain mencelah. Tuanku Muhriz memanggil Ismail menghadap ahead of schedule dan pertemuan itu berlangsung selama satu jam setengah. Kita ingatkan Ismail yang masuk sebagai menteri besar akan keluar sebagai Adun biasa seperti yang diumumkan Umno, sebaliknya Ismail melangkah keluar masih sebagai menteri besar!
Baiklah, kita ingat dengan titah baginda itu semua adegan dalam drama ini akan settle.

Tetapi, Zahid berkeras bahawa satu nama sahaja dipanjangkan kepada Tuanku Muhriz untuk diperkenankan sebagai menteri besar baharu, walaupun Ismail masih menjalankan tugas seperti yang dititahkan baginda.

Sepanjang hidup saya, saya ingatkan pemenjaraan dan mata lebam Anwar Ibrahim adalah the greatest unforgettable saga tetapi I must admit drama ini pun hebat juga. Apa yang pada awalnya dilihat sebagai pertembungan antara Umno dan Istana kini menjadi pergelutan antara orang Umno.

Kalau semua sepuluh ahli exco dilantik maka sepatutnya kemelut di Negeri Sembilan akan berakhir. Lantas, kenapa agaknya Zahid adamant untuk menggantikan Ismail, yang kini sudah mendapat perkenan Istana?

Kalau pimpinan tertinggi Umno nak buat skrip lain pun biarlah untuk drama lain di suatu hari nanti, mungkin selepas setahun atau dua tahun. Beri ruang kepada rakyat Negeri Sembilan bernafas, selepas tercungap-cungap kita menonton opera Melayu yang bercabang-cabang jalan ceritanya.
Saya doakan selamat untuk semua ahli politik terlibat dan mengharapkan suatu happy ending -- they all serve the rakyat with great service ever after.

57de9e1d8f19559c: What began as a political impasse over the absence of a state executive council and the inability to convene the state assembly has descended into further chaos, with a new candidate for menteri besar proposed to the Yang Dipertuan Besar while the incumbent remains in office.

It is understood that during their meeting two days ago, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir allowed Ismail Lasim to continue serving as menteri besar. So why is Umno proposing another candidate for the ruler's consideration? Could Negeri Sembilan end up with two menteris besar?
So, what happens next in Negeri Sembilan?

Ismail and Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi have both expressed their desire to resolve this crisis, regardless of who instigated it, so that the state government can administer sans the unnecessary drama.
Now, I fully support what appears to be the sincerity of these two Malay leaders.
As I understand it, Ismail took the first step towards breaking the deadlock by withdrawing a letter seeking to remove Tuanku Muhriz as the state's ruler.
Ismail requested an audience with the ruler – said to be granted for Friday morning – while the 10 state executive councillors withdrew their court action and were ordered to pay legal costs.
The epilogue to this convoluted saga was fast approaching, and the public was prepared to move on to a new chapter.
But, alas, came an unexpected twist in this drama.
Umno announced that Ismail had resigned.
I initially assumed the resignation intended to reset relations between the politicians and the constitutional ruler, starting with the menteri besar's departure.
It sounded like a reasonable move. After all, Ismail and the 10 executive councillors had done plenty to incur the ruler's displeasure, which even I found unforgivable.
So it seemed encouraging that Umno wanted to put the past behind it and start afresh.

However, the Negeri Sembilan palace has yet to verify the Juasseh assemblyman's resignation as menteri besar. The comptroller of the Negeri Sembilan royal household said the supposed letter was sent only by an individual named Hamidi, who claimed to be from a law firm.
Under the state’s constitution, the menteri besar must submit his resignation to the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, and it only takes effect with the ruler’s consent.
The palace's desire to verify the letter's authenticity certainly raises questions about it. At that point, Ismail seemed unsure which script he was supposed to follow.

Ismail's son spoke out, questioning the authenticity of the resignation letter and earning a rebuke from Zahid, who asked why family members were wading into the matter when it was an administrative issue.
Zahid has a point, but the letter itself remains perplexing.
And just as the public was trying to make sense of these conflicting scenarios, another unexpected development unfolded.
Tuanku Muhriz summoned Ismail for an audience ahead of schedule. Their meeting lasted an hour and a half.

We thought Ismail, who entered the palace as menteri besar, would emerge as an ordinary assemblyman, as Umno had announced. Instead, he walked out of the palace still holding the post of menteri besar!
So much for the audience with the ruler being the finale to this drama.
But Zahid remains adamant that only one name was submitted to Tuanku Muhriz for approval as the new menteri besar, even though Ismail is still carrying out his duties as instructed by the ruler.

For much of my life, I thought Anwar Ibrahim's imprisonment and black eye were part of the most unforgettable political saga I had ever witnessed. But I must admit, this drama is quite something, too.
What initially appeared to be a confrontation between Umno and the palace has turned into a power struggle within Umno itself.
Why is Zahid determined to replace Ismail, who now has the palace's consent to remain in office?

If Umno's top leadership wants to write another script, perhaps it should put it on hold for a year or two. Give the people of Negeri Sembilan some breathing space. This soap opera with its endless twists and turns has left us winded – though for the people's sake, I hope this saga finds some closure.

fbe1739af67044ec: The app gives short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of views of VotEDU on the App Store. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Moldova is a relatively small post-Soviet state with a population of three million people. A landlocked country, it has a long border with war-torn Ukraine and Romania; with the latter, it shares the same official language. The territory that is now Moldova was once part of the Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Union, and Russia has been meddling in its affairs.

Moldova has a large Russian-speaking population and a problematic unrecognized territory: Transnistria, which is basically controlled by Russia. It also has European aspirations and was officially named a candidate to join the European Union in 2022, after Russia invaded neighbouring Ukraine.

The country’s most recent parliamentary elections were held in September 2025, and despite the record influx of Russian disinformation and other meddling, elections were recognized as fair and democratic by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OCSE) observers. The pro-European Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) won the elections with a small majority.

The initiative supported by Digital Spark is an app called VotEDU, which answers basic questions about the democratic institution of elections for high school students in Moldova. It does so through short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages: Romanian, Russian, and English, and is the subject of this Spotlight story.
Global Voices interviewed the app’s developer, Vlad Garbuz, about the impact of Digital Spark and his initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Vlad Garbuz (VG): I started VotEDU, an independent civic-education project in Moldova, to help young people understand democracy before they vote for the first time. The idea began at the VOTech hackathon in Moldova. I joined Digital Spark because I wanted to turn it into a tool that students could use in everyday life and teachers could bring into class. The project helped me build the app and begin testing it with the young people it is meant for.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

VG: Young people meet politics every day through their feeds, long before they enter a polling station. In Moldova, many young people encounter misleading claims online. Yet many have very few easy ways of asking questions about elections and getting the answers they can understand.

That made me wonder how civic education could reach young people in the spaces where they already spend their time. VotEDU was the answer. It puts short lessons, simple explanations, and activities on their phones, so they can learn at their own pace.
GV: What are the key changes or activities that you implemented during your participation in the project?

VG: During Digital Spark, VotEDU developed into a civic-education app with nine units, 28 short lessons, quizzes, interactive activities, and a glossary of 136 civic terms. The content is available in Romanian, Russian, and English. All of the lessons have been reviewed for accuracy and political neutrality. Student privacy guided the app’s design. A short guide was also prepared for teachers.

VotEDU was represented at Moldova Digital Summit 2026, where several educators expressed interest in trying it in schools. The app is now being piloted with high school students in Moldova through its web version. It is also available on the App Store, with the Google Play version coming soon.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your beneficiaries and the community you serve? Please provide examples.
VG: Teacher feedback has highlighted the need for digital tools alongside Moldova’s electoral education textbook. VotEDU brings these topics into a format students can explore on their phones.

High school students in the pilot program are using the app and sharing feedback. The feedback tells us how easy the information was to access, as well as appreciation of the app’s design, quizzes, and illustrations. Together with teachers’ suggestions, this feedback is helping improve the content in the app and making it a better user experience.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

VG: I have learned that the design of a civic tool is part of its message. If an app is hard to understand, available in only one language, or careless with privacy, it may leave out the very people it hopes to reach.

Building VotEDU has made me more careful about how I explain civic topics. Each lesson needs to be accurate and fair, while still being simple enough to use on a phone. I now think more about whether young people feel comfortable asking questions and forming their own views, not just whether the information is online.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?
VG: The lesson I will carry forward is to start earlier. Young people should have a chance to understand democracy before an election campaign is asking for their attention.

I have also learned that a good idea needs to be tested with the people it is meant to help. Building VotEDU was only one part of the work. Now students are using it and telling us what they think. Their experience will help us see what works, what is still unclear to students, and what needs to change.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built?

VG: I will continue the pilot program and use feedback from students and teachers to improve VotEDU. I plan to bring it to more schools, including rural schools, and use short questions before and after the lessons to see what students learn.

In October 2026, I also demonstrated VotEDU at MEGAPHONE & e-Society in Skopje. I showed how digital tools can make civic education more useful and engaging for young people, and inspire others to try similar ideas. VotEDU is a project that can be adapted for different countries and topics. Making the project public and accessible is one of my objectives to ensure anyone can easily build something that will bring benefits to their local community.
Written by Daria Dergacheva
1fd2d6e1dc2cfd95: Donate to our Digital Communities Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Images via Canva and public domain.

Digital communications sparked new ways of forming communities: communities that spanned vast distances; that offered asynchronous interaction, innovative forms of constructing identities, and potentially enormous reach. These communities have provided connection for people who are isolated or marginalized, built powerful groups around both professional interests and unusual hobbies, and facilitated astonishing feats of knowledge-sharing and organizing, from Wikipedia to academic sub-field networks to hobby groups and fandoms.

But digital communities bring new challenges as well, from questions of moderation to questions of ownership. Almost all of them are built on the backbone of infrastructure owned by Big Tech — hardware at a minimum, usually several layers of software as well.

This is a risky place to put trust. Witness the sudden devastation when a platform is bought and sold, and what was accessible and inclusive becomes hostile; or the sudden change-to-terms-of-service maneuver, when a company leverages the trust of its users to exploit them for their sellable data. Increasingly hollowed-out echo chambers — toxic or just obliviously navel-gazing — make digital communities difficult and often dangerous to navigate. The proliferation of targeted ads, the risks of rapidly spreading mis- and disinformation, and, more recently, the insertion of large language model bots all illustrate this.

Sometimes it feels like it’s impossible to resist the tidal wave of AI slop and bot content and the all-pervasive mistrust of information engendered by the sheer amount of misinformation and disinformation we have seen produced this decade. But there are still ways to organize digitally.

The same social media that is polarizing Indian society is where young people have organized and continued to organize to resist the authoritarian Modi government. In Brazil, supporters of President Lula ran an organic, human-driven campaign that successfully beat algorithms weighted toward his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the October 2026 election. LGBTQ+ people in hostile environments often only have online spaces to find community and solidarity. People everywhere are rewilding the internet, reclaiming, reviving, and rebuilding communities everywhere in defiance of faceless, consolidated power.

In this month’s spotlight, Global Voices, in partnership with Ranking Digital Rights, will explore the multiverse of digital communities — starting with our own. We want to highlight specific communities, the tools and tactics they use to organize, resist, and overcome the algorithmic pressure from tech platforms, and show how digital communities thrive and persist the world over, defying overwhelming power asymmetries and rejecting pressure to accept the defaults.

20007bd249cf3ed0: From P Sundramoorthy

The Kuala Lumpur police chief's recent directive for policemen to fire when they encounter threats, including situations where they have doubts or feel threatened, raises an important question about the use of firearms by law enforcement in a civil democratic society.
The statement followed a serious incident in Gombak where a police officer suffered severe injuries in a machete attack.

Understandably, the safety and security of policemen must never be compromised. Officers who put their lives at risk to protect society deserve institutional support, protection and the authority to respond effectively to dangerous situations.
However, the broader question is whether a shoot-first approach is consistent with the principles of democratic policing.

Criminologically, policemen operate in unpredictable and potentially dangerous environments. They are expected to protect the public, prevent crime and enforce the law, sometimes while making split-second decisions. Their right to self-defence must be recognised and the government must provide the appropriate training, equipment and support.

Nevertheless, the authority to use firearms carries exceptional responsibility. In democratic societies, the determining factor should not simply be whether an officer feels threatened, but whether the threat is sufficiently immediate and serious to justify lethal force.
Differences in threats
There is an important distinction between a perceived threat, an actual threat and an imminent threat to life.

An officer’s subjective apprehension cannot, by itself, automatically justify discharging a firearm. The nature of the threat, the individual’s conduct, available alternatives and immediate danger to others must be objectively assessed.
International standards, particularly the United Nations Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials, emphasise necessity, proportionality and restraint.

Firearms should be used only in exceptional circumstances, particularly where there is an imminent threat of death or serious injury and less extreme measures are insufficient. The preservation of human life must remain paramount.

A policy that encourages officers to shoot whenever they experience uncertainty or apprehension could have unintended consequences. It may increase unnecessary fatalities, undermine public confidence and expose officers and the police institution to legal or disciplinary scrutiny.
Excessive or disproportionate force can weaken police legitimacy, public cooperation and effective crime prevention.
Equipping our police force

This does not mean expecting officers to hesitate when confronted with an immediate and potentially fatal attack. They must instead be equipped to make lawful and proportionate decisions under pressure.

Police services in established democratic societies generally emphasise structured use-of-force frameworks that incorporate de-escalation, conflict management, communication and alternatives to lethal force wherever practicable.
For Malaysia, this discussion should encourage greater transparency concerning police standing orders, firearms policies and procedures governing the discharge of weapons.
Public confidence requires firearm incidents to be documented and investigated without fear or favour, with independent scrutiny where death or serious injury occurs.
Accountability, however, must not become a mechanism for discouraging officers from taking necessary action when their lives or the lives of innocent members of the public are in immediate danger.
Police officers and other law enforcement personnel have a legitimate right and responsibility to protect themselves and the public.

When confronted with an imminent and serious threat, particularly an armed attack capable of causing death or grievous injury, they must have the authority and confidence to act decisively, including using lethal force where it is legally justified and necessary.
They should not be expected to expose themselves or innocent people to avoidable danger because of uncertainty about their authority to defend life.

Continuous training in firearms and the use of lethal force is essential. It must not be treated as a one-off exercise during basic training but be ongoing, regularly assessed and updated to reflect changing criminal threats, operational realities, technological developments and international best practices.

The SOPs governing firearms and lethal force must also be reviewed periodically and updated whenever necessary. They should clearly explain the circumstances in which firearms may be used, officers’ responsibilities, reporting requirements and post-incident procedures.
Ambiguous instructions place officers and the public at risk; clear, practical guidance is indispensable.

Ultimately, protecting police officers and protecting the public are not competing objectives. They are complementary responsibilities of a professional law enforcement service. Officers must not be expected to sacrifice their lives unnecessarily, nor should the public face an unrestricted use of lethal force.
The question is therefore not simply whether police should shoot or not. It is whether the circumstances legally, reasonably and objectively justify lethal force.

In a civil democratic society, officers must be decisive when confronting genuine and imminent threats to life, while restraint, professionalism, continuous training and accountability remain integral to the exercise of their authority.
The legitimacy of policing depends not merely on the ability to use force but on knowing when its use is justified and when it is not.
P Sundramoorthy is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research at Universiti Sains Malaysia.

ebc1d416786ba303: Microsoft's Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core. Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency's (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG).

STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: "The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened."
The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.
