ea2a682fdbb547e1: At The Money: Shopping Under Surveillance (November 18, 2026)

Ever feel like your most-used apps and favorite companies are playing games with you? Price changes from airlines, delivery services, and even Amazon seem to be all over the map. What does this mean for your wallet? L
Full transcript below.
About this week’s guest:
Lindsay Owens is CEO of the Groundwork Collaborative, a DC-based economic think tank and author of a new bestseller, “Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—and What That Means for Your Wallet.”
For more info, see:
Professional website
LinkedIn

Find all of the previous At the Money episodes here, and in the MiB feed on Apple Podcasts, YouTube, Spotify, and Bloomberg. And find the entire musical playlist of all the songs I have used on At the Money on Spotify
Transcript: Lindsay Owens, CEO of Groundwork Collaborative

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Ever feel like your most used apps and companies are playing games with you? Price changes from airlines, delivery services, even Amazon seem to be all over the map. What does this mean for your wallet?

To help us unpack all of this, let’s bring in Lindsay Owens. She’s CEO of Groundwork Collaborative. She’s also the author of a new book, Gouged: The End of a Fair Price and What That Means for Your Wallet. So let’s start out with some of the basics of surveillance capitalism and surveillance pricing that you describe in the book. Essentially, algorithms collecting all this data to try and guess what your willingness to pay might be.
Are we basically in a place where a price on the shelf for everybody, is that just a historical relic?

LINDSAY OWENS: Look, we’ve had price tags for almost 150 years now in this country. You know, for thousands of years we haggled. You went to the market, you picked out what you wanted, and then a negotiation commenced. But in the late 1800s, the Quakers felt like that wasn’t quite right. They thought haggling was unfair, all men should be treated equal, and they dispensed with the kind of greedy way that the Puritans were haggling, and they decided to use a fixed price.

And shortly after that, it was John Wanamaker, the iconic Philadelphia retailer, in his Wanamaker’s department store. He put the price tag on items for the first time, and we’ve been living under that kind of cultural and economic regime for nearly 150 years. But these days, I think the transparency and the predictability that a price tag provided is really under attack and at risk of extinction. Prices are changing, prices are more volatile, thanks to electronic shelf labels and algorithmic pricing. Prices are more deceptive. Sometimes you and I are charged different amounts for the same item thanks to personalized pricing or surveillance pricing.
So it really is a new frontier of pricing, and I would argue a new frontier of corporate profiteering.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. So let’s talk about some of the things that consumers can do, especially when it comes to online shopping or app shopping. What can we do to enhance our own digital privacy? How can we prevent stores from cranking up prices on us because of either where we live or our shopping history or any other information they know about us from online?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah. So the first thing I’ll say is, you know, I really don’t believe that it should be all of our jobs to duck and dodge and bob and weave and figure out how to beat the machine. I think we need fair and honest markets and fair and honest prices, and I think it’s the job of lawmakers to ensure that. But I also used to be a Hill staffer, so I know waiting around for Congress is not always your best bet.

So there are some things you can do. The first thing I like to say is they learn how much they can overcharge you by running experiments on you. Turn the experiment back around on them. You know, if you’re gonna buy your Christmas airplane tickets this year to go home and see Mom, sit down with your husband or your spouse and, you know, both of you fire up your computers at the same time and see if one of you gets a better deal on the tickets. There’s a good chance the ticket prices will be different for each of you. Go with whoever gets the cheapest price.

If you’re leaving a football game this weekend with a few friends and you’re gonna take an Uber home because you’ve had a couple beers, everyone fire up the Uber app at the same time, and probably one of you will get charged a lower price for the same ride to the same destination. Go with whoever gets the lower price. There is, I think, a simplicity in turning their experiments back around on them.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: A lot of us use loyalty programs. How do companies use the data for these programs where we think we’re getting a deal? How is that used against us?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, this is one of the saddest parts of the book, which is the revelation that you might be at risk of a loyalty penalty for using loyalty programs, right? You get really excited when you join a loyalty program in the beginning, ’cause you get promised all these perks and freebies and these inducements that get you to kind of hand over your data and shop attached to your loyalty card. But what we have started to see is the problem of the loyalty penalty. Once a company knows what you purchase on a regular basis, they figure that you’re a sure thing and they no longer need to push you any of those offers or discounts.

And there’s an example in the book from a Washington Post reporter who lived in a state that allowed him to request his data from Starbucks, and he got the 55-page report. And he learned that over time, as Starbucks knew he was a sure thing, he didn’t get any perks or freebies or discounts anymore. There was also a reporter recently from Wired magazine who requested his McDonald’s app data, by the way, so that was like a 500-page dossier.

I got to talk to him and I was like, I’m so excited to meet the Hamburglar. Like, you are really a serious customer. But one of the interesting things in his reporting was that McDonald’s had calculated this lifetime attrition score. Like, how likely is he to, like, you know, leave McDonald’s and go shop somewhere else, like Burger King? And his attrition score was zero.

They were like, he is absolutely hooked on McDonald’s. But these companies do use the data that they collect about you in loyalty programs, and they are pretty sophisticated data-harvesting operations in pricing and promotion decisions. And you can end up being penalized once they’ve got a full sense of your likely purchase history. The other thing they do, of course, which you may or may not care about, is they often bundle up your data and sell it, increasingly.

Companies like Kroger, you know, where 95% of transactions are attached to loyalty programs, they have an alternative profits book of business that is 30% of their net operating income. And a big piece of that is the sale of your data. So loyalty programs are a bit of a double-edged sword, I’d say.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. Tell us about dark patterns and drip pricing. Are companies really doing last-minute fees tacked on when you’re about to engage in a transaction?

LINDSAY OWENS: Oh yes. So drip pricing is the worst. It’s this practice of sort of luring you in with a teaser rate or a low initial price only to tack on, throughout the remainder of the transaction, drip, drip, drip, other fees, such that the total price you pay at the end is much higher than the teaser rate.

This is also, in some settings, called unbundling. Something that you’ve certainly experienced in the airlines, where, you know, the fare no longer includes things like your luggage or picking a seat, right? You have to pay extra for that. So, you know, drip pricing and junk fees are really tough, and they’re made much easier to use to exploit you in e-commerce because of things like dark patterns, the ways in which companies can manipulate user interfaces and make design choices that make it hard for you to see, you know, that these fees have been tacked on throughout the transaction.

We do, thanks to the Federal Trade Commission rulemaking that happened at the end of the Biden administration, now prohibit drip pricing in two sectors of the economy. So instead, you have to see the full and total price upfront. The first sector is short-term lodging. So if you’ve picked up an Airbnb or a Vrbo recently, you probably noticed that you can now see the full price of a week’s stay, inclusive of things like cleaning fees and stuff like that that used to be tacked on at the end.

And we also now require upfront pricing, or all-in pricing, in event ticketing. So you can see, you know, when you hover over a seat to pick a concert seat, you now see the full price of the ticket, not just the price of the seat. So it includes the price of the fees, and, you know, it doesn’t make the price any cheaper, but it does allow you to do a better job of comparison shopping, and it makes it such that you at least know the full price that you’re paying upfront before you start the transaction.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: What about subscription traps and roach motels? I have a handful of subscriptions and every now and then I try and cancel ’em and I get nowhere. Fortunately, I have a good relationship with my bank. We use the same corporate and personal bank, and when I say, “Hey, this is a fraud, they won’t let me cancel, stop paying this.” They’ve been pretty good about that, but I don’t think everybody has the same access to their private banker. What can you do about subscription traps and getting outta the roach motels?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, this is a tough one. A couple times in my life I’ve really been buried under subscriptions. Once when I was in high school, and I got pretty deep with the Columbia House records subscription programs,
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Everybody. Right? Hilarious.
LINDSAY OWENS: Oh man. It was just like, you know, you’re in
BARRY RITHOLTZ: High school. If you were in high school, you were a minor, you didn’t have contractual ability, and you could just send them a nasty letter.

LINDSAY OWENS: And that’s what I did. That’s in law school, I dealt with my Columbia Record House debt. I’m like, “Sorry, didn’t have contractual capacity as a 14-year-old. Bye-bye.” So eventually, but, you know, most times you don’t get that.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: And they were actually pretty good about canceling. You just had to remember to send the card in on time, and nobody did.

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah. The tough thing about the Columbia House was the negative option billing. So you picked out two discs at full price and then you got 12 discs for a penny. But then they would send you some discs that you didn’t select, and if you forgot to send them back, you had to pay full price for those too. So you could really end up kind of snowed under a pile of CDs. The other time in my life where I really got into trouble on subscriptions was right after I had my baby, and, you know, you’re not sleeping, you’ve got a lot going on.

And I ended up in a subscription for, like, a developmentally appropriate toy service. And actually it was a gift from a friend. She gave me three toy boxes, and at some point, like a year into my son’s life, I was like, why am I still getting these toy boxes? And I realized my friend had gifted me three months, but they had started charging me for them.
Right. So I think, you know, even though you never signed anything, you never agreed to anything. No, no. Oh, it was unbelievable.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: That’s an easy letter, CC’d to the state attorney general, and that’s the end of that. But still, I mean, good luck. What about the fact that these companies no longer have customer service branches? If you want to cancel satellite or cable, if you want to change something on your phone, it’s an hour of your life. It’s pretty horrendous.

LINDSAY OWENS: Yes. My organization has released model legislation that we call the Shopper’s Bill of Rights, and it includes 12 rights that we think shoppers should be guaranteed in the e-commerce and agent commerce era. And two of them include the right to a refund on the same payment method that you initially purchased it on, without battling a chatbot for three hours, and the right to cancellation the same way you signed up. If they auto-populated your address and your credit card information on the way in with one click, you can get out of that subscription with one click.

And New York City, actually, just about a week ago, implemented a click-to-cancel rule in the city. So companies operating in New York City have to give folks the same method of cancellation that they get for signing up for a subscription.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Let’s talk about something that’s kind of fascinating to me: the right to repair. So what started happening with everything from computers and printers to farm equipment, the company said, “You can’t fix this, you have to bring it back to us, and we’re gonna charge you an arm and a leg to do basic repairs,” or even things like buying cheaper toner for your printer. What about the right to repair and the right to shop for the components of that product?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, I think a lot of people are surprised to see this included in my book because they don’t always think of that kind of thing when they think of price gouging. But I absolutely think restraint of repair is a form of price gouging, and arguably a real daisy chain of price gouging, because they can, you know, charge you an arm and a leg for the initial product, then they charge you again for proprietary parts, then they might charge you again for proprietary labor, where, you know, you can’t fix it yourself, and maybe if you can’t fix it at all, you have to buy it again. So increasingly, companies use technology to make it hard to repair items. Car companies, you know, with engine control units that make it hard for, you know, your mechanic up the street to access what they need to fix your car.

John Deere, the tractor company, a real kind of corporate villain in the right-to-repair space, made it impossible for farmers to repair their combines, which, you know, makes it hard if it’s harvest season. You gotta wait for their dealer to come out and their repair shop to come out and fix it. There is an example in the book of the McDonald’s McFlurry. If you’ve ever wondered why you can always get french fries, but somehow the ice cream machine is always broken.

Well, it’s because Taylor Commercial Food Services, who owns the McFlurry machines, doesn’t let McDonald’s franchisees repair them themselves. So, you know, lots of these types of examples in the book, and, you know, thankfully there is, I think, a really burgeoning consumer movement around what we call the right to repair your own stuff. It’s run by a guy named Nathan Proctor at U.S. PIRG, the Public Interest Research Group, and they’ve had some big wins, including some memorandums of understanding with John Deere and even some movement at the federal level from the Federal Trade Commission on John Deere.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yeah, my experience with toner and printer was, one day I was about to order yet another cartridge for an HP laser printer, and I’m like, wait a second, I’ve paid something like 5x the cost of this printer. Let me use AI to find what’s a better alternative. And I ended up with, I went from an HP, I think it was an HP inkjet, to a Brother laser, unless I have it backwards, a Brother inkjet, whatever it was. The cartridges are like a fraction of the cost of the unit and are likely to be around that way for a long time.

But there was a thing a while ago where you could buy these just generic printer toner refills, and when HP figured that out, they would brick your printer, meaning it would just freeze and be dead. And that was it. How much control over our devices do manufacturers have, and what could we do about that?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, I mean, technically it’s illegal to void your warranty if you repair your own stuff. But we see examples all the time of companies threatening to void your warranty if you make repairs. So that’s one sort of form of retribution companies can impose. There are also some examples in the book of things like, you know, the Keurig coffee machine not working if you insert a non-Keurig brand cup, or the K-Cup, you know, or the GE refrigerator no longer spitting out water if you use a non-GE water filter.
Things like that. And, you know, there’s been a lot of litigation in this space, which has been helpful in kind of, I think, pushing back against some of this corporate overreach.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. Let’s talk about the power of public backlash. I remember not too long ago BMW proposed making the heated seats, like, a monthly subscription. I called my local dealer and said, “Cancel my deposits and gimme my money back. Cancel that deal. Take me off your list. You lost me as a BMW customer.” I’m wondering — and then there was an issue with Wendy’s with some of their pricing shenanigans. How significant is public backlash?

LINDSAY OWENS: Hugely, hugely significant. I mean, I really think one of the quickest ways that we can discipline companies who go too far with their pricing practices is to scream and yell and, like, share and tweet, right? It is absolutely the case that consumer backlash is a powerful force in convincing companies to go in a different direction. Voting with your wallet matters.

And throughout history, we’ve seen so many examples of consumer backlash really changing corporate behavior. One of the examples I love to talk about, which I include in the book, is, you know, actually in the mid-1990s, the CEO of Coke said in an offhanded interview to a Brazilian magazine that Coke was piloting installing thermometers in their vending machines — again, this was in the nineties — to hike the price of a Coke on a hot day. And he said he thought it was reasonable people would pay more on a hot day for an icy cold Coke out of the vending machine.

And it was the shot heard around the world. It was on the cover of every major newspaper. People were ticked about this, and they immediately had to walk it back. I mean, Pepsi really seized on the PR gaffe and, you know, saw their moment for an advantage, and Coke walked it back. And we saw that happen with Delta. Their partnership with Fetcherr was revealed by my organization, and, you know, Southwest and American jumped on it.

And I think that was a big part of why Delta walked back some of their plans. Obviously with the Instacart study my organization helped conduct, you know, consumer backlash was critical there. Two weeks later, you know, corporate issued a letter saying they would not use these practices. So I actually do think the quickest way to immediate action, by far, is consumer backlash.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s talk about a couple of companies that you spotlight as doing things right, like maintaining a cap on markups or freezing prices. One of the most obvious examples that comes to mind is Costco, pretty much universally beloved by their clients. What are they doing right?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah. So Costco is a little bit of a tricky example, but I use it in the book because I still think it’s a good one. I mean, their business model is a little different. They make a lot of their money from the subscription, the membership that you pay to shop in Costco.

But they do have a threshold on how much markup they will charge above their input costs. And they cap it at, I think it’s 14%. It depends. It varies a little if it’s a generic product, one of their own products, or if it’s a third-party product, but it’s a cost-plus pricing model.
62626f8cbcfd5bbe: Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability, for tasks like precision agriculture or search-and-rescue. But these featherweight microrobots couldn’t carry the electronics needed for navigation, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab. Now, the researchers have designed a flapping-wing microrobot with onboard sensors and computation, which can follow a complex trajectory and land precisely on a sunflower outside the lab’s motion capture environment. While the robot is still connected to an offboard power source, this demonstration highlights the potential of aerial microrobots to be used for precision agriculture in the future.  For instance, flying microrobots could weave through a field of almond trees or blueberry bushes to carefully pollinate delicate blossoms in regions where natural pollinator populations have been decimated by habitat loss. They could also hover near plants without causing damage, monitoring crop health and spotting pests before they become widespread. To enable onboard sensing and computation, the researchers developed a method to expand the artificial muscles that power the robot’s wings, increasing the net payload so the tiny robot could carry the necessary electronics. They also designed a sensor suite that can rapidly estimate the robot’s position and orientation without relying on an offboard motion capture system, and a miniature electronics package to securely hold the tiny computational components on the nimble vehicle. “This is a really important milestone for the research community. This is the first demonstration of an aerial microrobot that is sensory and compute autonomous. There are many situations, like pollination or industrial surveillance, where you can’t use a larger robot. Small-scale robots are uniquely positioned for these types of tasks, and if this thread of technology becomes successful in the future, it could be very promising,” says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-corresponding author of a paper on the robot. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Yi-Hsuan (Nemo) Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu, and Zhongtao Guan; co-corresponding authors Jonathan P. How, a Ford Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) and the Aerospace Controls Laboratory (ACL) at MIT; Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, an assistant professor at Cornell University; and others at MIT. The research appears today in Science Robotics. Increasing the payload The MIT researchers previously developed a swift, agile aerial microrobot with four wings, each powered by a set of soft actuators, or artificial muscles, that flap the wings rapidly so the bot can perform detailed maneuvers.  The robot, roughly the same size and shape as a microcassette, weighs less than a paperclip. To bring this tiny robot closer to real-world applications, the researchers need it to carry the additional weight from electronics for onboard sensing and computation, while still being fast, maneuverable, and robust to collisions. In this research, they developed a method to scale up the artificial muscles without hampering the robot’s performance. They carefully tuned the radius and length of the soft actuators, increasing their size by 50 percent while boosting the robot’s net lift forces by 46 percent.  “It is very difficult to scale up the actuators without causing the output power of the system to go down, which reduces the lift forces. We tuned the geometry of the robot very precisely so lift proportionally increases with the additional actuator weight,” Chen explains.  They were able to achieve a lift-to-weight ratio of 1.9, giving the robot more than enough lift force to carry the onboard electronics package they developed, which weighs only 244 milligrams.  The tiny electronics package contains the sensors, and microcontroller needed for onboard sensing and computation.  The researchers incorporated an inertial measurement unit to estimate attitude, an optical flow sensor to estimate lateral flight speed and position, and a time-of-flight sensor to measure height. But without the precision of the attached motion capture system, the robot does not know its absolute position, causing it to drift off course. Speedy sensing To overcome this challenge, the team designed a sensing algorithm to calculate the robot orientation, angular velocity, and position extremely quickly, simplifying the calculations to reduce the computational cost. They found that estimating position continuously at a faster rate yielded higher performance than a more accurate, slower estimation. “We spent a lot of time optimizing the selection of the sensors and position estimators so the robot would have very low drift. Our robot can now fly with positional accuracy that is comparable to flying with offboard cameras,” says Hsiao.  They integrated the sensors and computing components into a tiny electronics package, which they attached to a fiberglass substrate so it wouldn’t be thrown off by vibrations of the robot. “When you are talking about a computer which is that small, everything must be thought through carefully. There are so many factors to consider; it must do both perception and control, while fitting onto the robot and running fast enough that the vehicle will remain stable during flight,” How says. They tested the offboard computation capabilities of the aerial microrobot through a series of flight demonstrations, including hovering at different heights and following point-to-point trajectories. The robot maneuvered quickly and precisely, with positional errors of only a few centimeters. In addition, they demonstrated the robot’s potential for artificial pollination by using a joystick to send high-level position setpoints, guiding the aerial vehicle around several plants before carefully landing on a sunflower.  “This is quite difficult to do, even if you do have a motion-capture system,” Hsiao says. The researchers analyzed the vehicle’s power expenditures and found the electronics only consume about 6 percent of the total power, with the rest fueling the robot’s artificial muscles and wings.  They identified ways to further reduce power consumption from the electronics. This would allow for the addition of more components, like a camera that would enable the robot to recognize objects. The researchers are now working toward two goals: putting a camera onboard for autonomous object recognition and obstacle avoidance; and integrating power electronics and batteries onto the tiny robot, which would enable untethered flight in an outdoor environment.  This research was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), U.S. Office of Naval Research, U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and a Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

8fd900d387a7f388: Getting information does not equate to accessing justice
Originally published on Global Voices
Image courtesy the Hague Institute for Innovation in Law
By Zainab Malik

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine a woman facing eviction who turns to an AI chatbot for help. It explains her rights and drafts a letter to her landlord. But she cannot afford a lawyer, does not know where to submit the letter and has no institution that can enforce her rights fairly. The chatbot has made the law easier to understand, but has it brought her any closer to justice?

A September 2026 study by UK organization JUSTICE and the Administrative Fairness Lab found that one in six UK respondents who had experienced a legal dispute had used an AI chatbot. Researchers examined 77 conversations involving questions about rights, legal correspondence, complaints and court proceedings. Yet they could not establish whether these interactions helped resolve the disputes. We know more about how people use AI for legal help than whether it changes their circumstances.

That distinction matters. An estimated 1.5 billion people worldwide cannot obtain justice for their problems. HiiL’s Justice Needs Surveys, covering more than 150,000 people across 20 countries, show that only around four in 10 achieve a fair resolution. AI could help address this gap, but it is important to understand where its contribution begins and ends.
The promise of AI for justice seekers

People facing legal problems may not know whether what happened to them is unlawful, where to seek help or how to navigate an unfamiliar process. Legal advice is expensive, services can be difficult to reach, and institutions intimidating.

Purpose-built AI tools can explain rights clearly, organize information, prepare documents and identify relevant services. Voice-based tools may also reach people with limited literacy or without smartphones or reliable internet.

Early pilots are yielding promising results. In Australia, Hear Me Out, developed by the National Justice Project and the University of New South Wales, helps people identify the appropriate complaints body, understand the process and prepare supporting documents. Its pilot assisted more than 400 complaints, helping people turn experiences of injustice into complaints that can be pursued. In Nigeria, Citizens’ Gavel’s Podus AI helps people understand their legal rights, draft petitions and complaints, and identify the government agencies responsible for addressing them. Since its launch in March 2024, the platform has onboarded more than 33,000 users.
These are meaningful developments. But the number of tools and people assisted tells us only part of the story. What happens after someone submits a complaint?
When an answer is not a resolution

Understanding rights does not mean being able to exercise them. A tenant may know an eviction is unlawful but have nowhere to turn; a small business owner may prepare a claim but lack the means to pursue it. A person experiencing domestic abuse may face practical, financial or safety barriers to seeking protection.

Another challenge is getting the other party to participate. In dispute resolution, this is known as the “submission problem,” a concept developed by economists William Landes and Richard Posner. A process works only if both parties are willing to negotiate, accept mediation, or submit to a third-party decision. AI may help prepare a claim, but it cannot persuade a landlord to negotiate, compel an employer to pay wages, or make a business respond. Even when parties reach an agreement, there is no guarantee it will be respected. Without mechanisms to support compliance and enforce outcomes, an agreement on paper may have little practical effect.

There is also a growing challenge for the institutions receiving complaints. AI may make it much easier for people to submit them, potentially increasing demand on already overstretched public services. Recent UK reporting describes public bodies, councils and courts receiving a growing volume of AI-assisted submissions, some lengthy, repetitive and difficult to assess. Dubbed “AI clog,” the issue is not that more people are complaining — lowering barriers to redress is positive. The problem is that institutions may lack the capacity and resources to respond.

If AI increases the number of people approaching public authorities, those authorities must be equipped to meet the demand. This requires more than using AI to summarize documents or automate responses. It means better-designed complaints processes, adequately resourced institutions, trained staff and clear pathways for handling cases. Otherwise, technology risks making it easier to submit a complaint without making public services any more responsive.
Who owns the service?

Sustainability is another concern. A HiiL policy brief highlights the dependence of AI tools on external providers, proprietary platforms and uncertain funding. If a provider withdraws a service, what happens to the people relying on it?

HiiL’s exploration of voice-based AI support for local justice actors in Niger illustrates this risk. The aim was to make legal information available in local languages and support community intermediaries. But technology embedded in proprietary infrastructure can be difficult to maintain or transfer when a provider withdraws.

Ownership and governance therefore cannot be afterthoughts. Local justice providers and institutions need control over their tools, legal knowledge and data, as well as the resources to maintain and adapt services. Otherwise, technology intended to improve justice delivery may create new dependencies and disappear when people need it.
Making AI work for people seeking justice

AI for justice should be measured by more than chatbots launched, queries answered or documents generated. We need evidence that tools help people prevent problems, reach appropriate services, secure the participation of other parties and achieve fair outcomes.

This requires investment in tools designed around people’s problems and the providers best placed to address them. AI should connect users to human assistance, complement formal and informal justice mechanisms, and be supported by safeguards, accountability and sustainable financing. Crucially, public institutions must also be equipped to handle the increased demand that easier complaints procedures may generate. Evaluation should ask whether AI improves outcomes, for whom, under what conditions and at what cost. AI can make legal help more accessible and help people take action. But its promise will depend on whether the wider justice system can respond.

The ambition should not be to give everyone a free AI lawyer while leaving them waiting for an answer from the institutions responsible for upholding their rights. It should be to use technology to help those institutions work better, address people’s needs and deliver on their responsibilities fairly and effectively.
Zainab Malik is Senior Policy and Advocacy Advisor at HiiL.

528841cbf861a044: Most staples for Thanksgiving, including potatoes and cranberries, haven't jumped in price this year. Noah Samuel Franz on UnsplashInflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized. A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices. Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022, the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began. I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices. Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert: Go for frozen turkey Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels. The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report, published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions. It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill. A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time. As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in. Frozen turkey is among the Thanksgiving staples that haven’t seen big price jumps this past year. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh A mixed picture for side dishes Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider. Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data. Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper. Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive. Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5%, and up 2.6% for lettuce. More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors. Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply. Sauerkraut, a popular side dish in mid-Atlantic states, is likely to be pricier amid higher cabbage prices. Kelsey Todd on Unsplash Don’t forget dessert Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts. Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data. But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak, which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago. Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year. So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more. Where other savings can be found Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data. Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers. Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35, Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people. Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes. Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast. Elizabeth Canales receives funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

53bf28c36494803d: The activist admits his mental state has been negatively affected by the 10-year sentence increase
Originally published on Global Voices
Joshua Wong released from Lai Chi Kok Reception Centre on June 17, 2019. HKFP's File photo.

This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on November 16, 2026. The following version is edited and republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In a letter from a Hong Kong prison earlier this year, jailed activist Joshua Wong expressed dread over the looming sentence in his foreign collusion case. “Fretting about whether it’s 2032 or 2037, my mental state is hardly all right,” he wrote in Chinese, weighing when he might regain his freedom.
The agony inevitably stems from this: What if it’s 2037? Well, it’s easy [for people] to sympathise in the moment, but it’s difficult to be consistent, and it will only get harder.

The 30-year-old pro-democracy activist has already spent almost six years behind bars over various offences and was set for release in January 2026, until authorities charged him last year with conspiring to collude with foreign forces — the second case against him under the Beijing-imposed national security law. His case is one of the most high-profile examples of changing judicial norms in Hong Kong.
A prison letter Joshua Wong wrote to friend and former fellow student activist Louis Lee in February 2026. This photo was taken on September 30, 2026. Photo by Kyle Lam/HKFP. Used with permission.

On November 5, just two months before he was due to be released, a court sentenced him to 10 more years in prison for colluding with foreign forces. He is now expected to serve until late 2036, when he turns 40.

Standing in the courtroom as his new sentence was announced, Wong shook his head slightly and made notes, but appeared calm. Judge William Tam ruled that Wong’s offence was one of a “grave nature” under the national security law, which carries a minimum penalty of 10 years in jail and up to life imprisonment.
The judge knocked off three years from a 13-year starting sentence for Wong’s guilty plea.

In prison correspondence shared with HKFP by two close friends ahead of Wong’s sentencing, the former poster child of Hong Kong’s democracy movement had at times reflected on the weight of facing an additional decade behind bars. He expressed anxiety over fading from the memory of his friends — and from society at large. In one letter, Wong wrote:
I have no idea how much more I will lose in the passing of time. Responsibility is, in fact, response-ability. But who will respond? I can’t help but ponder and doubt.

Once a pro-democracy activist dedicated first and foremost to Hong Kong’s political future, Wong began campaigning as a charismatic, eloquent student leader who dared to stand up to the authorities — even to Beijing. Hong Kong is an overseas territory of China, and has increasingly been pressured to conform to China’s political goals in recent years, despite agreements that Hong Kong would retain “a high degree of autonomy” when handed over to China in 1997. A Netflix documentary about him is succinctly titled “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower.”

Yet, after years behind bars, Wong has changed. The teenager who focused single-mindedly on Hong Kong’s democracy movement has become even more caring for those around him despite being separated by prison walls, according to his friends.
Tiffany Chin, a former student activist who campaigned alongside Wong, said. The pair were once romantically involved and are now friends. She shared:
For me, it doesn’t feel like we’re the only ones supporting him. In fact, he has been supporting people on the outside in his own way.
And, with the political causes he once championed now firmly crushed, Wong has turned inward to reflect on himself. In another letter, he wrote:
We had held such high aspirations for society from a young age, we should hold ourselves to the same standard. Only by refusing a life of mediocrity can we be worthy of the world we envisioned.
From “robot” to caring friend

On a bright summer day in June 2025, while serving a sentence for subversion at Stanley Prison, Wong was arrested behind bars and brought to court the same day on a fresh charge of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces.
The prosecution came without warning. That day, Chin and Louis Lee, another longtime friend of Wong’s, rushed to the court after hearing the news, but failed to see him in person.

Authorities accused him of conspiring with Nathan Law — another high-profile, pro-democracy student activist — in 2020 to collude with foreign elements, citing Wong’s sharing of Law’s social media posts calling for international sanctions against Hong Kong as evidence.
The unexpected new charge was devastating to Wong. That month, he confessed he was under a lot of pressure — a vulnerability he rarely showed in the past, Chin said.

After so many prison terms and all the ups and downs over the last decade… he seldom openly showed vulnerability. So when he felt the need to say so bluntly that he was not OK, I truly believed he wasn’t.

Having begun campaigning at the age of 14, Wong has been in and out of prison throughout his years of activism. He now has a total of eight criminal convictions, including three separate offences linked to unlawful assembly and two national security offences.
Joshua Wong is photographed inside the Lai Chi Kwok Reception Centre on March 4, 2021. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.

Born in 1996 to a Christian family – one year before Hong Kong was handed over to China from British rule – Wong rose to prominence in 2011 when he co-founded student protest group Scholarism amid a public outcry against a proposed patriotic education curriculum.

The following year, Scholarism activists occupied the forecourt outside Hong Kong government headquarters and staged a hunger strike to protest what they described as a “brainwashing” curriculum. In a widely reported encounter, the teenager Wong twice refused to shake hands with then-city leader Leung Chun-ying, who visited the protest site alongside education officials.
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied behind Wong and his fellow student activists, forcing the government to back down and shelve the proposal.

But the teenage campaigner was also viewed as somewhat distant and domineering among the inner circle of Scholarism. Lee, who mainly handled protest logistics at that time, described his relationship with Wong as “almost like that of a boss and subordinate.”

Chin, who joined Scholarism around 2013, similarly described Wong as a deeply rational figure who seldom expressed his emotions. “Ten years ago, everyone described him as someone without many feelings,” she said. “Like a robot.”
Wong might even come across as “rude,” she added, noting that he rarely said thanks to others during that period.

A large part of Wong’s youth coincided with a period of escalating social movements in Hong Kong. Just two years after the anti-patriotic education protests, the city saw the 79-day Umbrella Movement in 2014. Wong, then aged 17, took centre stage in mobilising public support for student protesters, who demanded democratic reform and universal suffrage.

In a demonstration that sparked the Umbrella Movement, Wong and other student leaders led protesters into the forecourt of the government headquarters in an action dubbed “Reclaiming Civic Square,” seeking to escalate their campaign. That eventually resulted in Wong’s first criminal conviction.

In 2016, Wong and fellow student leaders Alex Chow and Nathan Law were found guilty of unlawful assembly. Though initially spared prison, Wong later served around 69 days behind bars – his first jail term – following a government appeal in 2017. His penalty was ultimately quashed by the Court of Final Appeal in 2018.

Scholarism disbanded in 2016. Wong and several former members, as well as young activists like Law, went on to establish Demosisto, a political party advocating for “democratic self-determination” in the city. Wong served as general secretary.
Lee and Chin did not join the new party, and they grew estranged from Wong during that period.

That year, Law was elected to the Legislative Council, making him the youngest lawmaker in Hong Kong history at the age of 23. He won over 50,000 votes, giving Demosisto a strong popular mandate. The prospect of youth democracy activism appeared bright at the time, but Law was eventually disqualified from his seat in 2017 following an oath-taking controversy.
From left: Joshua Wong, Agnes Chow, and Nathan Law, photographed on March 10, 2018. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.
Reconnections
It was only after Wong’s detention in late 2020 that Lee and Chin reconnected with him, beginning with an exchange of letters.

In 2019, citywide protests and unrest triggered by a controversial extradition bill engulfed the city. Wong and Demosisto were heavily involved in the protests, with the activist frequently lobbying foreign governments to impose sanctions on Hong Kong officials and halt the export of crowd control equipment to the city’s police force.

Then, in June 2020, Beijing imposed the national security law, effectively crushing political dissent in the city. Demosisto disbanded on the eve of the law’s enactment, while Nathan Law left Hong Kong in self-exile.
Written by Hong Kong Free Press

03692ec60cac1bbf: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn’t a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.”

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

43c6c4ac0068ccff: JAKARTA، Nov 18 — Indonesia’s central bank has raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to six per cent، a pre-emptive move aimed at stabilising the weakening rupiah and containing inflation amid heightened global economic uncertainty. Bank Indonesia (BI) Communications Department executive director Ramdan Denny Prakoso said the decision was made at the central bank’s two-day Board of Governors meeting which concluded on Wednesday. The meeting also saw the Deposit Facility rate raised by 25 basis points to 5.25 per cent and the Lending Facility rate by the same margin to 6.75 per cent. “The increase is a measure to further strengthen rupiah exchange rate stabilisation against the impact of rising global uncertainty، as well as a pre-emptive measure to keep inflation in 2026 and 2027 within the target range of 2.5 per cent، plus or minus one percentage point، ” he said in a statement on Wednesday. The latest increase marks BI’s first benchmark rate hike since June 18، when it raised the rate to 5.75 per cent، a level maintained for the following four months through October. Ramdan said the rupiah stood at Rp18,245 (RM4.11) against the US dollar on Tuesday، weakening 0.66 per cent from its end-October level، amid persistent global uncertainty and weak foreign investor sentiment in the domestic stock market. He said the central bank would continue directing monetary policy towards strengthening rupiah exchange rate stability while maintaining accommodative macroprudential measures to support lending to the real sector and preserve financial system stability. He said BI would also optimise foreign exchange intervention through offshore non-deliverable forward transactions، as well as spot and domestic non-deliverable forward transactions in the domestic market، alongside measures to strengthen banking liquidity. “Going forward، BI projects that the rupiah exchange rate will remain stable، supported by its commitment، attractive yields، inflation controlled within the target، and favourable domestic economic prospects، ” he said. Ramdan said global financial market volatility remained elevated due to continuing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East، growing political instability in Europe and expectations of further monetary tightening in the United States. He said BI expected global economic growth to remain weak at around 3.1 per cent in 2026، with inflation remaining elevated at approximately 4.6 per cent، prompting investors to reduce portfolio investments in emerging markets. Despite external pressures، he noted that Indonesia’s economy expanded by 5.47 per cent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026، accelerating from 5.29 per cent in the preceding quarter، supported mainly by domestic consumption and investment. He said BI projected Indonesia’s economy to grow between 4.9 and 5.7 per cent in 2026، while annual inflation eased to 3.23 per cent in October from 3.28 per cent in September، remaining within the central bank’s target range. On capital flows، Ramdan said foreign portfolio investment in Indonesia’s stock market recorded net outflows of US$900 million in the fourth quarter up to November 16، although overall capital flows registered net inflows of US$4.80 billion، supported by government global sukuk and bond issuances، as well as inflows into government securities. He said Indonesia’s foreign exchange reserves stood at US$146.8 billion at the end of October، equivalent to 5.3 months of imports، while bank lending grew 13.21 per cent year-on-year in the same month. e7bb5cbcc3bc3bfa: <!--kg-card-end: html--> A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

Gallup’s study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.

Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. “Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all,” the researchers wrote.

Most of the respondents (82%) said they’d used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, “although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships,” they wrote.

The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as “high quality” and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: “In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating.”

People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. “However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers also asked young people what they do online all day and the overwhelming majority (72%) said they spend their time scrolling short form content, mostly TikTok and Instagram. It’s also how they deal with loneliness, with six in 10 young people participating in this study reporting that they often or always scroll through online content when lonely.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> They also said scrolling works to dispel loneliness almost equally as well as hanging out with a friend in real life: “Although scrolling is more commonly used when young people feel lonely, those who use scrolling or in-person time as coping strategies report nearly identical levels of perceived helpfulness.”

Still, people who reported strong in-person friendships said they felt lonely less often, while online friendships have the same effect on loneliness regardless of how participants ranked the quality of those friendships. “No comparable difference appears across levels of online-only friendship quality,” the authors wrote. Having in-person relationships seemed to be what mattered most: “Higher loneliness is also more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.”

The relationships between loneliness, online friendships, and AI is complex and a person’s material conditions shape how they form friendships more than their access to a chatbot or how they use social media. The researchers’ analysis of young people who said they have no trusted adults in their lives makes that clear.

“Further analysis identifies several characteristics associated with having none of these friendship modes, but one stands out in particular: not having a trusted adult outside the family,” the researchers wrote. “This association remains substantial after accounting for country or residence, gender, age, urbanicity, and parent/ caregiver relationship quality.”

The study’s authors warned about reading too much into these results. “These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive,” they wrote. In general, people don’t have the same expectations of a chatbot that they do someone they know in real life.

“The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people’s relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly,” the study concluded.

461a1fe87414da12: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector.  Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference.  However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text.  For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts. Adaptation in action In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users.  These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict.  With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated. The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector.  Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data. In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy. And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text. “TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says. Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds. The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training. “It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.” In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion. This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.
